Agile: Processes & Wider Context.w: Initiating a project establishes solid foundations so the business understands the work needed to deliver the project product before committing to significant expenditure (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.4.1).

n.0: This is the purpose of starting up a project, which comes before initiation and asks whether the project is viable and worthwhile (book 13.2.1).
n.1: This is the purpose of managing a stage boundary, which supports the board's review of each stage (book 13.7.1).
n.2: This is the purpose of managing product delivery, which links the project manager with the delivery team (book 13.6.1).

Agile: Processes & Wider Context.q: A delivery team and its project manager agree the requirements for accepting, carrying out, reporting on and delivering a set of user stories. Which process has the purpose of controlling this link between the project manager and the delivery team?
o: Managing product delivery
Controlling a stage
Directing a project
Managing a stage boundary
Agile: Processes & Wider Context.w: Managing product delivery controls the link between the project manager and the delivery team by agreeing requirements for acceptance, execution, reporting and delivery of specialist products (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.6.1).

n.1: Controlling a stage is the project manager's process for assigning and monitoring work and keeping the stage within tolerances; the team side of the link is managing product delivery (book 13.5.1).
n.2: Directing a project is the board's process for key decisions and overall control; it does not manage the project manager's link with the delivery team (book 13.3.1).
n.3: Managing a stage boundary prepares information for the board's review of the stage and the next stage plan; it does not control work packages (book 13.7.1).

Agile: Processes & Wider Context.q: The board of a regional bus company wants to remain accountable for the success of its ticketing project while leaving day-to-day management to the project manager. Which process enables the board to do this through key decisions and overall control?
o: Controlling a stage
Starting up a project
Directing a project
Closing a project
Agile: Processes & Wider Context.w: Directing a project enables the project board to be accountable for the project's success by making key decisions and exercising overall control, while delegating day-to-day management to the project manager (PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.3.1).

n.0: Controlling a stage is the project manager's process for day-to-day control of a stage within tolerances, not the board's process (book 13.5.1).
n.1: Starting up a project checks that the prerequisites for initiation are in place; it is not the board's ongoing means of control (book 13.2.1).
n.3: Closing a project provides a fixed point to confirm acceptance of the project product; it does not provide ongoing board control (PRINCE2 7 manual 19.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Bronwen Hale, the commercial director, is explaining to Larkspur Rail's leadership team why Fair Fares will use agile ways of working. Release 1 is planned to go live in month four so that real usage data from passengers can shape Releases 2 and 3, and nobody yet knows how passengers will react to one-tap claims. Which explanation BEST describes the benefit of working this way on Fair Fares?
o: Adopting Scrum in all three teams will make delivery faster and raise the quality of the app, because the framework sets the pace of the work.
Agreeing the full feature list for all three releases at the start lets the board hold all three teams to a predictable, fixed scope for the ten months.
Short feedback loops from real passenger use let the teams adapt the later releases to what passengers need, cutting work on features of little value.
Releasing early means the board can extend the December end date if passengers ask for more features after Release 1 goes live.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Agile helps where work is complex and uncertain: rather than hunting for a perfect plan, teams stay adaptable, and feedback loops with continual improvement reduce waste and lead to better solutions (book 2.4, responsiveness and innovation). An early MVP release used by real passengers provides exactly that feedback for Releases 2 and 3.

n.0: This is the classic misconception the book warns against: adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value comes from the mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: Fixing every feature up front is the linear approach whose weakness is a lack of adaptability; with this much uncertainty agile favours staying able to pivot (book 2.2, 2.4).
n.3: The board has fixed the end date and budget, and PRINCE2 Agile keeps zero tolerance on time and cost; early feedback reshapes what is delivered, not when (Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: In sprint 3 of stage 2, the Coinbridge Payments developers stop joining the daily stand-ups they share with the app team. Instead they post short written updates when they have time, and two integration problems come to light a week late. Owen Thackeray, the app team's Scrum master, asks how to respond. Which action would restore the agile mindset characteristic that is lacking?
o: Agree with both teams that everyone joins the joint stand-ups, and keep blockers and integration work visible on a shared board.
Let the Coinbridge developers keep posting written updates, and ask Rhys Pengelly to summarize them for the app team every Friday.
Ask Gemma Lowther to remind her developers that the fixed-price contract requires them to deliver the integration on time.
Hold a separate weekly integration meeting for the two team leads, so that the developers can concentrate on building.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: The missing characteristic is transparency and rich communication: information should flow openly, through regular meetings and visible work status, so that obstacles are shared early and without fear (book 2.6.2). Bringing both teams back into the shared stand-up and making blockers visible restores it.

n.1: A weekly summary passed on by the project manager keeps information slow and filtered; it does not restore open, timely and rich communication between the teams (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Contract pressure does nothing to rebuild the open sharing of progress and obstacles that the teams have lost; the gap is in mindset, not in the contract (book 2.6.2).
n.3: This narrows the flow of information to two people and makes it less frequent, which is the opposite of transparency and rich communication across the teams (book 2.6.2).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: During initiation, the Fair Fares project board sets zero tolerance on time and cost for every level of plan but allows the Should have and Could have stories in each release to be flexed. Rhys Pengelly, the project manager, may reprioritize those stories with the product owners without asking the board, and must escalate if the Must haves for a release are forecast to be missed. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because the board authorizes the work release by release and reviews each one at a stage boundary.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the board has stated who may reprioritize the stories in each team.
Focus on products, because the Must have, Should have and Could have stories describe the products to be delivered.
Manage by exception, because tolerances let the board delegate day-to-day decisions and hear of a forecast breach.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Manage by exception sets tolerances for the performance aspects and delegates authority within them, with escalation when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. In agile it allows tolerance on what is delivered while restricting time and cost, which empowers teams within control (book 5.2.1.5, Table 5.1).

n.0: Stage-by-stage authorization is not what is described; the board is setting tolerances and the escalation point for flexing scope (book 5.2.1.4, 5.2.1.5).
n.1: Roles are mentioned, but the mechanism is delegated authority within set tolerances with escalation on a forecast breach, which is manage by exception (book 5.2.1.5).
n.2: Prioritized stories make flexing possible, but the decision being made is about tolerances and delegation, not about defining products (book 5.2.1.6, Table 5.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: At the project canvas workshop, Bronwen Hale says Fair Fares must at least reach the contract level of 80% of eligible app journeys receiving compensation automatically, to avoid the penalties from January. Any level above 80% would be welcome but is not required. Which performance aspect is she describing, and how should PRINCE2 Agile treat it?
o: Scope, fixed for the Must have stories that produce the 80% level and flexed for the Should and Could haves.
Benefits, fixed at the minimum viable level of 80% and flexed for any improvement above it.
Quality, fixed for the acceptance criteria of the matching model and flexed for the look of the screens.
Sustainability, fixed for the minimum contract criteria and flexed above those criteria.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: A measurable improvement with a minimum the business must reach and room for more is the benefits aspect. PRINCE2 Agile fixes benefits at minimum viability and flexes them above it (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).

n.0: Scope is what will and will not be delivered (the stories); the 80% is a measurable improvement the business expects, which is a benefit (book 1.3.2).
n.2: Quality covers the characteristics that make products fit for purpose; a target share of compensated journeys is a business improvement, not a product characteristic (book 1.3.2).
n.3: Sustainability concerns the project's impact on the wider environment; the compensation level is a measurable business improvement, so it is the benefits aspect (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Forty customer relations staff will join sprint reviews and test the new claim screens during stage 2. Apart from IT, few Larkspur staff have worked in an agile way, and Yusuf Bello reports that his team is unsure what is expected of them. Priyanka Desai, the agile lead, is asked how to raise their agile maturity. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to work?
o: Send each member of staff a guide to Scrum events and invite them to ask the app team when anything is unclear.
Introduce a digital backlog tool to customer relations first, so that staff can see the claim stories on screen before any coaching starts.
Coach Yusuf Bello and his supervisors in depth, and ask them to pass the new ways of working on to their staff.
Combine practical training with on-the-job coaching in real sprint reviews, set out in a training and coaching plan for the stages.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Agile maturity grows when people receive theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change, so that as many people as possible understand what is changing and why (book 2.7.3).

n.0: Informing people and leaving them to fend for themselves undermines the change and breeds frustration, a leading cause of resistance (book 2.7.3).
n.1: Tools before knowledge and skills do not build maturity; people first need to understand how the change applies to their work through training and coaching (book 2.7.3).
n.2: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why; coaching a few managers and relying on cascade leaves most staff without practical support (book 2.7.3).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: At a council meeting, Professor Alison Greer is asked why the Student Support Hub will be delivered with agile ways of working instead of one full design approved at the start. Demand has risen by 60% in four years, the wellbeing service is still working out how it will triage requests, and nobody is sure how students will prefer to ask for help. Which explanation BEST reflects why agile suits this project?
o: Adopting Scrum in both teams will make delivery faster and raise quality, whatever ways of working the wellbeing service keeps.
Agile lets the university fix every feature of the hub now and flex the budget and the go-live date as needs become clearer.
The right solution is uncertain, so short feedback loops with students and staff let the teams adapt quickly and reduce wasted work.
Agile lets the teams start building before the business justification is agreed, which saves time against the Welcome Week deadline.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Complex situations rarely have one perfect solution known at the start, so it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly. Feedback loops and continual improvement reduce waste and give better solutions to complex problems (book 2.4). Here the triage model and students' preferences are both uncertain.

n.0: This is the classic misconception: adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value comes from a change in mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile does the reverse: time and cost are fixed with zero tolerance, and what is delivered is flexed (book Table 3.1). The council has also said the budget is fixed.
n.3: Every PRINCE2 Agile project still needs business justification; it is tailored into a project canvas, not dropped (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: To prepare for the new hub, managers in the wellbeing service introduce a daily stand-up and a wall board of sticky notes for the triage redesign. However, every change to a triage step still needs written sign-off from a senior manager, and advisers are told to follow the new routine exactly as set out. Dr Kwame Mensah asks Jamal Hussain how this looks from an agile point of view. Which statement BEST describes the situation?
o: The service is doing agile without being agile: it has adopted agile routines, but staff are not allowed to adapt and decide for themselves.
The service is being agile, because daily stand-ups and a visible wall board show that the agile mindset is already in place among wellbeing staff.
The service is being agile without doing agile, because it has the right mindset but has not yet adopted a framework such as Scrum.
The service is both being and doing agile, because senior sign-off keeps each change within the tolerances agreed with the board.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Doing agile is the practical use of agile frameworks, techniques and terms; being agile means thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset with suitable self-management (book 2.3.1). Stand-ups and boards with rigid sign-off and fixed routines are doing agile without being agile.

n.1: Stand-ups and boards are visible practices; they do not show the mindset when staff cannot adapt or decide anything for themselves (book 2.3.1, 2.6.1).
n.2: The reverse is true: the service has adopted agile routines (doing) but restricts the freedom to think and act in an agile way (being) (book 2.3.1).
n.3: Tolerances are set for the project, not for every triage step; requiring senior sign-off for each change removes the self-management that being agile needs (book 2.3.1, Table 5.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain hears that wellbeing staff have seen three previous systems promised and then dropped. Before planning the initiation stage, he meets Tom Brierley and two other advisers to find out why those systems failed, and records what they say so that the Student Support Hub can act on it. Which principle is Jamal applying, and why?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because he is engaging internal stakeholders who will use the hub.
Ensure continued business justification, because past failures show whether the hub is likely to be worthwhile.
Tailor to suit the project, because he is adapting the method to the culture of the wellbeing service.
Learn from experience, because he is seeking lessons from earlier initiatives at the start and using them in the project.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Learning from experience means seeking, recording and acting on lessons throughout the project, starting with lessons from previous similar work in starting up (book 5.2, Table 5.1; assess previous lessons, Table 13.1). Jamal is gathering lessons from the three earlier systems.

n.0: Engaging stakeholders is part of defining roles and relationships, but Jamal's purpose here is to capture why earlier systems failed, which is learning from experience (book 5.2.1.3).
n.1: Continued business justification keeps checking that the project is desirable, viable and achievable; the stem describes gathering lessons, not reviewing justification (book 5.2.1.1).
n.2: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity and context; Jamal has not changed how the method is applied, he has collected lessons (book 5.2.1.7).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Midway through stage 2, the Release 1 burn-up chart shows that the web team will finish self-referral and booking before Welcome Week, but not the full self-help content library or a live chat option, both rated Should or Could haves. Professor Greer has said self-referral and booking are the minimum for Welcome Week, and the council has fixed the budget. Which response BEST applies PRINCE2 Agile fix and flex?
o: Move Release 1 to two weeks after Welcome Week, so that every planned feature can go live together for new students.
Keep the date and budget, launch self-referral and booking, and move the unfinished Should and Could haves to Release 2.
Drop booking from Release 1 and finish the self-help library instead, as the library costs less to complete in the time left.
Ask the council for extra funding to hire contract developers, so that the full Release 1 scope is ready for Welcome Week.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: PRINCE2 Agile fixes time and cost with zero tolerance and flexes scope: Must haves are fixed and Should and Could haves are flexed (book Table 3.1). Self-referral and booking are the stated minimum, so they go live on time and the lower-priority features move to a later release.

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan; delaying Release 1 past Welcome Week to protect lower-priority scope breaks the fixed date (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Booking is part of the minimum the university must offer, so it is a Must have and fixed; it cannot be traded for a lower-priority feature (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Cost has zero tolerance and the council has fixed the budget; extra funding to protect Should and Could haves flexes the wrong aspect (book Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Before Release 1, the university plans to send the 45 wellbeing staff a user guide and a recorded webinar on the new triage process, and then let them get on with it. Several staff have already said they feel the change is being done to them, and some have seen earlier systems dropped. Which action is MOST LIKELY to help staff adopt the new ways of working?
o: Send the guide and webinar as planned, and ask managers to report which staff have watched the webinar by the go-live date.
Train the senior managers in depth and ask them to pass the details on to their teams once Release 1 is live.
Combine short training with on-the-job coaching for staff in their own teams, planned to match each release of the hub.
Give staff early access to the case management tool first, so that they learn the new ways of working by using it.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: People need theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching to understand how changes apply to them; informing people and leaving them to cope breeds frustration, a leading cause of resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change (book 2.7.3).

n.0: This is informing people and leaving them to fend for themselves; tracking who watched a webinar measures compliance, not understanding (book 2.7.3).
n.1: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why; limiting training to managers and passing details on later leaves staff unsupported at go-live (book 2.7.3).
n.3: Introducing a tool first does not build the knowledge and skills people need; training and coaching should come first (book 2.7.3).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: At an early board meeting, the finance director asks Gwen Tallowby why Pinewick is using an agile approach for click and collect rather than specifying every website feature and store process in full before any work starts. The board accepts that customer behaviour in the pilot stores is hard to predict, and that the spring peak leaves no room to move the date. Which explanation BEST describes the benefit of working this way on this project?
o: Using Scrum and Kanban means the project will be delivered faster and at higher quality, because adopting an agile framework brings these gains with it.
Agile working allows the date and budget to move later on if feedback from the pilot stores shows that more features are needed before Easter.
Short feedback loops from Release 1 and the pilot stores let the teams learn what customers and staff need and adapt, reducing effort wasted on unused features.
An agile approach removes the need for the board to authorize each stage, so the teams can respond to customer feedback from the pilot stores without waiting for decisions.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Where a situation is complex and uncertain there is rarely one perfect solution, so it is better to stay adaptable. Feedback loops and continual improvement reduce waste and lead to better solutions, which is the responsiveness and innovation benefit described in book 2.4. Pinewick cannot predict how customers and stores will respond, so learning from each release and the pilot is the main gain.

n.0: This is the classic misconception the book warns against: adopting a framework does not by itself make delivery faster or better; the value comes from a change of mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: Time and cost have zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile by default, and the board has said neither can move; it is what is delivered that flexes (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Manage by stages still applies: the board authorizes one stage at a time and delegates day-to-day control within tolerances (book 5.2.1.4).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Six weeks into Stage 2, Nikhil Rao visits the store operations team. The team has set up a Kanban board, holds a short stand-up every morning and uses agile terms in its meetings. However, members wait for Sophie Draper to tell them which card to move next, and nobody questions the order of work even when a store is clearly blocked. Using the Agile Onion, which diagnosis is MOST accurate?
o: The team has taken on practices, the most visible layer, but the mindset at the core has not yet changed, so it looks agile without thinking in an agile way.
The team has taken on processes, the most visible layer, and now needs to add the practices layer by introducing more agile events such as retrospectives.
The team has reached the values layer, the innermost part of the onion, so the remaining gap is a lack of formal process from a framework such as Scrum.
The team has taken on principles, the layer that explains the why, so the problem lies in Sophie Draper's leadership style rather than in the team's understanding.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: In the Agile Onion, practices (techniques and activities such as boards and stand-ups) are the most visible part of agile adoption, and teams that stop there can look agile without the mindset. The mindset is the innermost layer that drives everything (book 2.6.1). A team that waits to be told what to do and never questions priorities is doing agile without yet being agile (book 2.3.1).

n.1: Practices, not processes, are the most visible layer, and adding more events would add more doing rather than change the way the team thinks (book 2.6.1).
n.2: Mindset, not values, is the innermost layer, and nothing in the team's behaviour shows that it has absorbed agile values; more framework process would not close the gap (book 2.6.1).
n.3: A team that has taken on the principles understands the why behind its work; members who never question the order of work have not reached that layer (book 2.6.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: During initiation, Patrick Dunne, who is new to agile, asks Nikhil Rao to bring two e-commerce team members and a manager from another department that has adopted agile to a session with the store operations team. They describe what helped and what went wrong in their first agile work. Patrick also agrees that the store team will hold a retrospective after each pilot store goes live and change its checklist before the next store. Which principle is Patrick applying, and why?
o: Tailor to suit the project, because he is deciding which agile frameworks and workshops the store operations team will use on the project.
Manage by stages, because the retrospectives divide the pilot into short periods that the board can review and authorize one at a time.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because he is bringing people from other departments into contact with the project team.
Learn from experience, because he is seeking lessons from earlier agile work and building inspect-and-adapt loops into the store roll-out.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Learn from experience means seeking and applying lessons from previous work at the start and throughout the project. Many agile concepts support it, such as short feedback loops, inspect and adapt, and retrospectives (book Table 5.1). Patrick gathers lessons from earlier agile adopters and builds a retrospective after each pilot store into the plan.

n.0: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity and context; the purpose here is to gather and apply lessons, not to choose frameworks (book 5.2.1.7).
n.1: Manage by stages concerns the board authorizing one management stage at a time; a retrospective after each store is a team learning loop, not a stage (book 5.2.1.4).
n.2: The visitors share their experience; they are not given roles, and nothing in the stem defines responsibilities or relationships in the project (book 5.2.1.3).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: In Stage 4, the release map shows the project is forecast to finish £60,000 over budget. A packaging supplier offers single-use cardboard boxes that would save £45,000 compared with the reusable crates, which the board set as the minimum sustainability criterion for all collection orders. Installing lockers at 14 stores instead of 20 would save £70,000, and the board has agreed that fewer lockers are acceptable. What should Patrick Dunne recommend?
o: Switch to cardboard boxes and install lockers at slightly fewer stores, because cost has zero tolerance and must be protected before the other aspects of the project.
Keep the reusable crates and install lockers at 14 stores, because sustainability is fixed at its minimum criteria while lower-priority scope can flex.
Keep the crates and all 20 lockers, and move the last stores' go-live to after Easter, so that the extra weeks spread the cost into the next year.
Keep the crates and all 20 lockers, and ask the board to raise the budget by £60,000, because the sustainability strategy has priority over cost.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: PRINCE2 Agile fixes time and cost with zero tolerance, fixes sustainability at its minimum criteria and flexes above them, and fixes scope for Must haves while flexing Should and Could haves (book Table 3.1). Reusable crates are the minimum sustainability criterion, and the board has said lockers can flex, so reducing lockers keeps the project within budget and on time.

n.0: Cardboard boxes would breach the minimum sustainability criterion, which is fixed; protecting cost does not justify falling below it (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Time has zero tolerance, and the board has said the service must be live in every store before Easter; delaying does not reduce cost either (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Cost has zero tolerance by default; the agile response is to flex what is delivered, here the lockers, rather than ask for more money (book Table 3.1, Table 5.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: In the store operations team's retrospectives, Sophie Draper answers most suggestions from the two trainers by explaining why the stores' current way of working is better. The trainers say they feel part of the team and enjoy working with Sophie, but they have stopped putting forward ideas. Nikhil Rao is asked for advice. Which action is MOST LIKELY to improve the situation?
o: Raise inclusion safety by holding a team social event so that the trainers feel accepted, while Sophie continues to decide which ideas are worth discussing.
Raise the team's agile maturity by sending the trainers on a Kanban course, as their suggestions show that they do not yet understand how flow works.
Build contributor safety by coaching Sophie to invite everyone's ideas first and to let the team agree which suggestions to try in the next cycle.
Ask Patrick Dunne to chair the retrospectives and rule on each suggestion, so that the trainers' ideas are judged by someone from outside the stores.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Psychological safety lets people speak up and challenge ideas without fear (book 2.7.4). Contributor safety means people are encouraged to share ideas and skills and their contributions are respected. The trainers already feel accepted, so the gap is in how their contributions are received, which Nikhil can address by coaching Sophie.

n.0: The trainers already feel part of the team, which is inclusion safety; the problem is that their contributions are dismissed, and this option leaves that unchanged (book 2.7.4).
n.1: Nothing suggests the trainers lack knowledge; training would not change the way their ideas are received in retrospectives (book 2.7.3, 2.7.4).
n.3: Having the project manager rule on ideas takes the retrospective away from the team and weakens self-management rather than building contributor safety (book 2.7.4, 13.6.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: During initiation, Joan Whitaker agrees that the Care Online digital team may work in two-week sprints, hold daily stand-ups and keep a backlog. However, she asks that her programme board approve every user story before it enters a sprint, and that the team follow the corporate project office's sprint checklist step by step without changing it. Which statement BEST describes the council's position?
o: The council is being agile without doing agile: its leaders think in an agile way, but the team has not yet adopted agile events or tools.
The council is doing agile without being agile: the team uses agile events and terms but is not allowed to apply an agile mindset.
The council is both doing and being agile, because the board keeps governance control while the team runs sprints, stand-ups and a backlog.
The council is being agile, because following a sprint checklist exactly is how a new team builds an agile mindset in its first stages.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Doing agile is the practical use of agile frameworks, processes, techniques and terminology; being agile is thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset with appropriate self-management. Sprints and stand-ups are in place, but approval of every story and a fixed checklist leave the team no room to adapt or decide, so this is doing without being (book 2.3, 2.3.1).

n.0: The reverse is true here: the agile events and tools are in place, but the leadership does not allow the mindset to be applied (book 2.3.1).
n.2: Governance and agile can coexist, but approving every story and fixing the routine removes the self-management that being agile needs (book 2.3, 2.3.1).
n.3: Following a framework rigidly without understanding why is the routine side of the being versus doing contrast; being agile means adapting and thinking critically (book 2.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: In the sprint 3 review, two occupational therapists explain that the self-assessment's timed pages will be hard for people with sensory impairments to complete. Two developers reply that therapists are not designers and that the pages follow the council's standard template, and the team moves on to the next item. Amy Fletcher wants to raise this at the retrospective. Which characteristic of the agile mindset is the team MOST in need of?
o: Empowerment, because the developers need more freedom to decide the page design without waiting for the therapists' approval.
Adaptability, because the team should inspect its release plan and adapt the sprint length to the therapists' availability.
Transparency and rich communication, because the review should have been recorded so that the therapists' points could be reread later.
Respect, because the team needs the empathy and open-mindedness to value every voice, including views from outside the digital team.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Respect in the agile mindset is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness: every voice is valued and diverse perspectives are welcomed. Dismissing the therapists because they are not designers shows a lack of respect, and their knowledge of users with sensory impairments is exactly what the team needs (book 2.6.2).

n.0: Empowerment is about autonomy and self-management; the developers already acted on their own view, and the problem is that they dismissed others (book 2.6.2).
n.1: Adaptability is inspecting and adapting in response to change; changing the sprint length does not address the developers brushing aside the therapists' views (book 2.6.2).
n.2: The therapists' points were raised openly in the review, so information did flow; what was missing was the willingness to value them (book 2.6.2).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: In starting up a project, Simon Archer asks Gita Bhatt what went well and what went badly when her two previous councils adopted agile, and he reviews the lessons from the council's last digital project with Helen Crowther. Later, every Care Online sprint ends with a retrospective, and the improvements agreed are carried into the next sprint. Which principle is being applied?
o: Learn from experience, because lessons are sought at the start and the short feedback loops of retrospectives turn them into improvements.
Tailor to suit the project, because Simon is adapting the method and its workshops to the council's low agile maturity before the project begins.
Manage by stages, because the retrospectives divide the project into short sprints that the board can review one at a time.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Gita's experience will shape the description of the agile coach role.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Learn from experience means seeking and applying lessons at the start, during and at the end of the project. In agile it is supported by retrospectives, inspect and adapt, and short feedback loops (book Table 5.1). Simon seeks lessons from Gita and from an earlier project, and the teams apply lessons sprint by sprint.

n.1: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity and context, for example by choosing frameworks and workshops; seeking and applying lessons is a different principle (book 5.2.1.7).
n.2: Manage by stages concerns the board authorizing one management stage at a time; retrospectives are learning events, not stage controls (book 5.2.1.4).
n.3: Nothing in the situation concerns who is accountable for what; Simon is gathering lessons and the teams are applying them (book 5.2.1.3).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: At the project canvas workshop, Sarah Pennington explains that, under the council's climate pledge, every project must meet minimum environmental criteria. For Care Online these are that the paper carers' assessment form is withdrawn and that first conversations no longer need a car journey to the person's home. Further measures to cut printing and travel are welcome if they fit the budget and timescale. Which aspect of project performance is being described, and how should PRINCE2 Agile treat it?
o: Benefits, fixed for minimum viability and flexed above it, because fewer home visits is the improvement the council expects to gain.
Scope, fixed for Must have features and flexed for Should and Could haves, because withdrawing the paper form is a feature.
Sustainability, fixed for the minimum criteria and flexed above them, because the pledge concerns the project's impact on the environment.
Sustainability, flexed in full like Should and Could scope, because zero tolerance applies to time and cost rather than to sustainability.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Sustainability is how the project affects the wider environment. PRINCE2 Agile fixes sustainability at its minimum criteria and flexes it above them (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1). The climate pledge sets the minimum; any extra measures are the flexible part.

n.0: Benefits are fixed at minimum viability, but the stem sets minimum environmental criteria from a climate pledge, which is the sustainability aspect (book 1.3.2, Table 3.1).
n.1: MoSCoW scope treatment applies to features by priority; the statement here sets environmental criteria, which is the sustainability aspect (Table 3.1).
n.3: Table 3.1 fixes sustainability for its minimum criteria, so withdrawing the paper form and removing the first-visit journey cannot be traded away; the flexible part is above that minimum.

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: The council has agreed to train ten social workers as Care Online product champions. The learning and development team proposes a two-day agile theory course for them in month one, after which the champions would go back to their teams and apply what they learned on their own. Gita Bhatt is asked for her view. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to build the agile maturity the council needs?
o: Run the two-day course as proposed, then measure each champion's agile maturity in the project closure workshop at month twelve.
Replace the course with a set of agile reading materials and videos, so that champions can learn at their own pace around caseloads.
Delay all training until Release 1 is live, so that the champions can learn agile from the finished product rather than from theory.
Combine the course with on-the-job coaching from Gita, set out in a training and coaching plan that follows the stages of the change.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: People need both theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching to apply a change; leaving them to fend for themselves breeds frustration and resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the agile change (book 2.7.3).

n.0: This leaves the champions on their own after the course, which the book warns undermines the change, and assessing maturity at closure is too late to help (book 2.7.3, 12.4.1).
n.1: Self-study is still theory with no practical coaching; the book pairs training with on-the-job coaching (book 2.7.3).
n.2: Champions need to understand the change while it is happening; delaying training until after Release 1 leaves them unprepared throughout stage 2 (book 2.7.3).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: During starting up, Graham Doyle asks Andrea Lucas why Smart Maintenance should use PRINCE2 Agile rather than one detailed plan fixed at the start. Hannah Reece expects the prediction model to need several months of real sensor data, and the maintenance engineers are not yet sure what the dashboard should show them. Which explanation BEST supports Andrea's choice?
o: Agile frameworks deliver faster and to a higher quality once they are adopted, so the twelve-month deadline before the aerospace contract will be easier to meet.
Agile removes the need for a fixed budget and end date, so the board can extend the project if the model takes longer to train.
The work is complex and uncertain, so staying adaptable and learning from feedback on each release beats seeking a perfect design up front.
Agile matches the way the software team already works, so the engineers and Senticore can keep their current ways of working unchanged.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely one perfect solution; it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly than to hunt for perfection. Here the model's usefulness and the engineers' needs will only become clear from real data and feedback, so frequent releases with feedback loops reduce waste (book 2.4).

n.0: This is the classic misconception: adopting a framework does not by itself bring faster delivery or higher quality; the value comes from a change of mindset and culture (book 2.3).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile keeps time and cost fixed with zero tolerance by default, and the board has fixed both here; agility flexes what is delivered, not the budget or date (Table 3.1).
n.3: The need for agile here comes from complexity and uncertainty, not from one team's habits; the engineers are central users whose feedback drives each release (book 2.4).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: At the first sprint review for Release 1, Stuart Bell and two other senior engineers give almost all of the feedback. Afterwards, two machine operators tell Tomasz Zielinski that they had ideas about the alert screen but felt their views would not count. Tomasz wants the reviews to show respect, a key characteristic of the agile mindset. Which change is MOST LIKELY to achieve this?
o: Run the feedback in small mixed groups so that every engineer and operator is heard, and record each group's ideas for the backlog.
Ask Stuart Bell to collect the operators' views before each review and present one combined set of comments on their behalf.
Invite the senior engineers to future reviews and send the operators a written summary of the decisions taken afterwards.
Ask the operators to email their ideas to Leanne Park after each review, so that she can decide which ones to add to the backlog.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Respect, as a characteristic of the agile mindset, is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness: every voice is valued and diverse perspectives are embraced (book 2.6.2). Small mixed groups let the operators, who use the machines every shift, be heard directly alongside the senior engineers.

n.1: Filtering the operators' ideas through the most senior engineer still leaves them unheard in the review, which is the problem Tomasz has noticed (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Leaving the operators out of the reviews removes their perspective altogether; respect means valuing all voices, not just the most experienced (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Sending ideas by email after the event keeps the operators out of the conversation and loses the rich, face-to-face exchange that the review provides (book 2.6.2).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: In initiation, Andrea Lucas records in the PID that the software team will keep its two-week Scrum sprints, Senticore will fit sensors to an agreed fitting schedule rather than in sprints, and the board will review a project dashboard instead of monthly written reports. Which principle is Andrea applying, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because she is setting out how each stage of the project will be planned, monitored and controlled by the board.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because she is agreeing how the three teams will work with the board and each other.
Focus on products, because she is making sure that each team, including Senticore, delivers well-defined outputs rather than simply carrying out activities.
Tailor to suit the project, because she is choosing the frameworks and artifacts each part of the project uses and recording them in the PID.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's size, complexity, risk and context; in PRINCE2 Agile that includes deciding which agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops to use, and the tailoring is recorded in the PID (book 5.2.1.7, Table 5.1).

n.0: Manage by stages is about the board authorizing one stage at a time and delegating control within it; Andrea is choosing ways of working, not stage controls (book 5.2.1.4).
n.1: That principle is about the right people in clear roles with stakeholders engaged; choosing sprints, fitting schedules and dashboards is a tailoring decision (book 5.2.1.3, 5.2.1.7).
n.2: Focus on products concerns defining and delivering well-specified outputs; Andrea's decisions are about how each team works and reports (book 5.2.1.6, 5.2.1.7).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Midway through Stage 3, the burn-up chart shows that the software team will deliver failure prediction and alerts for the ten trial machines by month 8; the project canvas lists these as Must haves. However, Senticore cannot fit sensors to every remaining Factory A machine by then, which is a Should have. The budget and end date are fixed. What should Andrea Lucas recommend?
o: Ask the board to move the Release 2 date back by four weeks, so that every Factory A machine is fitted before the alerts go live.
Fit as many remaining Factory A machines as the schedule allows, keep the Must haves, and re-plan the rest in the release map.
Agree a budget increase so that Senticore can add a second fitting crew and fit every Factory A machine by month 8.
Fit sensors to all of Factory A first, and move prediction and alerts for the ten trial machines into Release 3.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: PRINCE2 Agile sets zero tolerance for extra time and cost, fixes scope for Must haves and flexes it for Should and Could haves (Table 3.1). The board has also said the number of machines per release can change, so the remaining fittings are the part to flex.

n.0: Delaying the release flexes time, which has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, and the end date is fixed by the new aerospace contract (Table 3.1).
n.2: Raising the budget flexes cost, which has zero tolerance by default and which the board has fixed for this project (Table 3.1).
n.3: This protects a Should have by dropping Must haves from Release 2; scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves (Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Apart from the software team, nobody at Draycott has used agile before. For the start of Stage 2, Ruth Kenyon proposes sending the maintenance engineers and operators on a one-day course on agile theory, then leaving them to join sprint reviews and use the dashboard as they see fit. What should Andrea Lucas recommend instead?
o: Give each engineer a written guide to Scrum and the dashboard, so that they can refer to it whenever they need help.
Train the senior engineers in agile first, and let them pass what they have learned on to the operators later in the project.
Follow the course with on-the-job coaching in the engineers' own work, set out in a training and coaching plan for each stage.
Introduce a new task-tracking tool for the engineers first, so that they learn agile ways of working by using it every day.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: People need theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching to apply a change; informing them and leaving them to fend for themselves breeds frustration, a leading cause of resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the agile change (book 2.7.3).

n.0: A written guide only informs people; without coaching in their own work they are still left to fend for themselves (book 2.7.3).
n.1: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why; delaying the operators' learning leaves key users behind (book 2.7.3).
n.3: Early in a transformation the priority is building knowledge and skills through training and coaching, not introducing tools (book 2.7.3).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Three months into Repairs Reimagined, the service design team holds daily stand-ups, keeps a Kanban board and uses agile terms in every meeting. When tenant testing shows that a new phone script confuses callers, the team keeps using the script until Ian Thursby, the repairs director, has reviewed and signed off a change, which takes several weeks. Which statement BEST explains this situation?
o: The team is being agile but is not yet doing agile: it has the right mindset, but it has not adopted enough agile techniques and tools.
The team is both being and doing agile, because its stand-ups and Kanban board show that it inspects and adapts its work.
The team is doing agile but is not yet being agile, because it uses agile practices but is not allowed to adapt its work to feedback.
The team is neither being nor doing agile, because a Kanban board is a flow tool and is not part of agile ways of working.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Doing agile is the practical use of frameworks, processes, techniques and terms; being agile is thinking in an agile way and being allowed to apply that mindset within appropriate self-management (book 2.3.1). The stand-ups and board show the doing; waiting weeks for a director's sign-off before acting on tenant feedback shows the team is not free to adapt, so it is not yet being agile.

n.0: The team has adopted the techniques (stand-ups, Kanban, agile terms); what it lacks is the freedom to act on feedback, which is the being side (book 2.3.1).
n.1: Inspecting is not enough: the team cannot adapt the script for weeks, so the mindset is not being applied. Ceremonies alone do not show being agile (book 2.3, 2.3.1).
n.3: Kanban is one of the popular agile approaches, using visualisation and limits on work in progress (Glossary), so the team is doing agile.

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: In a team retrospective, Raj Malhotra notices that the staff who came from the repairs team talk over the newer contact centre advisers, whose ideas are often dismissed as 'not technical'. Raj introduces a round in which each person speaks in turn, and the team agrees to weigh every suggestion on its merits, whoever makes it. Which key characteristic of the agile mindset is Raj MOST LIKELY strengthening?
o: Respect, which is rooted in empathy and open-mindedness, so that every voice is valued and different perspectives are welcomed.
Empowerment, which gives the team autonomy to manage its own work and to make decisions about the call scripts without seeking approval.
Adaptability, which helps the team to inspect its results and change its ways of working in response to feedback.
Transparency and rich communication, which makes the status of the team's work visible to stakeholders outside the team.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Respect, as a key characteristic of the agile mindset, rests on empathy and open-mindedness: all voices are valued and diverse perspectives are embraced (book 2.6.2). Raj is making sure the advisers' views count as much as the repairs staff's.

n.1: Empowerment is about autonomy and self-management of the team as a whole; the problem here is that some members' views are dismissed by others (book 2.6.2).
n.2: Adaptability is inspection and adaptation in response to change; Raj is not changing the work in response to results but making sure all members are heard (book 2.6.2).
n.3: Making work status visible to stakeholders is transparency; the issue in the retrospective is how members treat one another's ideas (book 2.6.2).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: During initiation, Deborah Kiely points out that many tenants do not use the internet and some do not read English well. The teams therefore add a phone route into the new reporting service and plan translated text updates, so that what the project delivers meets the needs of all tenants. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Tailor to suit the project, because the teams are adapting the method's processes and artifacts to the project's context.
Ensure continued business justification, because the teams are checking that the investment is still desirable and viable.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the teams are engaging tenants as stakeholders in the project.
Focus on products, because the teams are defining what the outputs must do so that they meet users' needs and expectations.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Focus on products means delivering well-defined outputs that meet users' expectations, which sets clear expectations and avoids unnecessary work (book 5.2.1.6, Table 5.1). Adding a phone route and translated updates so the service works for all tenants is shaping the products around user needs.

n.0: Tailoring adapts the way the method is applied (frameworks, artifacts, workshops); here the teams are changing what the products must do (book 5.2.1.7).
n.1: Nothing in the situation re-tests whether the project is still worth the investment; the change is to the products' features (book 5.2.1.1).
n.2: This principle is about having the right people in clear roles; the action described changes the outputs so they meet users' needs (book 5.2.1.3).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Midway through Stage 4, the burn-up chart shows that the teams cannot finish everything planned for Release 3 by month 12. Tenant-chosen appointment slots for all homes are Must haves; video reporting and a live engineer tracker are Could haves. Ian Thursby suggests a two-month extension so that no features are lost. What should Sally Greaves, the project manager, recommend?
o: Agree the two-month extension, because the Must and Could haves together give tenants the full benefit of Release 3.
Keep the month 12 end date and the budget, deliver the Must haves and drop or defer the Could haves that will not fit.
Ask the board for extra budget to add agency contractors to both teams, so that every feature can be finished by month 12.
Re-label some Must haves as Should haves, so that the end date can be met without referring the change to the board.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: By default PRINCE2 Agile allows no tolerance on time or cost at any plan level, fixes scope for Must haves and flexes Should and Could haves (book Table 3.1). The board has also said budget and timescale will not change, so the Could haves give way.

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, and the board has fixed the twelve months; extending to protect Could haves breaks the fixed aspect (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Cost also has zero tolerance, and the £1.3 million is fixed; the aspect to flex is lower-priority scope (book Table 3.1).
n.3: Scope is fixed for Must haves; downgrading them to hit the date would drop essential features and avoid the governance that a change to them needs (book Table 3.1, 11.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.q: Joy Ansah's contact centre has high staff turnover, and advisers fear that online reporting will lead to job losses. To prepare them for the new diagnosis guide in Release 2, Joy plans to email every adviser a copy of the guide with a short explanation and then leave them to use it on live calls. Which approach would BEST build the agile maturity needed for this change?
o: Combine training on the guide with on-the-job coaching, set out in a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change.
Send the guide by email as planned, then monitor call handling times so that the advisers who struggle can be identified and replaced.
Train the team leaders in depth and ask them to pass the guide on to their own advisers once the release has gone live.
Delay all training until Release 3, so that advisers learn the whole new service at once when it reaches all homes.
Agile Practitioner: Mindset & Principles.w: Under agile maturity, people need both theoretical training and practical on-the-job coaching; informing people and leaving them to fend for themselves breeds frustration, demotivation and resistance. PRINCE2 Agile suggests a training and coaching plan mapped to the stages of the change (book 2.7.3).

n.1: Informing people and leaving them to cope is exactly what undermines the change; it would deepen the advisers' fears (book 2.7.3).
n.2: As many people as possible should understand what is changing and why, through training and coaching, not second-hand after go-live (book 2.7.3).
n.3: The guide arrives in Release 2; coaching should be mapped to the stages of the change rather than held back to the end (book 2.7.3).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: At a board meeting, Dominic Faraday asks why Fair Fares needs organizational change management when the app will do most of the work of paying compensation. Yusuf Bello's 40 staff will move from checking claims by hand to handling unusual cases and possible fraud. Which explanation BEST answers Dominic's question?
o: OCM is a supplier activity that Coinbridge Payments should cover under its fixed-price contract, as its payment service drives the change.
OCM replaces the communication management approach, so that one change plan can hold every message to staff and passengers.
OCM is needed to agree new pay terms with customer relations staff before go-live, as financial reward is what makes a change stick.
The benefits rely on staff adopting new ways of working, so OCM plans the move to the target state and evolves the culture so it lasts.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to a target state (book 4.2.1). Fair Fares only realizes its benefits if customer relations staff work differently, and the change management approach should consider how the culture evolves so changes are not rolled back.

n.0: OCM is how Larkspur itself moves from its current to its target state; it cannot be handed to the payment supplier, whose contract covers building the payment feature (book 4.2.1).
n.1: The communication management approach remains a separate management approach; OCM does not replace it, though communication is one input to how the change is managed (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.2: The book points to evolving the culture, not money, compliance or communication alone, as the way to stop changes being rolled back (book 4.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Matteo Ricci wants passengers to trust the one-tap claim and, later, payments made without a claim, so that use of the app grows quickly after each release. He asks who should be engaged as a key influencer to shape how regular passengers see the change. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited?
o: Nigel Ormsby, because as passenger panel chair and a daily commuter he has a network and credibility among regular passengers.
Gemma Lowther, because Coinbridge Payments runs the card payments that passengers will receive under the new service.
Bronwen Hale, because as commercial director she holds the budget for customer-facing services and received the mandate for Fair Fares.
Hollie Brennan, because she checks the stories against their acceptance criteria and knows how the claim screens behave.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Key influencers are people who, through their network, can shape the perception of the majority affected by a change and so most influence adoption and benefits (book 4.2.2). Among regular passengers, the panel chair who commutes daily has that reach; seniority, technical skill or supplier status do not provide it.

n.1: Gemma commits the supplier's staff and owns its contract; she has no network among passengers through which to shape their view of the change (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Seniority and budget make Bronwen a natural project executive, but they do not give her influence over how regular passengers perceive the change (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Technical knowledge of the screens does not make Hollie someone passengers listen to; a key influencer shapes the majority's perception through a network (book 4.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: In stage 3, the Coinbridge Payments team works from its own offices in another city and follows its own company's ways of working. Its developers are unsure which decisions about the payment screens they can take themselves and which need Larkspur's agreement, and several small questions have waited days for an answer. What should Rhys Pengelly do to lead this cross-organization team MOST effectively?
o: Ask the Coinbridge developers to send every design question to him, so that he can decide each one quickly for both organizations.
Agree clear decision boundaries with Gemma Lowther and the product owners, such as a delegation matrix, for the Coinbridge developers.
Leave each design decision to Coinbridge, as the fixed-price contract makes the supplier responsible for the design of its work.
Require the Coinbridge team to move into Larkspur's offices for the rest of the project, so that questions can be answered face to face.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: When teams work across organizations and cultures, PRINCE2 Agile advises setting clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that shows what each party decides or advises on (book 4.3.1, 7.4.3). This lets the Coinbridge developers act quickly within agreed limits.

n.0: Routing every question through the project manager creates a bottleneck and bypasses the product owners; it removes self-management instead of setting boundaries for it (book 4.3.1, 7.3.1).
n.2: Without agreed boundaries, decisions affecting Larkspur's passengers would be made by the supplier alone; the guidance is to define what each party decides or advises on (book 4.3.1).
n.3: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer; teams across organizations and locations need clear boundaries and planned ways of working together (book 4.3.1, 4.3.3).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: From stage 2, the app team works in Larkspur's head office three days a week, the data team works fully remotely, and the Coinbridge team is based in another city. Fatima Zahra says her team feels cut off and hears about decisions late. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to improve communication across this hybrid set-up?
o: Ask each team to send a weekly written status report to Rhys Pengelly, who will circulate a combined summary to all three teams each Monday.
Require all three teams to work at Larkspur's head office five days a week until Release 3 is live, so questions are answered in person.
Agree how information flows between teams, hold in-person days for key people around planning and reviews, and allow informal time online.
Send the same monthly project newsletter to all three teams, so that everyone receives identical messages at the same time.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Remote and hybrid teams need a more deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together. Synchronized co-location days for key people help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3, 4.4).

n.0: Periodic reports are not enough on their own and can be biased; they also keep the flow one-way rather than building the relationships a hybrid set-up needs (book 4.4).
n.1: Mandating co-location is not the effective response; hybrid and remote teams need a deliberate, structured approach to working together (book 4.3.3).
n.3: Generic one-way messaging is rarely effective; communication should be two-way and tailored to the groups involved (book 4.4).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Before stage 2, the app team realizes that none of its members has tested an app with a screen reader, although about 12% of Larkspur's passengers have told it they have a disability or long-term condition. Owen Thackeray wants the team to close this gap without delaying Release 1. Which action follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on building agile teams?
o: Ask Sasha Ellery to move the accessibility stories out of Release 1 until a team member has completed an external course.
Help the team build a skill matrix of current and planned skills, with a training plan for accessibility testing on the team dashboard.
Offer a cash bonus to the first developer who gains an accessibility certificate, to reward the individual effort this will need.
Ask Rhys Pengelly to assign the accessibility testing to one named developer and record the duty in that person's written role description.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Building agile teams includes empowering them with training plans: the team skill matrix shows current and planned skills and the gaps, and visual management on the team dashboard keeps progress transparent (book 4.5, 7.4.1).

n.0: The app must meet accessibility standards, so deferring the work avoids the gap rather than building the team's capability (book 4.5).
n.2: Value-based incentives in the book are peer-assessed rewards for behaviour that models agile values, balanced with intangible motivators; a race between individuals does not build the team (book 4.5).
n.3: Assigning the work from above sidesteps the team's own planning and leaves a single point of failure; the guidance is to empower the team through training plans (book 4.5).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: At a project board meeting, a council member asks why the Student Support Hub needs organizational change management. In her view, the web team and Northmere will build the hub, and once it is live the wellbeing staff will simply have to use it. Which explanation BEST answers her question?
o: OCM gives the board a way to instruct staff to use the hub by a set date, and clear instructions with a deadline are what make staff comply.
OCM is needed because the change management approach cannot be used outside a project, so another discipline must cover the wellbeing service's 45 staff.
OCM is mostly a record of the training given, because frequent releases of the hub are what make staff adopt the new ways of working.
The service must move from its current way of triaging to a new target state, and the change lasts if the culture adopts it rather than rolling back.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to the target state (book 4.2.1). Building the hub does not change how 45 staff triage requests; the culture has to evolve so that the change is not rolled back once the project ends (book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).

n.0: Making change stick depends on evolving the culture, not on compliance with instructions; staff who have seen three systems dropped are unlikely to adopt the hub because of a deadline (book 4.2.1).
n.1: The change management approach can be tailored for use outside a project, for example to describe the target state for the business (book 4.2.1, Table 4.1).
n.2: Frequent releases support adoption, but OCM is the whole transition from current to target state, including culture and communication, not a training record (book 4.2.1, 4.2.4).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Dr Kwame Mensah wants the wellbeing staff to adopt the new triage process before Welcome Week. Many staff fear that a digital route will make support feel impersonal, and some doubt the hub will last. Jamal Hussain asks who should be engaged as a key influencer to shape how the staff see the change. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited, and why?
o: Dr Kwame Mensah, because as director of the service he has the authority to require staff to use the new process.
Tom Brierley, because he is respected by his colleagues, so his views can shape how many staff see the hub.
Ian Prothero, because Northmere supplies the records system and can explain how the link to the hub will work.
Dr Ruth Sefton, because she must approve the handling of health data and can reassure staff that it is secure.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: A key influencer is someone who can shape the perception of the majority and, through their network, most affect the adoption of the change (book 4.2.2). Tom Brierley is respected by the staff who must change, and his open doubts mean his support would carry weight with colleagues who share them.

n.0: Formal authority is not the same as influence over colleagues' perceptions; the key influencer is the person with network and credibility among those affected (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Ian Prothero is the supplier's account manager; he has no network among the wellbeing staff whose adoption matters (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Dr Sefton is a specialist approver; reassurance on data is useful, but she does not have the peer network that shapes how staff see the change (book 4.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: In stage 2, the Northmere developers work from their own offices under their company's rules, while the university web team works on campus. The two teams must agree how the hub exchanges data with the records system, but they have never met, and misunderstandings over the shared data fields have already cost a sprint. Which action BEST builds the working relationship between the two teams?
o: Agree regular days when key people from both teams work together in person, and set aside online time for less structured conversation.
Require all the Northmere developers to work on campus every day until Release 1 is live, so that the teams can share one room.
Limit contact between the teams to written requests passed through Jamal Hussain, so that the per-iteration agreement with Northmere is protected.
Leave the two teams to build their own relationship, as self-managing teams decide for themselves how they will work together.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Teams that work apart need a plan for how they will use their time together and build social cohesion. Sync co-location days for key people and teams, plus time for less structured conversation online, are the aids PRINCE2 Agile suggests (book 4.3.3).

n.1: Mandating full co-location for another organization's staff is not the effective answer; planned co-location days for key people build cohesion without it (book 4.3.3).
n.2: Channelling all contact through the project manager reduces collaboration and rich communication, which is what caused the misunderstandings (book 4.3.3, 4.4).
n.3: Self-management works within clear boundaries; leading teams across organizations means planning how people work together, not leaving it to chance (book 4.3.1, 4.3.3).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: The wellbeing staff work across both campuses, and many work part-time or remotely, so they often miss face-to-face meetings about the new triage process. Jamal Hussain is drafting the communication management approach and asks how communication should be handled for this group. Which explanation BEST fits PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Hold all briefings in person on the main campus, because rich communication needs people to be in the same room together.
Send one weekly email to all 45 staff, because a single message for everyone keeps the information on the change consistent.
Plan a deliberate structure: agreed formats and channels, the key relationships, and set times for structured and informal contact.
Rely on a formal monthly report to the service, because informal conversations about the change cannot be controlled by the project.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Remote and hybrid working need a more deliberate, structured approach to communication: clarity on how information flows and in which formats, the key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together (book 4.4). This group works in a hybrid way across two campuses.

n.0: Rich communication is not limited to face-to-face meetings, and in-person briefings would keep excluding the part-time and remote staff who already miss meetings (book 4.4).
n.1: Generic one-way messaging is rarely effective; communication should be bidirectional and tailored to groups, with listening as well as broadcasting (book 4.4).
n.3: Most communication happens outside formal channels and should be accepted and supported; periodic reports on their own are not enough (book 4.4).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: For Release 1, Dr Kwame Mensah forms a triage team of eight advisers from both campuses to handle self-referrals. They have not worked together before, and several are unsure which changes to the triage questions they may make themselves and which need his approval. Which action BEST helps build this into an agile team?
o: Kwame writes the team's values and decision rules himself and circulates them, so that the advisers can start triaging without delay.
Pay a monthly bonus to the advisers who close the most self-referral requests, so that the team is motivated to work quickly.
Ask each adviser to email Kwame a daily summary, so that he can approve any change to the triage questions before it is made.
Hold a session where the team co-decides its values and agrees which decisions it can take and which must be escalated.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Building agile teams starts with co-deciding team values and accountabilities, so that the team knows the boundaries of its self-management and when decisions must be escalated (book 4.5).

n.0: Values and accountabilities should be co-decided by the team; values written by a manager do not build shared ownership (book 4.5).
n.1: PRINCE2 Agile suggests value-based incentives that reward behaviour modelling agile values, balanced with intangible motivators; a bonus for volume can reward rushing urgent cases (book 4.5).
n.2: Approving every change centrally removes self-management; the team needs agreed boundaries, not daily approval (book 4.5).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: At the starting up workshop, Gwen Tallowby asks why the project needs organizational change management (OCM). In her view the project will deliver the website features, the collection points and the staff training, and store managers can then be told to use them. Bill Rowntree points out that store managers are already worried about extra work at the busiest time of year. Which explanation BEST answers Gwen's question?
o: OCM is a communication activity, so Lucy Fenn's national campaign in February will give store managers and customers the information they need to adopt the service.
OCM moves Pinewick from its current way of working to the target state and helps the culture evolve, so stores keep running collections after the project ends.
OCM is needed to secure compliance, so area managers should audit each store and record any that fail to use the new collection process correctly.
OCM begins once the project closes and the stores take over the service, so it should be planned by Bill Rowntree's team as part of business as usual.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to the target state. When deciding how much of it to plan, the book asks the project to consider the evolving culture and how to make sure changes are not rolled back once the transformation is over (book 4.2.1). Delivering the products is not enough; store managers have to adopt and keep the new way of working.

n.0: Communication is part of OCM, but a national campaign aimed at customers does not address store managers' concerns, and making change stick depends on evolving the culture rather than on messaging (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.2: Audit and compliance may show who is not using the process, but they do not make the change last; the book points to evolving the culture (book 4.2.1).
n.3: OCM covers the transition from current to target state, which runs alongside delivery; frequent releases and user involvement during the project support adoption (book 4.2.1, 4.2.4).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Patrick Dunne wants a key influencer to help the 85 store managers accept click and collect before the pilot begins. He learns that Sophie Draper has run the store managers' peer forum for five years and is widely trusted by other managers, who often copy changes she makes at the Wrexham store. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to be the key influencer for store managers?
o: Bill Rowntree, because as head of store operations he has the formal authority to instruct area managers and store managers to adopt the new process.
Gwen Tallowby, because as retail operations director she received the mandate and is accountable to the board for the performance of the stores.
Elena Marsh, because Tallis supplies the stock system that store managers rely on, and she can explain how live stock levels will work in stores.
Sophie Draper, because she is a store manager with a trusted network among her peers, whose views shape how other managers see the change.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Key influencers are people who can shape how the majority perceive a change and who, through their network, most influence its adoption and the realization of benefits (book 4.2.2). Sophie is a fellow store manager, runs the managers' peer forum and is copied by others, so her view will shape how store managers see click and collect.

n.0: Formal authority can secure compliance, but a key influencer is chosen for network and credibility among the people adopting the change, not for position (book 4.2.2).
n.1: Gwen is senior and accountable, which suits governance, but nothing suggests store managers look to her as a peer whose example they follow (book 4.2.2).
n.2: A supplier can explain the system, but the key influencer is the person whose network shapes store managers' perception, not a technical specialist outside Pinewick (book 4.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Two Tallis developers join the e-commerce team's refinement sessions and sprint reviews to advise on the new stock interface. After a few weeks there is friction: the e-commerce developers expect Tallis to accept their design choices, while the Tallis developers believe they should decide the interface's data format and update frequency. Tallis works to its own quarterly release cycle. What should Patrick Dunne do to lead this cross-organization team MOST effectively?
o: Agree with Elena Marsh and both teams a delegation matrix showing which interface decisions Tallis makes, which it advises on and which the e-commerce team makes.
Ask Elena Marsh to move the Tallis developers onto the e-commerce team's two-week sprints, so that both organizations follow one framework and timetable.
Route all questions about the interface through himself and Elena Marsh, so that developers in the two organizations no longer need to negotiate the design directly.
Ask the two Tallis developers to work at Pinewick's head office every day until Release 1, so that the teams resolve their differences face to face.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: When people work across organizations and cultures, the book advises setting clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that makes clear what external specialists decide and what they advise on (book 4.3.1, 7.4.3).
