The friction here is about who decides, so making decision rights transparent addresses its cause.

n.1: Tallis has said it cannot change its cycle for one customer, and putting everyone on one framework would not settle who decides what about the interface (book 4.3.1).
n.2: Funnelling questions through two managers slows communication and reduces collaboration, and it still leaves decision boundaries unclear (book 4.3.1, 2.6.2).
n.3: Requiring daily co-location is not the effective answer; planned co-location days can help, but the friction comes from unclear decision rights (book 4.3.3).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Three members of the store operations team work from their own stores in Cardiff, Leeds and Exeter, while the two trainers are based at head office. The team has always reported progress by email, and Patrick Dunne notices that the store-based members often learn about decisions days after the trainers. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to improve communication in this hybrid team?
o: Ask each member to send Sophie Draper a fuller weekly email report, so that she can pass a single summary on to everyone at the end of each week.
Ask the three store-based members to relocate to head office for the whole of Stage 3, so that the team can work together in one place every day.
Agree how information will flow, keep the Kanban board online for all, hold structured and informal video time, and plan in-person days for key events.
Let the two head office trainers make day-to-day decisions, as they share an office, and ask the store-based members to concentrate on preparing their own stores.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Remote and hybrid teams need a more deliberate, structured approach to communication: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, identifying key relationships and agreeing both structured and unstructured time together (book 4.4). Planned co-location days for key people and moments help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3).

n.0: Periodic written reporting is not enough on its own and keeps information flowing one way and late, which is the problem the team already has (book 4.4).
n.1: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer for a team spread across stores; the book suggests planned co-location days instead (book 4.3.3).
n.3: Splitting decisions by location creates a two-tier team and damages the social cohesion and collaboration a hybrid team needs (book 4.3.3, 2.6.2).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Bill Rowntree wants to keep the store operations team motivated through the busy Stage 4 roll-out. He proposes a cash bonus for each member based on how many stores they personally take live, ranked in a league table that he will publish to all store managers. Nikhil Rao is asked for advice. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on building and leading agile teams?
o: Keep Bill's individual bonus but show the league table to the team rather than to all store managers, to reduce the public pressure on members.
Replace the bonus with a personal target for each member, set by Sophie Draper and reviewed against each member's results at the end of the stage.
Avoid incentives, because motivation in an agile team comes from personal values and is best left to each member to manage for themselves.
Use peer-assessed recognition for behaviour that reflects the team's agreed values, balanced with purpose and recognition, instead of individual targets.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: The book suggests motivating agile teams through value-based incentives, such as peer-assessed points for behaviour that models agile values, balanced with intangible motivators such as purpose and recognition and with personal values. Team values can be used in peer-based assessments in retrospectives (book 4.5).

n.0: Rewarding individual go-live counts still sets members against each other, which works against collaboration; hiding the table does not make the incentive value-based (book 4.5).
n.1: Manager-set individual targets do not reflect values the team has agreed or peer assessment, which the book recommends (book 4.5).
n.2: The book does not leave motivation to chance; it recommends value-based incentives balanced with intangible motivators and personal values (book 4.5).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: At an early board meeting, Joan Whitaker asks why Care Online needs organizational change management at all. In her view, once the online service works and the interface to the case system is live, staff and the public will simply use it. Simon Archer notes that Paul Henshaw has said the change will create more work for the front door team, and that many social workers fear their judgement will be bypassed. Which explanation BEST answers Joan?
o: OCM is needed because it controls changes to the project's baseline, so that requests from front door staff and social workers are assessed formally.
OCM is needed because it replaces the communication management approach with a single plan for training social workers and front door staff.
OCM is needed because the benefits depend on staff and the public adopting new ways of working, and the culture must change for that to last.
OCM is needed because the grant conditions require a separate change management team to report on the project's outcomes every quarter.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to the target state. Working software does not deliver benefits on its own: people must adopt the change, and culture decides whether it is adopted and whether it is rolled back later (book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).

n.0: Controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issues practice, not of OCM (book 11.1, 4.2.1).
n.1: The communication management approach is part of the people guidance that supports OCM; OCM does not replace it (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.3: The grant needs a quarterly report of spend and outcomes, but nothing in the scenario calls for a separate team; the reason for OCM is adoption of the change (book 4.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Simon Archer wants front-line social workers to see online self-assessment as support for their professional judgement rather than a threat to it, so that they follow up online assessments promptly. He wants to work with one key influencer who can shape how social workers across the county see the change. Using the Additional information (People), who is the BEST choice?
o: Dr Rajesh Iyer, because he leads practice standards for all social workers and is trusted by front-line staff across the county.
Joan Whitaker, because as assistant director she chairs the department's programme board and has formal authority over the service.
Bev Lomax, because she chairs the carers' network and can explain to others how carers will benefit from the online assessment.
Amy Fletcher, because she has run user research with carers and older people and understands how the service will be used.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Key influencers are people who, through their network and credibility, most shape how the majority see a change and so drive its adoption and benefits (book 4.2.2). Rajesh leads practice standards for all social workers and is trusted by front-line staff, so his view will carry with the group Simon needs to reach.

n.1: Formal seniority is not the same as influence; Joan prefers traditional reporting and is not described as trusted by front-line social workers (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Bev is a strong influencer for carers, but the group to reach here is social workers, and she is not part of their network (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Amy understands users, but she sits in the digital team and has no described standing among front-line social workers (book 4.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: In stage 3, the Abacus Care Software developers build the case system interface from their own offices in another region, while the council's digital team works in county hall. The two teams have so far met only on formal calls about change requests, and integration problems are taking days to resolve. Which action is MOST LIKELY to build the social cohesion the two teams need?
o: Require the Abacus developers to work from county hall every day until Release 2 is live, so that both teams sit together.
Agree co-location days for key people from both teams around integration points, and make time for less structured conversation online.
Route all contact between the teams through Martin Sallis and Simon Archer, so that technical discussions stay within the fixed-price contract terms.
Ask both teams to send each other a weekly written status note, so that each team knows what the other has finished and what is next.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Leading teams across organizations and locations means planning how people work together and building social cohesion, for example by syncing co-location days for key people and teams and allowing time for less structured conversation online (book 4.3.3).

n.0: Mandating full-time co-location is not the effective answer; planned co-location days and good hybrid working build cohesion without it (book 4.3.3).
n.2: Funnelling contact through two managers cuts the direct, rich communication between the teams that integration work needs (book 4.3.3, 4.4).
n.3: Periodic written reports are not enough to build trust and cohesion, and they can be biased towards what seems acceptable (book 4.4).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: The Care Online digital team works together in county hall, while the social workers and occupational therapists who help with research and testing join from offices and home visits across a rural county, with little spare time. Oliver Grant notices that decisions made in quick office conversations are not reaching the practitioners. Which statement BEST explains how communication should be handled in this hybrid team?
o: Office conversations should stay the main channel, because most communication happens outside formal channels and cannot be planned.
The practitioners should receive the monthly highlight report, because periodic reporting keeps remote members informed without taking their time.
Each update should go to all practitioners in one identical message, because consistent wording makes sure nobody receives a different account.
The remote part needs a deliberate approach: agree how information flows and in which formats, and set structured and unstructured time together.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Remote working needs a more deliberate, structured approach than co-location: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, the key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together. A hybrid team combines co-located and remote working, so its remote members need this structure (book 4.4).

n.0: Informal communication should be accepted, but relying on office conversations is exactly what is leaving the remote practitioners out (book 4.4).
n.1: Periodic reporting alone is insufficient and can be biased; it does not give remote members a two-way flow of information (book 4.4).
n.2: Generic messaging is rarely effective; messages should be tailored to each group and the flow should be two-way (book 4.4).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Helen Crowther wants to motivate the digital team and the practitioners who work with it during stage 2. She proposes a monthly gift voucher for the developer who completes the most story points. Oliver Grant is concerned that this could damage the collaboration the team has built. Which approach BEST follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on motivating agile teams?
o: Keep the voucher but base it on story points per hour worked, so that part-time practitioners can compete fairly with full-time developers.
Let team members award points to colleagues whose behaviour models the team's agreed values, alongside recognition and a clear sense of purpose.
Replace the voucher with a bonus for the whole team if Release 1 is live by month four, with progress shown on the project dashboard.
Ask Helen to rate each person's contribution at the end of every release and show the resulting ranking on the team dashboard for everyone to see.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: PRINCE2 Agile suggests value-based incentives, such as peer-assessed points or a fictional currency for behaviour that models agile values, balanced with intangible motivators such as purpose and recognition, and with personal values (book 4.5).

n.0: Rewarding individual output still sets team members against each other; the book points to peer-assessed rewards for behaviour that models agile values (book 4.5).
n.2: A deadline bonus rewards output against a date rather than behaviour that models the team's values, and leaves out intangible motivators (book 4.5).
n.3: A manager's ranking is neither peer-based nor tied to the team's agreed values, and it works against self-management (book 4.5).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: At the project canvas workshop, Graham Doyle says Smart Maintenance is a technology installation, so organizational change management (OCM) is not needed. The maintenance engineers are proud of their skills and doubt the predictions, and after closure the maintenance team will run the dashboard as part of normal work. Which explanation BEST shows why OCM matters here?
o: OCM is the practice that controls changes to the project's baseline, so it is needed whenever the engineers ask for new dashboard features.
OCM moves the organization from its current to its target state, and evolving the culture helps stop engineers reverting to old ways after closure.
OCM replaces the communication management approach, so it gives the project one place to brief the engineers and the union about the project.
OCM sets the tolerances for adoption, so the board can decide how far the engineers' use of the new dashboard may slip before an exception is raised.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current state to its target state. Making the change last means evolving the culture so that changes are not rolled back after the transformation (book 4.2.1). Moving from reactive and calendar maintenance to prediction-led work, with sceptical engineers, is exactly this kind of change.

n.0: Controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issues practice, not OCM (book 11.1, 4.2.1).
n.2: OCM does not replace the communication management approach; communication is one of the things considered when planning the change (book 4.2.1, 4.4).
n.3: Tolerances are set through manage by exception for the performance aspects; OCM is about the transition to new ways of working (book 5.2.1.5, 4.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Andrea Lucas wants a key influencer to help the maintenance engineers at Factory A accept the dashboard's predictions. Engineers there tend to follow colleagues whose practical judgement they trust, and several doubt that a computer can tell them when a machine will fail. Using the people list, who is the BEST choice of key influencer for this group?
o: Graham Doyle, because as operations director he is the most senior person on the project and holds the budget for both factories.
Hannah Reece, because as data science lead she can explain in detail how the prediction model reaches each of its results.
Dev Patel, because as Senticore's account director he knows the sensors well and commits the teams that fit them.
Stuart Bell, because his long experience and standing with colleagues let him shape how the other engineers see the change.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Key influencers are people who can shape the perception of the majority and, through their network, most influence adoption of the change (book 4.2.2). Stuart Bell has 30 years' experience and is respected by colleagues; winning over a respected sceptic carries far more weight with the engineers than a formal instruction.

n.0: Seniority and budget give formal authority, but a key influencer is chosen for network and credibility among the affected group (book 4.2.2).
n.1: Hannah is a technical specialist and the model's builder; engineers who doubt the computer are more likely to follow a trusted peer (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Dev Patel works for the supplier and sits outside the engineers' network, so he has little influence over how they see the change (book 4.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: During Stage 2, Senticore's fitting crews and Draycott's production staff argue on the shop floor about who can decide when a machine may be stopped and where on each machine a sensor may be mounted. Two fittings are delayed while people wait for answers. What should Andrea Lucas do to lead these teams across the two organizations?
o: Agree clear boundaries, such as a delegation matrix showing which decisions the fitters may take and which they advise on.
Ask Dev Patel to make all decisions about machine stops and sensor positions, as Senticore holds the fixed-price contract.
Require every decision about machine stops and sensor positions to be referred to her, so one person is accountable.
Ask Jim Halligan to settle each dispute as it arises, as he represents the engineering staff on the shop floor.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: When people work across organizations and cultures, PRINCE2 Agile advises setting clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that shows what external parties decide and what they only advise on (book 4.3.1).

n.1: Machine stops affect Draycott's production and sensor positions affect safety certification; handing all such decisions to the supplier ignores those boundaries (book 4.3.1).
n.2: Routing every decision through the project manager creates a bottleneck and undermines self-management within agreed boundaries (book 4.3.1).
n.3: The union representative speaks for staff interests but has no authority over production schedules or fitting decisions; the gap is unclear decision rights (book 4.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: The software team works at head office two days a week and from home on the others. Factory B engineers join sprint reviews by video while Factory A engineers attend in person, and the Factory B engineers say they miss much of what is decided. Which approach to communication BEST fits this hybrid arrangement?
o: Require everyone to attend every review in person at Factory A, so that all decisions are made face to face.
Send all the engineers the same written summary after each review, so both factories get identical information.
Agree how information flows and in what formats, with structured and informal time together and some in-person days.
Ask Ruth Kenyon to brief the Factory B engineers once a month, so that they hear decisions from their own manager.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Remote and hybrid teams need a deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows, suitable formats, key relationships, and agreed structured and unstructured time together. Synchronized co-location days for key people help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3, 4.4).

n.0: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer for distributed teams; the book advises planned in-person days alongside structured remote working (book 4.3.3).
n.1: Generic one-way messaging is rarely effective; communication should be two-way and tailored to each group (book 4.4).
n.3: Periodic one-way briefings are not enough on their own; the engineers need to take part in the flow of information and feedback (book 4.4).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: The maintenance engineers and operators trialling the dashboard are expert machinists, but few have read sensor trend charts or judged how confident a prediction is. Tomasz Zielinski and Ruth Kenyon want to build these skills over the three releases. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on building agile teams?
o: Rank the engineers each month by how many predicted failures they act on, and pay the top three a bonus.
Use a team skill matrix of current and planned skills, agree a training plan from it, and show it on the team dashboard.
Ask Hannah Reece to read all the trend charts for the engineers, so that gaps in skills do not slow the trial down.
Recruit a data analyst to join the trial team, so that the engineers can concentrate on their machining work.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: PRINCE2 Agile suggests empowering teams with training plans, using a team skill matrix that shows current and planned skills, and using visual management such as team dashboards (book 4.5, 7.4.1).

n.0: Value-based incentives reward behaviour that models agile values, often peer-assessed and balanced with purpose and recognition; an individual ranking on one metric works against teamwork (book 4.5).
n.2: Relying on one specialist leaves the skill gap in place and makes the team dependent on Hannah; the aim is to build the team's own capability (book 4.5).
n.3: Adding a specialist does not develop the engineers, who will run the dashboard after closure; a skill matrix and training plan build their skills (book 4.5).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: At the starting up workshop, Ian Thursby says that organizational change management is unnecessary for Repairs Reimagined: once the portal, scripts and parts list are delivered, advisers and engineers will simply start using them. Sally Greaves disagrees. Which statement BEST explains why OCM matters for this project?
o: OCM takes the place of the project's management approaches, so that the board can direct the change without needing a project canvas.
OCM is needed because the project uses agile delivery, whereas a project delivered in a linear way would not change how people work.
OCM makes sure the Coastline contract is renegotiated first, so that engineers are paid for each new way of working they adopt.
OCM moves the organization from its current to its target state, and evolving the culture stops the new ways of working being rolled back.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: OCM is the means by which an organization moves from its current to its target state (book 4.2.1). Delivering products does not change how people work; the change management approach should consider the evolving culture and how to make sure changes are not rolled back after the transformation (book 4.2.1, 4.2.3).

n.0: OCM works alongside the project; the change management approach is one of the management approaches, and business justification is still needed (book 4.2.1, 6.3.1).
n.1: Any project that changes how people work needs its change managed; the delivery method does not remove that need (book 4.2.1).
n.2: Contract terms belong to the commercial management approach; OCM is about moving people from the current to the target state and making the change stick (book 4.2.1, 7.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Joy Ansah's advisers fear that online reporting will cost them their jobs, and a staff survey shows that they trust what colleagues tell them far more than messages from managers. Sally Greaves wants a key influencer to help shape how advisers see the change. Which person in the scenario is BEST suited to this, and why?
o: Joy Ansah, because as contact centre manager she has formal authority over the 28 advisers and can instruct them to support it.
Kyle Morgan, because as an experienced adviser and informal leader who trains new starters, his network can shape most advisers' views.
Winston Clarke, because as chair of the tenants' panel he can explain to advisers how much tenants want to report repairs online.
Amara Okeke, because as data and insight analyst she can show advisers the evidence on call waiting times and repair satisfaction.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Key influencers are people who can shape the perception of the majority and, through their network, most influence adoption of the change (book 4.2.2). Kyle is an informal leader trusted by advisers and trains new starters, so his credibility reaches the affected group.

n.0: The survey shows advisers trust peers more than managers; a key influencer works through network and credibility, not formal authority (book 4.2.2).
n.2: Winston influences tenants, not the advisers whose perception needs shaping; he lacks a network inside the contact centre (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Evidence helps, but a key influencer is someone whose network shapes the majority's view; Amara is a specialist, not a trusted voice among advisers (book 4.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: Coastline Property Services engineers are trialling the new parts list on the pilot estate. They keep phoning the service design team to ask whether they may add parts to the list, use a different supplier or change appointment lengths, and work stalls while they wait for answers. Frank Tolley says his engineers want to help but are unsure what they are allowed to decide. What should Sally Greaves do?
o: Agree a delegation matrix with Frank Tolley and the team, showing which decisions engineers can make and which need agreement under the contract.
Ask Ian Thursby to instruct Coastline's engineers directly under the repairs contract, so that the association's managers decide each of the questions they raise.
Bring the engineers into the service design team's daily stand-ups, so that the whole team can make each of the decisions they need.
Record each question as an issue in the issue register, so that the project board can decide on each one at its next meeting.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: When teams span organizations, leaders should set clear boundaries within which people can flex, for example a delegation matrix that makes clear what each party decides or advises on (book 4.3.1, 7.4.3). This lets Coastline's engineers act without waiting while respecting the contract.

n.1: Routing every decision through a director slows the work further and ignores that Coastline's engineers are managed through Coastline; clear boundaries are needed instead (book 4.3.1).
n.2: Daily stand-ups with 90 field engineers are impractical and still leave unclear who decides what; the gap is the lack of agreed decision boundaries (book 4.3.1).
n.3: These are routine operating decisions, not issues for the board; escalating them would stall the trial further (book 4.3.1, 11.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: The digital team of three works from home most of the week, while the service design team works together in the association's office. The two teams must agree how the portal's online reporting form matches the new phone scripts, and misunderstandings have already caused rework. Which approach to communication is MOST appropriate for this hybrid arrangement?
o: Require the digital team to work in the office every day, so that the two teams can communicate face to face as one co-located team and stop the rework.
Rely on the board's quarterly written reports, which give both teams a single, formal record of decisions about the form and scripts.
Plan it deliberately: agree how information flows and in which formats, hold co-location days for key people and keep some unstructured time.
Let each team communicate in its own way, as remote and co-located teams need the same approach and little extra planning.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Remote and hybrid working needs a more deliberate, structured approach: clarity on how information flows and in which formats, identifying key relationships, and agreeing structured and unstructured time together; sync co-location days for key people help build social cohesion (book 4.3.3, 4.4).

n.0: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer; the book suggests planned co-location days and deliberate online arrangements (book 4.3.3).
n.1: Periodic reporting is insufficient and far too slow for two teams aligning their work every iteration (book 4.4).
n.3: Remote and hybrid teams need a more deliberate and structured approach than co-located ones, not the same approach (book 4.4).

Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.q: The service design team brings together staff from the contact centre, the repairs team and tenant engagement. In the first iterations, members disagree about who can approve changes to call scripts and when a decision must go to the project manager, and some changes are made twice. What should the team do FIRST to address this?
o: Ask Joy Ansah to approve each script change before it is used, because most of the scripts are used by the advisers in her contact centre.
Complete a team skill matrix, so that the team can see the current and planned skills of each of its members.
Introduce peer-assessed bonus points, so that members are rewarded for behaviour that models the agile values.
Co-decide the team's values and accountabilities, including the limits of its self-management and when a decision must be escalated.
Agile Practitioner: People & OCM.w: Building agile teams starts with co-deciding team values and accountabilities, so that members know the boundaries of self-management and when decisions must be escalated (book 4.5). That is exactly the gap causing duplicated changes.

n.0: Adding a manager's approval removes self-management and slows the team; the team needs agreed accountabilities and escalation limits (book 4.5).
n.1: A skill matrix shows capabilities and training needs; it does not settle who decides what or when to escalate (book 4.5, 7.4.1).
n.2: Value-based incentives support motivation, but they do not resolve unclear decision rights and escalation (book 4.5).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: At the starting up workshop, Yusuf Bello warns that paying compensation without a claim could make it easier for people to obtain payments they are not owed. Nothing of this kind has happened yet, but he wants the concern managed throughout the project. Which practice is designed to handle this concern, and why?
o: Issues, because it collects and assesses events that are causing a deviation from what has been agreed.
Risk, because it identifies, assesses and controls uncertain events that could affect the project's objectives.
Quality, because it defines the users' requirements and the acceptance criteria the payment feature must meet.
Business case, because it judges whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The risk practice identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty so that the project is more likely to meet its objectives; it answers 'what if something unexpected happens, and how do we respond?' (book 10.1). A possible rise in fraud has not happened, so it is a risk to be managed, not an issue.

n.0: The issues practice deals with events that have happened or deviations from the baseline; possible future fraud is an uncertainty, not yet an issue (book 11.1).
n.2: Quality documents what users require and how it will be met; Yusuf's concern is an uncertain future event, which the risk practice handles (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: The business case practice keeps the justification under review, and a major risk may appear on the canvas, but identifying, assessing and controlling the uncertainty is the risk practice (book 6.1, 10.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: In starting up a project, Bronwen Hale leads the development of the project canvas from the mandate. Release 1, which detects delays and pre-fills a claim for one-tap confirmation, has to be live by the end of month four so that usage data can guide Releases 2 and 3. How should Release 1 be reflected in the project canvas?
o: Show Release 1 as the first benefit of the project, measured by the number of new features passengers can use.
Leave Release 1 out of the canvas and describe it in the team plan that the app team writes for its first sprint.
Record Release 1 as a Could have in the scope section, so that it can be dropped if the budget comes under pressure.
Identify Release 1 as the minimum viable product, so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Where an MVP is used, the project canvas should identify it so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late (book 6.3.2). Release 1 is described as the MVP and is time-critical because its usage data guides the later releases.

n.0: Features are outputs, not benefits; a benefit is a measurable improvement such as the share of eligible journeys compensated (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.1: A team plan is a detailed plan for the next iteration; the canvas itself should identify the MVP so that a forecast delay can be escalated (book 6.3.2, 8.3.2).
n.2: Release 1 is the MVP whose usage data guides Releases 2 and 3; treating it as a Could have would let the core of the project be dropped, and cost has zero tolerance in any case (book 6.3.2, Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Matteo Ricci wants personas to help the teams understand what different passengers need from Fair Fares. A marketing analyst offers eleven profiles based on age band, income and ticket type, already written from survey data. Which approach to personas follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Write up to five fictional, needs-based personas, such as a commuter who uses a screen reader, in a workshop with team members.
Adopt the eleven profiles as written, because survey data on age, income and ticket type gives the most reliable view of passengers.
Build one persona for each member of the passenger panel, using their real names, so that the teams can test directly with them.
Ask the analyst to merge the profiles into five demographic groups and send them to the teams before the first sprint.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Personas help identify and articulate benefits for users. PRINCE2 Agile advises writing them in a cross-functional workshop with development team members, keeping them fictional, basing them on needs rather than demographics, and using no more than five for new products or pilots (book 6.4.1).

n.1: Demographics such as age and income no longer predict shared needs, and eleven personas is more than the five the book suggests for new products (book 6.4.1).
n.2: Personas should be fictional, which widens the room for innovation, so real panel members' names and profiles should not be used; one persona for each of the panel's 30 members would also be far above the suggested maximum of five (book 6.4.1).
n.3: The number is right, but the personas would still rest on demographics and be written by one person rather than in a cross-functional workshop with team members (book 6.4.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Bronwen Hale refines the project canvas. Under expected benefits she lists 'a new compensation feature in the Larkspur app', 'the delay matching model' and 'personalized journey alerts'. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the canvas has to show the main features of the project product so that the board can see what will be delivered.
Yes, because each item can be released early, which lets the benefits management approach plan for early benefits.
No, because these are outputs; the benefits should be measurable improvements, such as the share of eligible journeys compensated.
No, because benefits belong in the benefits management approach and should be left out of the project canvas.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome; an output such as a feature or a model is never a benefit (Glossary, book 6.3.2). The canvas benefits section should list expected, measurable benefits with tolerance, for example the proportion of eligible journeys compensated or fewer staff hours spent checking claims.

n.0: The canvas does show the project product and main features, but in its scope section; listing them as benefits confuses outputs with benefits (book 6.3.2).
n.1: Frequent releases do enable earlier benefits, but that does not turn the released items into benefits; they remain outputs (book 6.3.2).
n.3: The project canvas does include benefits, expected and measurable with tolerance; the benefits management approach covers how they will be managed and reviewed (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Rhys Pengelly and Gemma Lowther agree how the work under Coinbridge's fixed-price contract will support agile delivery: a stable Coinbridge team with a set cost per sprint, an agreed definition of the minimum viable product, and the steps for a formal variation if the supplier's scope changes. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure.
In the role descriptions for the Coinbridge team.
In the commercial management approach.
In the quality management approach.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The commercial management approach describes how procurement and contracts will support agile product development, for example fixed teams and costs per iteration, a definition of the MVP and tolerances, and an agreed Definition of Done (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: This shows who is involved, how they relate and arrangements such as co-location or remote working; it does not hold procurement and contract terms (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).
n.1: Role descriptions set out each role's responsibilities; the contract model, costs per sprint and variation steps belong elsewhere (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The quality management approach records quality techniques, standards and testing methods, not how the supplier contract supports agile delivery (book 9.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Fair Fares has three delivery teams: the in-house app team, the Coinbridge Payments team and the in-house data team. Rhys Pengelly is drafting the project management team structure and wants it to follow PRINCE2 Agile guidance for a project with several teams. Which structure should he propose?
o: One project manager, one chief product owner setting priorities across the teams, and a product owner for each team.
A project manager for each team, with Rhys coordinating the other two and reporting on all three to the project board.
One product owner, Sasha Ellery, prioritizing every story for all three teams, with no chief product owner role.
One project manager who also acts as product owner for all three teams, with a team coach working in each team.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: With multiple teams, PRINCE2 Agile keeps one project manager, possibly several product owners (typically one per team), and a chief product owner who sets priorities across the teams; team coaches work with one or two teams (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

n.1: With several teams PRINCE2 Agile keeps one project manager; the extra roles appear at team level as product owners (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).
n.2: Each team has its own product owner, and a chief product owner sets priorities across teams; one PO for three teams leaves no cross-team user representation (book 7.3.1).
n.3: The project manager has authority over the product owners and agrees work packages with them, so combining the PM with every PO role removes that structure (book 7.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Early in stage 2, Rhys Pengelly, who is used to traditional projects, starts assigning daily tasks directly to individual developers in the app and data teams and asks them to report to him each evening. The product owners hear of the changes afterwards. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager runs the project day to day for the board and has to keep each stage within its tolerances.
Yes, because the project manager acts as a servant leader, linking the governance roles with the delivery teams.
No, because daily tasks should be set by the project board through the release map for each stage.
No, because the project manager should agree work with the product owners, who direct their own team members.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, and the product owner, a version of the team manager, is the only role with direct authority over delivery team members. Work is agreed between the PM and the PO as sets of user stories (book 7.3.1).

n.0: This describes the project manager's role correctly, but day-to-day control is exercised by agreeing work packages with the product owners, not by directing developers (book 7.3.1).
n.1: A servant leader supports and enables the teams; assigning their daily tasks and demanding evening reports is the opposite of that stance (Table 7.2).
n.2: The board works at stage level through the release map and tolerances; it does not plan daily tasks, which the team plans for its iteration (book 8.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: The project board needs someone to represent the user community, own the project backlog and set priorities across the app, Coinbridge and data teams, for example making sure the claim and payment screens follow one consistent style. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the chief product owner role?
o: Sasha Ellery, senior product manager.
Matteo Ricci, head of digital products.
Bronwen Hale, commercial director.
Nigel Ormsby, chair of the passenger panel.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The chief product owner represents the user community, owns the project backlog, keeps it aligned with the team product backlogs and sets priorities across teams (book Table 7.2). Matteo sets the direction for all digital channels and already works with users and the passenger panel.

n.0: Sasha has prioritized the app team's stories for years, which suits the product owner role for that one team; the CPO prioritizes across all teams (Table 7.2).
n.2: Bronwen received the mandate and holds the budget, which fits the project executive role, accountable for the project, rather than the user-side CPO role (Table 7.2).
n.3: Nigel is a valuable source of passenger feedback and influence, but he advises Larkspur from outside as a passenger; he does not set the direction of its digital channels or prioritize work across the teams (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Dominic Faraday, a board member, keeps asking for a Gantt chart and long written reports, and other senior managers outside IT are unsure how agile delivery fits Larkspur's governance. The board wants someone to coach its members, support Rhys Pengelly and remove organization-level blockers to agile working. Who in the scenario is BEST suited to the agile coach role?
o: Owen Thackeray, Scrum master for the app team.
Rhys Pengelly, project manager.
Matteo Ricci, head of digital products.
Priyanka Desai, agile lead in IT.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The agile coach mentors and facilitates across the organization, removes systemic blockers to agile adoption, such as a board member resisting dashboards, and supports the board, project assurance and the project manager with expert agile knowledge (book Table 7.2). Priyanka has coached departments and senior managers.

n.0: A Scrum master fits the team coach role, working closely with one or two teams on self-management, not coaching the board and removing organization-wide blockers (Table 7.2).
n.1: Rhys is new to agile delivery and is himself someone the agile coach should support; the PM role runs the project day to day (Table 7.2).
n.2: Matteo's user focus and authority over digital channels suit the chief product owner role, not mentoring leaders in agile ways of working (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, the university's quality team asks for evidence that each release of the Student Support Hub has been tested with real students, and the hub must work with screen readers. Jamal Hussain wants to settle what the users will accept and how that will be checked. Which practice addresses this concern, and why?
o: Quality, because it documents the users' requirements of the project products and how they will be met.
Progress, because it monitors actual achievements against those planned and forecasts the project's objectives.
Risk, because failing an accessibility check is an uncertain event that could affect the project's objectives.
Issues, because a release that has not been tested with students will deviate from the agreed baseline.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The quality practice documents the users' requirements of the project products and establishes how they will be met; it answers 'what is acceptable to users and how is it measured?' (book 9.1). Accessibility standards and testing with students are quality requirements and quality methods.

n.1: Progress compares actual achievements with plans and forecasts objectives; it does not define what users will accept or how products are checked (book 12.1).
n.2: A failed check is a possible threat, but defining acceptable quality and how it is verified is the quality practice, not the risk practice (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: Nothing has deviated yet; the issues practice controls changes to the baseline, while the quality team's request is about defining and meeting requirements (book 9.1, 11.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Jamal Hussain is drafting the benefits management approach. Professor Greer wants evidence of benefits, such as fewer paper forms printed and shorter waits for a first appointment, well before the project closes in month 14. How should the approach reflect this?
o: Plan a single benefits review after the project closes, because benefits cannot be realized until all three releases are live.
Treat the on-time go-live of each release as the benefit, because meeting each date shows that value has been delivered.
Leave benefits out of the approach until Release 3, because the early-warning feature is expected to bring the largest benefit to students.
Use the releases to deliver benefits early, and set out when and how each benefit will be measured and reviewed after each release.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases so that benefits can be delivered early, and it sets out how benefits will be measured, reviewed and by whom (book 6.3.2). Iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project, not only after closure (book 6.3.1).

n.0: Most benefit confirmation happens after closure, but iterative releases let some benefits be realized and measured during the project (book 6.3.1).
n.1: A go-live date is a time target and a release is an output; a benefit is a measurable improvement such as shorter waiting times (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.2: Release 3 may not be built at all, subject to ethics review; Releases 1 and 2 already bring measurable benefits that the approach should plan for (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain assembles the project brief for the Student Support Hub. Professor Greer wants the brief to show clearly how the agile approach will shape the project, as most university leaders are used to annual plans. Which content is MOST appropriate to add to the brief?
o: A fixed list of every feature in all three releases, so that the council can approve the whole scope before initiation starts.
The scope and quality areas that can flex by priority, the agile techniques chosen and their benefits, and how releases affect operations.
The web team's task plans for its first three sprints, so that the board can approve the work each developer will do on the hub in stage 2.
The design of the web team's online dashboard, so that the board can see how sprint progress will be reported to it each week.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project brief outlines the flexible areas of scope and quality criteria based on prioritization, the agile techniques and approaches chosen with their expected benefits, and, because of incremental delivery, more detail on the impact on operations and maintenance (book 6.3.2).

n.0: Fixing every feature in advance removes the flexibility on scope that agile relies on; Must haves are fixed but Should and Could haves flex (book 6.3.2, Table 3.1).
n.2: Task-level plans are produced by the team for the next iteration in managing product delivery, not by the board in starting up (book 8.3.2).
n.3: Team dashboards are co-created by each team in the project kickoff workshop; the board pulls information from the project dashboard (book Table 13.8, Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Professor Greer refines the project canvas. It shows one cost figure of £950,000 and one forecast of benefits, which assumes that all three releases, including the early-warning feature, will be delivered. The ethics committee has not yet reviewed the early-warning feature. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the budget is fixed, so a single cost figure and a single benefits forecast give the board all it needs.
Yes, because the canvas is a one-page summary, so alternative outcomes should be kept for the full business case.
No, because the canvas should show best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios, such as benefits without Release 3.
No, because benefits belong in the benefits management approach and should not be forecast on the project canvas.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: When the business case is tailored into a project canvas, the canvas should outline best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios (book Table 5.2). Release 3 depends on an ethics review, so the board needs to see whether the hub is still justified if it is not built.

n.0: A fixed budget does not remove uncertainty about benefits; the forecast depends on a feature that may never be approved (book Table 5.2).
n.1: The canvas is a one-page visual business justification, and in PRINCE2 Agile it is the business case; it should still outline the different scenarios (book 6.3.2, Table 5.2).
n.3: The project canvas includes expected, measurable benefits with tolerance; the benefits management approach covers how they will be managed and reviewed (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Early in stage 2, Northmere developers change two shared data fields without telling the web team, while web developers wait for approvals they do not need. Jamal Hussain wants to make clear, for each type of decision about the link to the records system, who decides and who must be involved, such as Rebecca Lyle or Dr Ruth Sefton. Which technique should he use?
o: A team skill matrix, showing each developer's strengths and gaps on the two team dashboards.
The commercial management approach, setting out the delivery model for Northmere's work.
A delegation matrix, showing for each decision area who decides and who is involved.
A user story map, showing the order in which the integration stories will be delivered.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: A delegation matrix makes responsibilities and decision authority transparent: for each decision area it shows who decides and who is involved (book 7.4.3). Here both teams are unsure which decisions they can take.

n.0: A team skill matrix shows capabilities, strengths and gaps to assign people and plan training; it does not set decision authority (book 7.4.1).
n.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contract arrangements, such as the per-iteration payment, not who decides each technical question (book 7.3.2).
n.3: A story map breaks products into user stories and orders them; it does not make decision rights clear (book 8.3.2.4).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Jamal Hussain records how the people working on the hub will work together: the days when key people from the web team, Northmere and the wellbeing service meet in person, and the shared online boards that keep each team's work visible to the others. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure.
In the commercial management approach.
In the role descriptions for each team member.
In the quality management approach.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The project management team structure shows who is involved and how they work together, including working practices that reflect agile and the arrangements for co-located or remote teams, with the tools used for transparency and rich communication (book 7.3.2).

n.1: The commercial management approach covers procurement and the form of contract, such as Northmere's per-iteration payment, not day-to-day working arrangements (book 7.3.2).
n.2: Role descriptions set out each role's specific responsibilities; working practices and co-location arrangements sit in the team structure (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The quality management approach covers quality techniques, standards and responsibilities, including agile testing, not how teams meet and share their work (book 9.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During stage 2, Professor Greer and Peter Langley start emailing two web team developers directly with new tasks for the current sprint, including early work on the early-warning feature. The developers begin the work without telling Rebecca Lyle, the web team's product owner. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project executive is accountable for the project and can direct the work of any team member.
Yes, because self-managing developers may take on work from any senior stakeholder who supports the project.
No, because the project manager is the role that should assign each task to the individual developers.
No, because the product owner directs the team's work, so new requests should go through her and the product backlog.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the product owner is a version of the team manager and the only role with direct authority over the delivery team members; the project manager agrees work with the PO as sets of user stories (book 7.3.1). New work should reach the team through the PO's product backlog.

n.0: The executive is accountable for the project, but direct authority over delivery team members sits with the product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.1: Self-management works within the tolerances and work agreed through the product owner, not on requests from any senior stakeholder (book 7.3.1).
n.2: The project manager has direct authority over the product owner, not over individual developers; the PO directs the team (book 7.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: The Student Support Hub needs a chief product owner to represent its users, who include students and the wellbeing staff who will use the case view, to own the project backlog and to set priorities across the web team and the Northmere team. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the chief product owner role?
o: Rebecca Lyle, senior digital product manager.
Dr Kwame Mensah, director of student wellbeing.
Maya Kowalczyk, students' union vice-president for welfare.
Professor Alison Greer, pro vice-chancellor.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The CPO represents the user community, owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams (book Table 7.2). Kwame Mensah knows students' needs in detail and leads the wellbeing staff who will use the case view, so he can speak for both user groups.

n.0: Rebecca Lyle has managed the web team's backlog for two years, which suits the product owner role for that one team rather than representing users across teams (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Maya Kowalczyk represents students, but not the wellbeing staff who will also use the hub; she is better placed to help recruit and voice the student design panel (book Table 7.2, 4.2.2).
n.3: Professor Greer received the mandate and holds the budget, which fits the project executive role accountable for the project (book Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: The project board wants someone independent of the delivery teams and of the wellbeing service to monitor whether agile practices and governance checks are being followed, and to advise the board and Jamal Hussain on risks, exception reports and their impact on the project canvas. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the project assurance role?
o: Chloe Hartley, Scrum master for the web team.
Rebecca Lyle, senior digital product manager.
Daniel Ferreira, head of the web team.
Sinead Walsh, quality and enhancement manager.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, builds quality and governance checks into delivery, and advises the board and project manager on issues, risks, exception reports and impacts on the canvas (book Table 7.2). Sinead Walsh reviews services against standards and is independent of the wellbeing service and the teams.

n.0: Chloe Hartley works inside the web team as its Scrum master, which fits the team coach role; she is not independent of a delivery team (book Table 7.2).
n.1: Rebecca Lyle manages the web team's backlog and fits the product owner role, so she would be assuring her own team's work (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Daniel Ferreira heads the web team that builds the hub, so he is on the supplier side and not independent of the delivery teams (book Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: At the starting up workshop, Bill Rowntree says that no store should offer click and collect until its stock accuracy is at least 97%, because customers would otherwise arrive to find items missing. Patrick Dunne wants this requirement defined, together with how it will be measured in each store, by the practice designed for that purpose. Which practice should handle it, and why?
o: Risk, because it identifies, assesses and controls uncertain events, such as stock accuracy failing to improve, that would affect the project's objectives.
Progress, because it compares actual achievements in each store against those planned and controls any deviations that would cause an exception.
Business case, because it judges whether the investment in each store is and remains desirable, viable and achievable for Pinewick.
Quality, because it documents the users' requirements for the project's products and establishes the means by which they will be met.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The quality practice documents what users require of the project's products and sets up how those requirements will be met; it answers what is acceptable to users and how that is measured (book 9.1). A minimum stock accuracy of 97% before a store goes live is an acceptance requirement of that kind.

n.0: The chance that accuracy will not improve in time is a risk, but defining the 97% requirement and how it is measured is the job of the quality practice (book 9.1, 10.1).
n.1: Progress monitors achievement against plan and handles exceptions; it does not define what is acceptable to users (book 12.1).
n.2: The business case practice keeps the justification for the investment under review; it does not set the acceptance criteria a store must meet (book 6.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: In starting up a project, Gwen Tallowby leads the project canvas workshop. The finance director has said he will support the project if there is evidence that click and collect increases total sales, rather than moving existing sales from home delivery into stores. How should the benefits section of the project canvas reflect his concern?
o: List the click and collect service in all 85 stores as the main benefit, because it is the product the finance director is being asked to fund.
State a measurable benefit, such as the net rise in total sales at stores offering collection compared with similar stores, with a tolerance.
Record the number of reservations made through the website as the benefit, because each reservation represents an extra sale for Pinewick.
Leave the benefits section blank until after closure, because benefits are confirmed once the service has run through a full spring peak.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The benefits section of the project canvas sets out expected benefits that are measurable and have a tolerance (book 6.3.2). A benefit is a measurable improvement that the investing organization sees as an advantage, so a net increase in sales, measured against comparable stores, answers the finance director directly.

n.0: The service in 85 stores is the project's output, part of its scope; an output is not a benefit (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.2: Reservations could simply move sales from home delivery into stores, so counting them does not measure the net improvement the finance director asked about (book 6.3.2).
n.3: The canvas must show expected benefits now to justify the investment; benefits are confirmed later, but they must be defined from the start (book 6.3.1, 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Patrick Dunne drafts the benefits management approach. Release 1, live stock levels by store on the website, is due in month 3, long before the full service is live in all stores. Market research shows that a third of customers have travelled to a store and found an item out of stock. How should the benefits management approach treat Release 1?
o: Measure no benefits until Release 3 is complete, because the benefits of click and collect come from the full service operating in all 85 stores.
Treat Release 1 as an output for the e-commerce team to accept, because the benefits of each release are reported in the end project report.
Plan to measure early benefits from Release 1, such as fewer wasted trips to stores, because frequent releases are planned to deliver benefits early.
Plan to measure Release 1 benefits in the post-project benefits review, because benefits are realized once products are in use by customers after the project.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases so that benefits can be delivered early (book 6.3.2), and iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project rather than after it (book 6.3.1). Release 1 goes live in month 3 and addresses wasted trips, so its benefits can be measured from then on.

n.0: Waiting for the full service throws away the early benefits that frequent releases are planned to deliver (book 6.3.2).
n.1: The end project report compares performance with the PID; benefits are measured as set out in the benefits management approach, and Release 1 can start delivering them during the project (book 6.3.2, Table 12.1).
n.3: Release 1 is in live use from month 3, so its benefits can be measured during the project; leaving them to the post-project review loses early evidence (book 6.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: At the end of Stage 3, sales data from the 10 pilot stores show that about half of the collection orders came from customers who would otherwise have bought online for home delivery. Patrick Dunne updates the project canvas with the pilot results and a revised expected case, and asks the board to confirm that Release 3 is still justified before it authorizes Stage 4. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the business justification must remain valid throughout, so the canvas is updated with real results for the board to review at the stage boundary.
Yes, because the revised canvas allows Patrick to raise the budget for Stage 4 to pay for the extra marketing needed to attract new customers to stores.
No, because the budget and date cannot change, so the business case was settled when the board authorized the project and does not need revisiting.
No, because benefits are measured after the project closes, so the pilot results should be held back for the post-project benefits review.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Ensure continued business justification requires a valid justification throughout the project (book 5.2.1.1). At a stage boundary the board reviews the current stage and confirms continued business justification before approving the next stage (book 13.7.1). Updating the canvas with real pilot results gives the board the evidence it needs.

n.1: Cost has zero tolerance by default; the canvas is updated to test the justification, not to increase the budget (book Table 3.1).
n.2: Fixed time and cost do not remove the need to check justification; the board confirms it at every stage boundary (book 5.2.1.1, 13.7.1).
n.3: The pilot results are real evidence about viability, and checking viability at the stage boundary depends on them; some benefits can be realized during the project (book 6.3.1, 13.7.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Patrick Dunne and Elena Marsh agree how Tallis will work with the project. The new stock interface will be delivered in Tallis's quarterly releases, both parties will use an agreed Definition of Done for the interface, and Tallis will report its progress through the project dashboard. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure, because it describes who is involved in the project and how the teams and people work together.
In the commercial management approach, because it sets out how the supplier arrangement will support agile delivery and how progress is tracked.
In the role descriptions, because they describe the specific responsibilities that Elena Marsh and the Tallis developers have in the project.
In the risk register, because the dependency on Tallis's quarterly release cycle is the main uncertainty that could affect Release 1.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The commercial management approach makes sure procurement and contracts support agile product development, for example through an agreed Definition of Done, the delivery model, and guidelines for tracking and reporting (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3). The agreed working terms with Tallis belong there.

n.0: The project management team structure covers who is involved, their relationships and arrangements such as co-location; the terms of the supplier arrangement belong in the commercial management approach (book 7.3.2).
n.2: Role descriptions set out the responsibilities of roles in the project management team; they do not hold the terms on which a supplier delivers (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The dependency may also be logged as a risk, but the agreed way of working with the supplier is a commercial arrangement, not a risk record (book 7.3.2, 10.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: At the start of Stage 3, the store operations team and Patrick Dunne disagree about who should decide matters such as the order in which the pilot stores are prepared, changes to collection-point signage and the timing of staff training sessions. Sophie Draper says her team keeps waiting for approvals it may not need. Which technique should Patrick use with the team?
o: A team skill matrix, completed with the team, showing which members have the skills needed to make each type of decision about the pilot stores.
A product flow diagram, showing the order in which pilot stores, signage and training must be completed and who signs off each step.
A responsibility chart drawn up by Patrick and Bill Rowntree and issued to the team, setting out which decisions each member may take.
Delegation poker, so that Patrick and the team agree the level of delegation for each decision area and record it in a delegation matrix.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Delegation poker is a collaborative technique for defining how decisions are made within teams (book 7.4.2), and a delegation matrix makes responsibilities and decision authority transparent, showing who decides and who is involved for each decision area (book 7.4.3). The dispute is about decision rights, so these techniques address it.

n.0: A team skill matrix shows capabilities, strengths and gaps; it does not settle who has authority to decide (book 7.4.1).
n.1: A product flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products, not who makes which decisions (book 8.4.2).
n.2: A chart imposed by managers does not involve the team; delegation poker agrees decision levels collaboratively, which supports self-management (book 7.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Patrick Dunne proposes that Fran Okonedo, the e-commerce team's Scrum master, also act as team coach for the store operations team. Fran has coached a Kanban team before and will facilitate the store team's workshops and help it manage itself, while Sophie Draper looks after the team's work and backlog. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the team coach is accountable for delivering the work packages of both teams, which keeps the two teams' work aligned.
Yes, because a team coach works closely with one or two teams, helping them to self-manage and facilitating their workshops.
No, because each delivery team must have its own dedicated team coach, so the store operations team needs a separate coach.
No, because coaching a team that is new to agile is the agile coach's role, so Nikhil Rao should coach the store operations team.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: A team coach works closely with one or two specific teams, helping them self-manage, facilitating team workshops and coaching agile practices; a Scrum master fits this role (book Table 7.2, 7.3). Coaching both teams is within that span, and the team's work stays with its own lead.

n.0: Delivering allocated work within agreed tolerances is the product owner's responsibility, not the team coach's (book Table 7.2).
n.2: The book says a team coach can work with one or two teams, so a coach shared by two teams is acceptable (book 7.3, Figure 7.2).
n.3: The agile coach works across the organization on systemic blockers and supports leaders; team-level coaching is the team coach's role (book Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Pinewick's board asks Patrick Dunne to propose who should take the project executive role. The person must be accountable for the project, approve the tolerances within which the teams make agile decisions, and act as a role model for agile adoption across the business. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the project executive role?
o: Marcus Lindell, because as head of e-commerce he owns the website and app roadmap and represents online customers' needs.
George Ahmed, because as head of internal audit he can give the board independent assurance that the project is controlled.
Gwen Tallowby, because she received the mandate and is accountable to the board for the store performance the project must improve.
Bill Rowntree, because as head of store operations he manages the area managers and store standards that the roll-out will change.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The project executive is accountable for the project and its strategic alignment, approves the tolerances for agile decision-making and acts as a role model for agile adoption (book Table 7.2). Gwen was given the mandate by the board and answers to it for store performance, which the project exists to improve, so she is the natural person to hold that accountability.

n.0: Marcus represents online customers' needs and owns the roadmap, which suits a user-facing role such as chief product owner rather than overall accountability (book Table 7.2).
n.1: George's independent audit view suits a project assurance contribution, which checks how the project is run on the board's behalf; he was not given the mandate and is not accountable for the project's outcome (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Bill speaks for store operations, an important user and stakeholder group, but he was not given the mandate or the accountability for the project's success (book Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Patrick Dunne needs a product owner for the e-commerce team. The person will own the team's product backlog, keep it aligned with the project backlog and agree sets of user stories with Patrick as work packages. Using the scenario's people list, who is BEST suited to the product owner role for the e-commerce team?
o: Anita Shah, because she already manages the e-commerce team's backlog and works day to day with the team that will build the features.
Fran Okonedo, because as the team's Scrum master she runs its sprint events and knows how the team plans and estimates its work.
Marcus Lindell, because he owns the roadmap for the website and app and represents online customers' needs across Pinewick.
Nikhil Rao, because he helped the e-commerce team adopt agile and understands how it turns customer needs into new features.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The product owner is a version of the team manager role: they own one team's product backlog, keep it aligned with the project backlog, prepare user stories and agree work package descriptions with the project manager (book Table 7.2). Anita already manages the e-commerce team's backlog.

n.1: A Scrum master fits the team coach role, which helps the team self-manage and facilitates its workshops (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Marcus owns the roadmap across channels and represents customers, which fits the chief product owner role, prioritizing across teams, rather than one team's backlog (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Nikhil is an agile coach, a role that works across the organization on systemic blockers rather than owning a team's backlog (book Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Early in stage 2, Sarah Pennington asks Simon Archer how the board will see, month by month, whether the work completed so far puts Care Online on course to finish by the grant deadline, and what will happen if it starts to look as though the agreed tolerances will be exceeded. Which practice is designed to answer Sarah's question?
o: Plans, because it defines the products to be delivered and the means of delivering them, with estimates of when and at what cost.
Risk, because it identifies, assesses and controls the uncertain events that could stop the project from meeting its grant deadline and budget.
Progress, because it compares actual achievement with the plan, forecasts the objectives and controls deviations causing an exception.
Issues, because it collects and assesses deviations from what was agreed and controls any changes to the project's baseline.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The progress practice establishes mechanisms to monitor and compare actual achievements against those planned, to forecast the project's objectives and continued viability, and to control any deviation that would cause an exception (book 12.1).

n.0: Plans set out what will be delivered and estimate when and how much; comparing actual work with the plan and forecasting is the progress practice (book 8.1, 12.1).
n.1: Risk handles uncertain events; Sarah wants a regular comparison of actual with planned work and a forecast, which is progress (book 10.1, 12.1).
n.3: Issues controls changes to the baseline; controlling deviations that would cause an exception belongs to progress (book 11.1, 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: At the project canvas workshop, the group lists possible entries for the benefits section of the Care Online project canvas: the online carers' self-assessment form; the community support directory; text message updates for people tracking their case; and a fall in the average wait for a first assessment from eight weeks to four. Which entry should be recorded as a benefit, and why?
o: The online carers' self-assessment, because it is the minimum the council must deliver to respond to the inspection findings.
The community support directory, because carers and the public will start using it as soon as Release 1 goes live in month four.
Text message updates, because a feature that people use to track their case counts as a benefit once it has been delivered.
The fall in the average wait for a first assessment, because it is a measurable improvement that the council sees as an advantage.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome that the investing organization sees as an advantage; an output such as a form, directory or feature is never a benefit in itself (Glossary, book 6.3.2). The canvas benefits section holds expected, measurable benefits with their tolerance.

n.0: The carers' self-assessment is an output, even though it is the minimum to deliver; it would be identified as the MVP, not as a benefit (Glossary, book 6.3.2).
n.1: The directory is an output; its use may lead to benefits, but the directory itself is not a measurable improvement (Glossary).
n.2: A delivered feature is an output; any benefit would be the measurable improvement that the feature leads to (Glossary, book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: The grant conditions require the council to report outcomes to the government department every quarter, and Sarah Pennington wants some benefits to be visible well before month twelve. During initiation, Simon Archer is preparing the benefits management approach for Care Online. What should it include?
o: Plans for frequent releases so that benefits start early, with measures, tolerances and reviews of those benefits from Release 1 onwards.
A single measurement of benefits in a post-project review after month twelve, since benefits are confirmed after the project closes.
A count of features delivered each quarter as the outcome measure, since the features are what the grant is paying for.
A cross-reference to the project canvas in place of its own content, as the canvas already lists the expected benefits and tolerances.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The benefits management approach defines the actions and reviews for realizing and measuring benefits. In agile, frequent releases are planned so that benefits arrive early, and some benefits can be confirmed during the project rather than all after closure (book 6.3.1, 6.3.2).

n.1: Benefits are mostly confirmed after closure, but iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project, which is what the grant and Sarah need (book 6.3.1).
n.2: Features are outputs, not outcomes or benefits; the measures should track the improvements the features bring (Glossary, book 6.3.2).
n.3: The canvas states the expected benefits, but the benefits management approach is still needed to set out how they will be realized, measured and reviewed (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Simon Archer points out that the £1.1 million grant has already been awarded and the cabinet has approved the spend. He proposes that the Care Online project canvas be finalized at the end of initiation and not reviewed again, so that the board can concentrate on delivery. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the investment decision was made when the grant was awarded, so the board's remaining role is to oversee delivery of the releases.
