Yes, because the project canvas is a one-page artifact that replaces the detailed business case and so needs little upkeep.
No, because a publicly funded project should replace the project canvas with a full written business case before delivery starts.
No, because the justification must stay valid throughout, so the canvas should be checked and updated as releases deliver and learning grows.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Ensure continued business justification requires the project to remain desirable, viable and achievable throughout its life. In PRINCE2 Agile the project canvas is the business case, and it should be checked and maintained, for example at stage boundaries when the board confirms continued justification (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1, 13.7.1).

n.0: Approved funding does not remove the need to keep checking that the project is still worthwhile; every project needs continued justification (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).
n.1: The canvas is a suitable replacement for the business case, but being concise does not exempt it from being checked and kept up to date (book 6.3.2).
n.2: The verdict is right, but the project canvas is a suitable business case for an agile project; the fault is freezing it, not its format (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During initiation, Simon Archer and Martin Sallis discuss how Abacus will work on the case system interface. Abacus normally quotes for each fixed-price change request, which takes about six weeks. They agree instead on a fixed Abacus team and cost for each two-week sprint, a shared Definition of Done, and tolerances around the Release 2 interface. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the project management team structure, because it describes who is involved in the project and how the people will work together.
In the commercial management approach, because it sets out procurement and contract arrangements that support agile product development.
In the role descriptions, because Martin Sallis's responsibilities as the supplier's account manager need to be defined for the project.
In the risk register, because the six-week quoting time is a threat to the Release 2 date that needs a planned response.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The commercial management approach sets out how procurement and contracts will support agile delivery, for example fixed delivery teams and costs per iteration, the MVP and tolerances, and an agreed Definition of Done (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: The team structure covers who is involved, their relationships and working arrangements such as co-location; contract form and payment per sprint belong in the commercial management approach (Table 7.3).
n.2: Role descriptions set out project roles and their responsibilities, not the contract terms under which a supplier works (Table 7.3).
n.3: The old quoting time might have been recorded as a risk, but the agreed contract arrangements themselves belong in the commercial management approach (Table 7.3, Table 10.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Care Online has two delivery teams: the council's digital team and the Abacus team building the case system interface. Simon Archer is drafting the project management team structure and wants it to be clear who decides priorities when the two teams' work competes for the same release. Which structure follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: A project manager for each team, both reporting to the board, with the chief product owner deciding priorities within each team's backlog.
One project manager who prioritizes the user stories across both teams' backlogs, supported by a team coach working in each team.
One project manager; a product owner per team who owns its backlog; and a chief product owner setting priorities across both teams.
One product owner covering both teams' backlogs, who also represents the user community on the board in place of a chief product owner.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: With several teams there is one project manager, a product owner for each team (a version of the team manager role, owning that team's product backlog), and a chief product owner who represents the users and sets priorities across the teams (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

n.0: A multi-team project still has one project manager, and each team's product backlog is owned by its product owner rather than the CPO (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).
n.1: Setting priorities across teams is the chief product owner's job, not the project manager's (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).
n.3: The product owner is a team-level role; representing the user community and prioritizing across teams belong to the chief product owner (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Social workers have high caseloads and work across a rural county. During initiation, Simon Archer records in the project management team structure that practitioners will join the digital team remotely for fixed two-hour slots in each sprint, using video calls and a shared online team dashboard, with a co-located session at the start of each release. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the team structure should record co-location and remote arrangements, with tools for transparency and rich communication.
Yes, because practitioners are not members of the delivery team, so their involvement can be arranged outside the project's governance.
No, because practitioners should be co-located with the digital team for every sprint if agile ways of working are to succeed.
No, because remote working arrangements belong in the communication management approach rather than in the team structure.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The project management team structure records who is involved and how they work together, including arrangements for co-located or remote teams and the agile techniques and tools that keep work transparent and communication rich (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3). Planned remote slots, a shared dashboard and periodic co-location suit busy practitioners.

n.1: The practitioners take part in the team's research and testing, so their involvement sits within the project's structure; this reason does not explain why the arrangement is sound (book 7.3.1, Table 7.3).
n.2: Mandating co-location is not the effective answer for people spread across a county; planned remote and hybrid arrangements are recognized (book 4.3.3, Table 7.3).
n.3: Co-location and remote arrangements are part of the project management team structure in Table 7.3; the communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication (book 4.4).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Care Online needs a project executive who will be accountable for the project and for the grant that funds it, keep it aligned with the council's strategy, and approve the tolerances within which the teams make agile decisions. Using the Additional information (People), which person is BEST suited to the project executive role?
o: Joan Whitaker, because she chairs the department's programme board and is used to approving detailed plans in advance.
Sarah Pennington, because she received the mandate for Care Online and is accountable for the government grant that funds it.
Helen Crowther, because she manages the digital team that will build most of the online service and knows its capacity.
Simon Archer, because he is an experienced project manager from the corporate project office and knows PRINCE2 7 well.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The project executive is accountable for the project, keeps it aligned with strategy and approves the tolerances for agile decision-making (Table 7.2, Table B.1). Sarah received the mandate and is accountable for the grant, so she holds the business accountability the role needs.

n.0: Joan chairs a departmental programme board, but she is not described as accountable for this project or the grant, and a liking for detailed advance plans is no reason to hold the role (Table 7.2).
n.2: Helen manages the people who will build the service, which points to the supplier side rather than to accountability for the investment (Table 7.2).
n.3: Simon is the project manager, who runs the project day to day for the board within tolerances; the executive role sits above him (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: The Care Online digital team needs a team coach who will work closely with it, help it manage itself, facilitate its team workshops, improve communication and help it write user stories. Using the Additional information (People), which person is BEST suited to the team coach role for the digital team?
o: Gita Bhatt, because she has led agile adoption in two other councils and will support the council's leaders and teams for six months.
Helen Crowther, because as head of customer and digital services she line manages the digital team and can direct its work.
Amy Fletcher, because she has led research with carers and older people and can make sure the team builds what users need.
Oliver Grant, because as the digital team's delivery manager he already runs its sprint planning sessions and retrospectives.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The team coach works closely with one or two teams, helps them self-manage, facilitates team workshops such as planning and retrospectives, and coaches agile practice; a Scrum master fits this role (Table 7.2, Table B.1). Oliver already runs the digital team's sprint planning and retrospectives.

n.0: Gita's background fits the agile coach role, which works across the organization on systemic blockers rather than inside one team (Table 7.2).
n.1: Line managing and directing the team's work does not fit a role whose purpose is to help the team manage itself (Table 7.2).
n.2: Amy's research skills suit work on user needs and testing, but she is not described as facilitating the team's workshops or ways of working (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: At the project canvas workshop, Stuart Bell asks how the engineers will know what the dashboard must do before they accept it, and how that will be measured on the shop floor. Andrea Lucas says this concern is handled by one of the PRINCE2 Agile practices. Which practice, and why?
o: Quality, because it documents the users' requirements of the project's products and sets out how they will be met and checked.
Plans, because it defines the products to be delivered, who will build them and how, and estimates when and at what cost.
Progress, because it compares what has been achieved with what was planned and forecasts whether objectives will be met.
Business case, because it judges whether the dashboard is and remains desirable, viable and achievable for the business.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The quality practice documents the users' requirements of the project products and establishes how they will be met; it answers what is acceptable to users and how that is measured (book 9.1). Stuart's question is about acceptance criteria and how they are checked.

n.1: Plans set out what is delivered, by whom, how, when and at what cost; they do not define what users will accept (book 8.1, 9.1).
n.2: Progress monitors actual achievement against plan and forecasts; it does not define acceptance criteria (book 12.1).
n.3: The business case practice judges whether the investment stays worthwhile; users' acceptance criteria belong to quality (book 6.1, 9.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: In initiation, Graham Doyle is refining the project canvas with Andrea Lucas. He wants the benefits section to show what Draycott will gain, with a tolerance, so that the board can later judge whether the investment paid off. Which entry belongs in the benefits section of the project canvas?
o: Sensors fitted to all 60 machining centres across both factories by the end of month 12.
A predictive maintenance dashboard in daily use by all 22 maintenance engineers across both factories after Release 3.
Weekly improvements to the dashboard released by the software team once Release 1 is live.
A measured fall in unplanned breakdown costs from last year's £1.8 million, within an agreed tolerance.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome that the investing organization sees as an advantage. The project canvas records expected, measurable benefits with a tolerance (Glossary, book 6.3.2). Lower breakdown costs are such an improvement.

n.0: Fitted sensors are an output (a specialist product), not a benefit; outputs belong in the scope section (Glossary, book 6.3.2).
n.1: A dashboard in use is an outcome built on outputs; the benefit is the measurable improvement it brings, such as lower breakdown costs (Glossary).
n.2: Weekly releases are a way of delivering, not a measurable improvement for the business (Glossary, book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Andrea Lucas is drafting the benefits management approach in initiation. Release 1 goes live at month 4 on ten Factory A machines, and Ruth Kenyon expects fewer breakdowns on those machines soon afterwards. Graham Doyle suggests that benefits should not be measured until after the project closes at month 12. What should the benefits management approach do?
o: Leave all benefit measurement until after closure, as benefits are confirmed once the project has ended.
Plan measurement of breakdown costs from Release 1 onwards, with tolerances and responsibilities, so early benefits are tracked.
Record the expected benefits in the release map, as the release map serves as both the project plan and the stage plan.
Measure benefits by counting the user stories delivered in each sprint, as these show the value the software and trial teams have added.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases to enable early delivery of benefits, and sets out measurement and tolerance guidance and responsibilities (book 6.3.2). Confirming benefits happens mostly after closure, but iterative releases can realize some during the project.

n.0: Some benefits can be realized during the project through iterative releases; the approach should plan to measure them from Release 1 (book 6.3.1, 6.3.2).
n.2: The release map shows releases, timing and features; how benefits will be measured and reviewed belongs in the benefits management approach (book 8.3.2, 6.3.2).
n.3: User stories delivered are outputs, not benefits; benefits are measurable improvements such as reduced breakdown costs (Glossary).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: After the PID is approved, Graham Doyle tells Andrea Lucas that because the budget and end date are fixed, the project canvas will not be revisited until closure, when benefits will be checked. Release 1 is due at month 4, and Graham has said it is the minimum needed to show whether continuing is justified. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because time and cost have zero tolerance, so the cost side of the canvas cannot change during the project.
Yes, because benefits are mostly confirmed after closure, once the dashboard has been in use for some time.
No, because justification must stay valid throughout, so the canvas should be checked as Release 1 shows its value.
No, because once the PID is approved the project canvas should be replaced by a full written business case.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Ensure continued business justification requires the justification to remain valid throughout the life cycle (book 5.2.1.1). Release 1 is the stated minimum for continuing, so the canvas must be checked against the evidence it produces, not left until closure.

n.0: Zero tolerance on time and cost does not keep the justification valid; benefits, risks and value can all change and must be reviewed (book 5.2.1.1).
n.1: Benefits are largely confirmed after closure, but the justification still has to be checked throughout, especially at the Release 1 decision point (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).
n.3: The project canvas is a suitable replacement for the business case and is refined, not swapped for a written document, as the project goes on (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: In initiation, Andrea Lucas and Dev Patel agree how Senticore's fixed-price contract will support agile delivery: sensors will be fitted release by release, the minimum viable product is the ten Release 1 machines, and a fitting is not complete until it meets an agreed Definition of Done. Where should these arrangements be recorded?
o: In the commercial management approach, as it covers how procurement and the contract support agile delivery.
In the project management team structure, as it shows how Senticore's fitters work with the other teams.
In the role descriptions, as they set out the responsibilities Dev Patel holds in the project management team.
In the quality register, as it records the planned and completed quality activities for each sensor fitting.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The commercial management approach makes sure procurement and the form of contract support agile product development, for example by defining the MVP and tolerances, an agreed Definition of Done and how the supplier tracks and reports (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.1: The project management team structure shows who is involved, their relationships and working arrangements such as co-location, not contract terms (Table 7.3).
n.2: Role descriptions set out each role's responsibilities; the terms of Senticore's contract belong in the commercial management approach (Table 7.3).
n.3: The quality register records individual quality activities and their results; it does not hold contractual arrangements (Table 9.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: During Stage 2, the software team and the engineers' trial team disagree about which dashboard features matter most. Leanne Park wants a data export that would help the software team's testing, while the engineers want a simpler alert screen first. Andrea Lucas is asked how priorities across the teams should be set. Which arrangement follows the organization practice?
o: Andrea decides the priorities herself, because the project manager has direct authority over every member of each team.
Leanne decides, because as the software team's product owner she owns the backlog that the dashboard features come from.
The chief product owner sets priorities across the teams, and each team's product owner orders its own backlog to match.
Each team keeps its own priorities, and the team coach resolves conflicting features at the next team retrospective.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: With several teams, PRINCE2 Agile has one chief product owner who represents the users and sets priorities across teams, while each team's product owner owns that team's product backlog and keeps it aligned with the project backlog (book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

n.0: The project manager has direct authority over the product owners, not over delivery team members, and setting user priorities is the CPO's job (book 7.3.1).
n.1: A product owner owns one team's backlog but does not prioritize across teams; that is the chief product owner (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).
n.3: The team coach helps a team self-manage and facilitates its workshops; cross-team priorities are set by the chief product owner (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Two weeks before Release 1, Andrea Lucas is worried about the dashboard. She starts holding her own morning meeting with the software developers, telling each one which tasks to work on that day, and informs Leanne Park afterwards. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager runs the project day to day on behalf of the board within the agreed tolerances.
Yes, because close to a release date the project manager should take direct control of the delivery team's work.
No, because daily task allocation for the software team should be carried out by Tomasz Zielinski as team coach.
No, because the product owner directs the delivery team, and the project manager agrees the work with the product owner.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, and the product owner is the only role with direct authority over delivery team members. The PM and PO agree work as sets of user stories within tolerances (book 7.3.1).

n.0: The PM does run the project day to day, but through work packages agreed with the product owner, not by directing developers (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).
n.1: Nothing in PRINCE2 Agile gives the PM direct control of team members near a release; authority runs through the product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.2: The team coach helps the team self-manage and facilitates workshops; it is not a task-allocating role (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Graham Doyle needs to appoint a chief product owner for Smart Maintenance. The role must represent the engineers and operators who will use the dashboard in both factories, own the project backlog and set priorities across all three teams. Using the people list, who is BEST suited to this role?
o: Leanne Park, the software team lead, who manages the software team's backlog and works with engineers on requirements.
Ruth Kenyon, the head of maintenance, who leads the engineers in both factories and will own the dashboard afterwards.
Stuart Bell, the senior maintenance engineer at Factory A, who has 30 years' experience and is respected by colleagues.
Graham Doyle, the operations director, who received the mandate and holds the capital budget for both factories.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The chief product owner represents the user community, owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams (Table 7.2). Ruth leads the 22 engineers across both factories and will own the dashboard after the project, so she speaks for all its users.

n.0: Leanne manages one team's backlog, which fits the product owner role for the software team, not a role prioritizing across all teams (Table 7.2).
n.2: Stuart is respected but works at Factory A only and has no authority over the engineers at Factory B; he suits a key influencer role (book 4.2.2).
n.3: Graham received the mandate and holds the budget, which fits the project executive, who is accountable for the project rather than representing users (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: The board wants someone to monitor, independently of Andrea Lucas and the teams, whether Smart Maintenance follows PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, and to build governance and quality checks into each release. Using the people list, who is BEST suited to the project assurance role?
o: Mei Chen, the quality manager, who is responsible for the aerospace quality system and approves maintenance changes.
Tomasz Zielinski, the Scrum master, who knows agile practices well and already works closely with the software team.
Colin Ashby, the production manager for Factory A, who plans the machine schedules and knows the factory well.
Robert Kale, the quality director, who is independent of operations and reports directly to the board.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, integrates quality and governance checks into iterative delivery and advises the board and PM (Table 7.2). Robert already carries out independent checks of major projects for the board and is independent of operations.

n.0: Mei runs the aerospace quality system that approves the project's maintenance changes, so she is part of the work being checked and is not described as independent of operations (Table 7.2).
n.1: Tomasz works inside the software team, which fits the team coach role; assurance needs someone independent of the teams (Table 7.2).
n.2: Colin is a stakeholder whose machines are affected and who reports within operations; he is not independent of the project (Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Deborah Kiely asks how the project will decide whether the new online reporting form is acceptable to older tenants and to tenants whose first language is not English, and how that will be measured before the form goes live across all homes. Which practice is designed to answer this question, and why?
o: Business case, because it judges whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable for the association.
Quality, because it documents what users require of the project's products and establishes how those requirements will be met.
Progress, because it compares what has actually been achieved with what was planned and forecasts the project's objectives.
Plans, because it defines which products are needed and who will produce them, how, where, when and at what cost.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The quality practice documents the users' requirements of the project products and establishes the means by which they will be met; it answers what is acceptable to users and how that is measured (book 9.1, 9.3.1).

n.0: The business case practice supports investment decisions; it does not set or check what users will accept from a product (book 6.1).
n.2: Progress tracks achievement against plans and controls exceptions; defining and measuring acceptability to users is quality (book 12.1, 9.1).
n.3: Plans set out what is to be delivered and by what means; the acceptance criteria users require and how they are checked belong to quality (book 8.1, 9.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: In the project initiation workshop, the teams plan to write personas for the new repairs service. Deborah Kiely suggests basing them on the association's tenant profile data, with one persona for each age band, ethnic group and household type, which would give 14 personas. How should the personas be developed?
o: Write up to five fictional personas based on tenants' needs, such as reporting by phone, in a cross-functional workshop with the team.
Use the 14 profiles, because personas built on age, ethnic group and household type make sure every group of tenants is represented.
Base each persona on a real member of the tenants' panel, using their name and history, so that the personas are accurate.
Ask Amara Okeke to write the personas from the tenant satisfaction and repairs data on her own, so that they are evidence-based and quick to produce.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Personas help articulate specific benefits for users. They should be written in a cross-functional workshop with team members, kept fictional, based on user needs rather than demographics, and limited to no more than five for pilots or new products unless agile maturity is high (book 6.4.1).

n.1: Demographics no longer predict shared needs, and 14 personas exceeds the suggested maximum of five for a new service at low agile maturity (book 6.4.1).
n.2: Personas should be fictional; abstraction widens innovation and avoids designing for a few individuals (book 6.4.1).
n.3: Personas are written collaboratively in a cross-functional workshop with team members, not by one analyst (book 6.4.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Margaret Oyelaran is leading the development of the project canvas for Repairs Reimagined. She wants it to show the board's minimum expectation of a measurable fall in second visits, which currently affect 30% of repairs. Where and how should this be shown in the project canvas?
o: In the scope section, as an epic for Release 2 that the diagnosis guide and parts list will deliver.
In the major risks section, as a threat that second visits may not fall if engineers do not use the parts list.
In the costs section, as the saving the board expects to use to fund Release 3 and the AI assistant pilot.
In the benefits section, as an expected, measurable benefit with its current baseline of 30% and a tolerance.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The project canvas includes a benefits element: expected, measurable benefits with tolerance (book 6.3.2, Table 6.1). A fall in second visits is a measurable improvement the association expects, so it is a benefit, with the minimum the board expects reflected in its tolerance.

n.0: Scope lists the project product and its epics, which are outputs; the fall in second visits is the measurable improvement those outputs should bring (book 6.3.2, Glossary).
n.1: That threat could be a major risk, but the board's expected improvement itself is a benefit to be measured (book 6.3.2).
n.2: The costs element records the estimated costs of the project; the expected fall in second visits is a benefit (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Amara Okeke and Sally Greaves draft the benefits management approach. To keep the effort small, they plan to measure repair satisfaction and second visits once, at a benefits review six months after the project closes, even though Release 1 goes live on the pilot estate in month 4 and Release 2 in month 8. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because benefits are confirmed mainly after closure, when the products are in operational use and their effects can be measured.
Yes, because the benefits management approach is agreed in initiation and does not need to change while the releases are delivered.
No, because frequent releases are planned so that some benefits arrive early, and reviews should measure them as each release goes live.
No, because benefits should be measured by the project executive in person, rather than by an analyst or the project manager.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases to enable early delivery of benefits, and iterative releases can realize some benefits during the project (book 6.3.1, 6.3.2). With releases in months 4 and 8, reviews should measure satisfaction and second visits as each release goes live, so the board can see whether the minimum improvement is on track.

n.0: Confirming benefits is mostly after closure, but iterative releases realize some benefits during the project; a single post-project review misses the early evidence (book 6.3.1).
n.1: The approach is agreed in initiation, but that does not justify ignoring benefits that the releases deliver during the project (book 6.3.2).
n.3: The benefits management approach sets out responsibilities for measurement; nothing requires the executive to measure benefits in person, so this is not why the plan is weak (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Ian Thursby and Frank Tolley are agreeing how Coastline will take part in the project. They want to record how the pay-per-job contract will support trialling new ways of working in short iterations, the Definition of Done for new engineer procedures, and how Coastline will track and report its part of the work. In which management product should this be recorded?
o: The project management team structure.
The role descriptions.
The commercial management approach.
The benefits management approach.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The commercial management approach sets out how procurement and contracts will support agile product development, for example costs per iteration, the MVP and tolerances, an agreed Definition of Done and how the supplier tracks and reports (book 7.3.2, Table 7.3).

n.0: The team structure shows who is involved, their relationships and working arrangements such as co-location; contract terms with Coastline go in the commercial management approach (book 7.3.2).
n.1: Role descriptions set out each project role's responsibilities; they do not hold the contractual arrangements with a supplier (book 7.3.2).
n.3: The benefits management approach covers how benefits are measured and reviewed, not how the supplier contract supports iterative work (book 6.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: At the project kickoff workshop, the service design team needs to see who can facilitate tenant testing, who can write call scripts and who understands repair diagnosis, and where training is needed before Release 2. Which technique should the team use, and where should the result be shown?
o: A team skill matrix, completed by the project manager and shown on the project dashboard.
A team skill matrix, completed together by the team and shown on the team dashboard.
A delegation matrix, completed by the team and shown in the role descriptions.
Delegation poker, played by the team and recorded in its team plan.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The team skill matrix gives an overview of capabilities, strengths, gaps and development areas, helping assign people and identify training needs. It is completed collaboratively in the project kickoff workshop and, for delivery teams, shown on the team dashboard (book 7.4.1, Table 13.8).

n.0: The matrix is completed collaboratively by the team, and a delivery team's matrix belongs on its team dashboard, not the board-level project dashboard (book 7.4.1).
n.2: A delegation matrix shows who decides what; it does not map skills, gaps and training needs (book 7.4.3).
n.3: Delegation poker defines decision-making levels within a team; mapping skills and training needs is the team skill matrix (book 7.4.2, 7.4.1).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Halfway through Stage 2, Ian Thursby is unhappy with the service design team's pace. Each Monday he emails individual team members the tasks he wants them to complete that week, bypassing Raj Malhotra, the team's product owner, who agrees the team's work with the project manager. Is this an appropriate application of the organization practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the repairs director manages the in-house repairs team and can direct the staff who joined from that team.
Yes, because a senior manager may step in to direct the work when a team's pace threatens the stage's tolerances.
No, because the chief product owner should assign each member's tasks, as it is the role that sets the priorities across all the teams.
No, because the product owner holds direct authority over the team, and work reaches it as user stories agreed with the project manager.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: In the PRINCE2 Agile structure the project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, and the product owner is the only role with direct authority over delivery team members; the PM and PO agree work as sets of user stories (book 7.3.1). A director emailing tasks to individuals bypasses this structure and undermines self-management.

n.0: Line management outside the project does not give Ian authority over the delivery team; within the project, work reaches the team through its product owner (book 7.3.1).
n.1: If tolerances are threatened, the project manager deals with it and escalates to the board if needed; a director does not take over the team's work (book 7.3.1, Table 12.1).
n.2: The CPO prioritizes the project backlog across teams; it does not assign individual tasks, and authority over team members sits with the product owner (book 7.3.1, Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: Repairs Reimagined needs a chief product owner who will represent tenants as the main user community, own the project backlog and set priorities across the service design and digital teams. Which person in the scenario is BEST suited to the chief product owner role?
o: Deborah Kiely, because she works closely with the tenants' panel and knows tenants' needs well.
Raj Malhotra, because he facilitates the service design team's iterations and prioritizes its work with tenants.
Ellen Price, because she leads the digital team that configures the tenant portal.
Margaret Oyelaran, because she received the mandate and is accountable for performance.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: The CPO represents the user community, owns and refines the project backlog with user input and sets priorities across teams (book Table 7.2). As head of tenant engagement, Deborah works closely with the tenants' panel and understands tenants' needs, and her remit spans both teams.

n.1: Prioritizing one team's work with users is the product owner's role; the CPO sets priorities across all teams (book Table 7.2).
n.2: Ellen leads the digital team's technical work; she does not represent tenants across the whole project (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Accountability for the project and receiving the mandate fit the project executive; the CPO represents users and owns the project backlog (book Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.q: The board wants someone independent of the project manager to check that the project follows PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, to build governance checks into the iterative delivery, and to advise the board on exception reports and risks. Which person in the scenario is BEST suited to the project assurance role?
o: Amara Okeke, because as data and insight analyst she measures the service's performance and tenant satisfaction.
Sally Greaves, because as project manager she makes sure risks are identified, assessed and controlled.
Dr Laura Benn, because her governance and assurance role lets her monitor independently and advise the board.
Ian Thursby, because as repairs director he manages the Coastline contract and the in-house repairs team.
Agile Practitioner: Business Case & Orga.w: Project assurance monitors adherence to PRINCE2 Agile principles and agile practices, integrates quality and governance checks into iterative delivery, and advises the board and PM on issues, risks and exception reports (book Table 7.2). Laura's governance and assurance role, reporting to the audit and risk committee, makes her independent of the PM.

n.0: Measuring service performance suits testing or benefits measurement; it is not independent oversight of governance and adherence to the method (book Table 7.2).
n.1: The board wants someone independent of the project manager; Sally cannot assure her own management of the project (book Table 7.2).
n.3: Ian is a senior business manager with a strong interest in the contract outcome, not an independent governance specialist (book Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In stage 2, Rhys Pengelly needs to forecast which Release 1 stories the app team can complete by the end of month four. The app team's velocity has ranged from 18 to 34 story points per sprint over its last six sprints, while the Coinbridge team reports a steady 40 points per sprint. How should Rhys forecast the app team's progress?
o: Use the Coinbridge team's steady 40 points per sprint, as it is the more reliable figure and story points are shared across teams.
Use the app team's own average velocity from recent sprints, and update the forecast after each sprint as actual figures come in.
Use the app team's highest figure of 34 points, so that the forecast shows what the team can achieve when it is stretched.
Ask the app team to estimate every Release 1 task in hours now and build a fixed plan from those estimates for the release.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile favours empiricism: start the work, measure how much gets done and forecast from that rate, using the team's own velocity rather than another team's (book 8.3). Velocity is an average rate per timebox and is refined as each sprint adds actual data.

n.0: Velocity should come from the team doing the work; story points are relative to each team, so another team's rate cannot forecast the app team (book 8.3).
n.2: Picking the best sprint produces an optimistic target, not an empirical forecast; velocity is an average rate refined as each sprint adds data (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.3: Predicting all the work in detail up front is rationalism; PRINCE2 Agile favours empiricism, measuring the actual rate of work and forecasting from it (book 8.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In the project initiation workshop, the three teams need to break the Fair Fares epics into user stories, group the stories into the three releases and show that payment to the card in Release 2 depends on the matching model. Rhys Pengelly had started a product breakdown structure. Which technique does PRINCE2 Agile recommend for this?
o: Build a user story map from the passengers' activities and turn it into a release map showing the releases and dependencies.
Finish the product breakdown structure first, then turn it into a Gantt chart listing each team's tasks for the ten months.
Draw a cumulative flow diagram of the epics, so that the teams can see which stories belong in which release.
Ask each team to write a team plan covering all its sprints, then combine the three team plans into the project plan.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, built from user activities and broken into stories. Turning the story map into a release map groups the stories into releases and defines the interdependencies (book 8.3.1, 8.3.1.1).

n.1: The book recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, and a ten-month task list is not how agile plans are built (book 8.3.1).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram tracks work items in each workflow state over time to reveal bottlenecks; it does not group stories into releases (book 12.4.2).
n.3: A team plan is a detailed plan for the next iteration, produced when a work package is accepted, not a long-range plan for every sprint (book 8.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: To satisfy Dominic Faraday, Rhys Pengelly spends the first two weeks of initiation building a detailed Gantt chart that lists every task for all three teams in every sprint up to December. He asks the teams to follow it and to report any task that slips. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a full baseline of tasks lets the board judge progress against an agreed schedule at each stage boundary.
Yes, because time and cost have zero tolerance, so each task has to be fixed in advance to protect the end date.
No, because task-level planning should be done by each team for the next sprint, under a high-level release map.
No, because a Gantt chart should be prepared by project support rather than by the project manager.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Planning in PRINCE2 Agile is done just in time: a high-level release map at stage boundaries, and task-level planning for the next iteration in managing product delivery, produced by the team in its team plan (book 8.3, 8.3.2).

n.0: Stage boundaries use a high-level release map; a ten-month task baseline cannot hold when the work is uncertain and would be judged on activity rather than delivered value (book 8.3).
n.1: Zero tolerance on time and cost is protected by flexing lower-priority scope, not by fixing every task in advance (Table 3.1, 8.3).
n.3: Who draws the chart is not the problem; the problem is planning every task months ahead instead of just in time (book 8.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: At the end of sprint 4, the app team says the 'confirm claim with one tap' story is almost done. The screens work, but the screen reader checks in the team's Definition of Done have not been run. Hollie Brennan, the test automation engineer, asks how the story should be reported. How should the team treat it?
o: Report it as not done and return it to the product backlog, so that Sasha Ellery can reprioritize the remaining work.
Count it as done for the sprint review, as the screens work, and add the screen reader checks as a new story.
Show it as 90% complete on the team dashboard and give it part of its story points in the velocity figure.
Remove the screen reader checks from the Definition of Done for Release 1, so that the story can be accepted now.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The Definition of Done is a shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet to be complete. An item is either done or not done, with no 'almost done'; unfinished work returns to the backlog for reprioritization (book 9.3.2.2).

n.1: A partly done story may be split only so that the part reported as done meets the Definition of Done; here the screens themselves have not passed the DoD's screen reader checks, so counting them as done hides incomplete work (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: There is no 'almost done' under a Definition of Done: an item is done or not done, and partial credit distorts velocity (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: The app must meet accessibility standards; weakening the team's agreed DoD to pass a story undermines the quality the passengers need (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: The app team reports that the Larkspur app carries a large amount of technical debt from a rushed redesign two years ago, and that it is slowing work on the claim screens. Sasha Ellery asks how the debt should be handled during Fair Fares. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Pause feature work for two months while the app is rewritten, then start the Release 1 stories once the code has been rebuilt.
Defer work on the debt until Release 3 is live, because refactoring changes how the app behaves for passengers and adds risk before the deadline.
Make the debt visible, set a tolerance for it and plan refactoring into sprints, raising an exception if it is forecast to exceed that.
Record the debt as a Won't have in the product backlog, so that it no longer counts against the team's velocity.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Technical debt is work owed before a job is truly complete, and it accrues interest. PRINCE2 Agile allows tolerances to be set on it, with an exception if it is forecast to become too significant; refactoring improves internal structure without changing external behaviour (book 9.4.1, 9.4.2).

n.0: A two-month pause would put the fixed Release 1 date and the December end date at risk; the debt should be managed alongside delivery (Table 3.1, 9.4.2).
n.1: Refactoring changes internal structure without changing external behaviour, and leaving debt to grow lets its interest slow every later release (book 9.4.1, 9.4.2).
n.3: Labelling the debt Won't have hides work that is still owed; technical debt should be visible and controlled with tolerances (book 9.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During initiation, Rhys Pengelly drafts the quality management approach. It records Larkspur's accessibility standards, the app team's automated testing, the testing methods Coinbridge uses for its payment work, and how the passenger panel will try each release before it goes live. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because agile ways of working and agile testing methods, including suppliers', should be recorded in the approach.
Yes, because recording the testing methods in the approach removes the need for a Definition of Done in each team.
No, because Coinbridge's testing methods belong in its contract and should be kept out of Larkspur's approach.
No, because user testing by the passenger panel should be recorded in the quality register, not in the approach.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The quality management approach sets out quality techniques, standards, roles and responsibilities. Agile ways of working must be incorporated, documented and assured in it, and agile testing methods, including those of suppliers, should be recorded there (book 9.3.2, Table 9.1).

n.1: The approach and the team Definition of Done do different jobs; each team still needs its own DoD, linked from its product backlog (book 8.3.2.1, 9.3.2.2).
n.2: The book says agile testing methods, including suppliers', should be recorded in the quality management approach (book 9.3.2).
n.3: The quality register records each planned and completed quality activity and its result, but the approach is where the methods and who is involved are described (book 9.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In the project initiation workshop, the participants assess the Fair Fares Agilometer. Gemma Lowther confirms that Coinbridge's fixed-price contract was signed before the project started and that any change to its scope will need a formal variation. Which Agilometer slider does this MOST directly affect?
o: Level of collaboration.
Ease of communication.
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally.
Advantageous environmental conditions.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The 'advantageous environmental conditions' slider assesses whether the overall working environment supports agile, including contracts that do not inhibit agile working (book 10.3.2.2). A fixed-price contract needing formal variations for any scope change pulls this slider down.

n.0: Collaboration concerns how closely the parties work together day to day; the contract terms are part of the wider working environment (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: This slider is about how easily all parties can communicate; a contract variation clause does not change that directly (book 10.3.2.2).
n.2: This slider concerns how easily benefit can be delivered through regular partial deliveries; the contract's terms fall under environmental conditions (book 10.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: At a team planning workshop, the Coinbridge team and its product owner agree two responses to the risk that payments made without a claim attract fraud: a check that the card being paid matches the ticket purchase, and a daily limit per account. Both responses need development work in the coming sprints. How should these responses be managed?
o: Add them to the product backlog with the user stories, prioritized alongside them, and keep the risk in the risk register.
Keep them in the risk register and ask the team to fit the work in once its sprint commitments are complete.
Record them in the Agilometer under level of collaboration, so that the board can track them at each agile enablement workshop.
Raise an exception report to the board, as responses to fraud fall outside the tolerances given to the team.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds risk responses and user stories together, so that response work is prioritized and planned like any other item (book 10.4.1). The risk itself stays recorded in the risk register (Table 10.1).

n.1: Response work kept outside the backlog is not prioritized or planned and may never be done; the book puts it in a risk-adjusted product backlog (book 10.4.1).
n.2: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working itself; it is not where responses to a product risk such as fraud are planned (book 10.3.2).
n.3: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; planning risk responses is normal work within the team's delegated authority (Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Rhys Pengelly runs a full risk workshop during initiation and records the results in the risk register. He tells the teams that new risks will be gathered again at each stage boundary, and that sprint planning and retrospectives should concentrate on delivery. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because stage boundaries are where the board reviews whether the project's risks remain acceptable.
Yes, because keeping sprint events focused on delivery helps protect the fixed December end date.
No, because new risks should be identified by project assurance rather than by the project manager.
No, because risk identification should be a fixed part of every planning session and retrospective.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile adapts the five risk steps to iterative working: identifying risks is a fixed part of every planning session and team or project retrospective, and implementing and communicating responses are part of the continuous iteration cycle (book 10.3.1).

n.0: The board does review risk at stage boundaries, but that does not replace identifying risks continually within the iterations (book 10.3.1).
n.1: Leaving risk out of sprint events does not protect the date; risks found late are more likely to threaten it (book 10.3.1).
n.2: Risks can surface anywhere and are gathered by the teams in their events; it is not a task reserved for project assurance (book 10.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In stage 3, Matteo Ricci asks for passengers to be able to receive compensation into a digital wallet as well as to their card. This would add a new epic to the project backlog and change the scope of Coinbridge's fixed-price contract. How should this request be handled?
o: As a detail change, agreed between the Coinbridge product owner and the team at the next team planning workshop.
As a trade, swapping the wallet epic for Coinbridge stories of similar effort so that the project backlog keeps its size.
As a request for change to the project baseline, assessed formally and decided by the board or delegated change authority.
As an off-specification, raised by Hollie Brennan because the payment feature will not meet its original specification.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A new or changed requirement that changes the project backlog is a change to the project baseline and must be handled formally, decided by the project board or by those with delegated change authority (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2). Coinbridge's contract would also need a formal variation.

n.0: A change that alters the project backlog is a baseline change; detail changes are those that leave the project backlog unaffected (book 11.3.2).
n.1: Trading absorbs small changes within the existing backlog; a new epic that alters the backlog and the supplier contract needs a formal decision (book 11.3.2, 11.4.1).
n.3: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; this is a proposal to change the baseline, which is a request for change (book 11.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During a sprint in stage 2, the passenger panel finds the wording on the claim confirmation screen confusing. Sasha Ellery agrees with the app team to add a story to rewrite the wording and to move a Could have story of similar size to a later sprint. The project backlog is unchanged and the board is not involved. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager has the authority to approve any change to the stories during a stage.
Yes, because this is a detail change within the project backlog, traded at team level with the product owner.
No, because each change found by users has to be logged as a request for change and decided by the board.
No, because changes should wait until the sprint has ended and be raised at the team retrospective.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change, handled informally at team level. Trading swaps requirements of similar effort so the change is absorbed without growing scope, with priorities agreed with the product owner (book 11.3.2, 11.4.1).

n.0: The change was not approved by the project manager, and changes to the project baseline need the board or delegated change authority; this one is a team-level detail change (book 11.3.2).
n.2: Changes that do not affect the project backlog are detail changes handled informally at team level; formal board decisions are for baseline changes (book 11.3.2).
n.3: Agile embraces change; trading lets a small change be absorbed without disrupting the iteration, and the retrospective is for reflecting on how the team works (book 11.4.1, Table 13.14).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Dominic Faraday asks for a written report of at least ten pages every month. Rhys Pengelly wants to give the project board the information it needs on progress while following PRINCE2 Agile guidance. What should Rhys propose?
o: Weekly copies of the three team dashboards, sent to every board member so that they can follow the status of each task.
A project dashboard the board pulls from, with the release burn-up and current risks and issues, updated in progress reviews.
A monthly ten-page highlight report written by project support for Dominic, with the three team dashboards attached as an appendix.
A Gantt chart updated each month to show the percentage complete of every task for each of the three teams.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project dashboard replaces the highlight report. It is updated and reviewed in progress review workshops and the board pulls information from it, including release status, burn charts and current risks and issues (book Table 12.1, 12.3.2.1).

n.0: Team dashboards replace checkpoint reports and are used by the project manager; the board's view is the project dashboard, pulled rather than pushed (Table 12.1).
n.2: In PRINCE2 Agile the project dashboard replaces the highlight report; a long pushed report adds effort without giving the board a current, visual view (Table 12.1).
n.3: Progress in agile is tracked by what is delivered, for which burn charts suit every level; percentage-complete tasks say little about value delivered (book 12.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Midway through stage 2, the Release 1 burn-up chart shows that, at the current velocity, the app team will finish all the Must have stories on time, but about a third of the Should and Could have stories will not be done by the end of month four. Rhys Pengelly asks the board to move the Release 1 date back by three weeks so that every story can be included. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the burn-up chart forecasts the finish date, and the board should act on the forecast it shows.
Yes, because an exception has occurred, so the board has to decide how the release should be re-planned.
No, because the board should have been asked to add budget for extra people rather than extra time.
No, because time has zero tolerance; the Should and Could haves should be flexed, as the Must haves are on track.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile fixes time and cost and flexes what is delivered; burn charts track that flexing, and an exception arises only when a tolerance, such as delivering the Must haves, is forecast to be exceeded (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).

n.0: Burn charts do forecast completion, but the right response here is to flex lower-priority stories, not to move a date that has zero tolerance (book 12.3.1).
n.1: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded: the Must haves are on track and flexing Should and Could haves is within tolerance (Table 12.1, Table 3.1).
n.2: Cost also has zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile, so asking for more budget breaks the same rule as asking for more time (Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During initiation, Rebecca Lyle and the web team need to size about 120 user stories for the hub so that Jamal Hussain can draft a first release map. Time is short, and Daniel Ferreira does not want the team to spend days debating each story. Which estimating approach is MOST suitable?
o: Magic estimation, with the whole team quickly placing the stories in order of relative size with little discussion of each.
Ask Daniel Ferreira to estimate all 120 stories himself in story points, so that the developers' time is kept for building.
Use the Northmere team's past velocity to size the web team's stories, as Northmere has delivered similar integration work.
Estimate each story in hours with the most experienced developer, then add up the hours to fix the Release 1 end date.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Agile estimation is relative and draws on the whole team. Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique for early planning that sizes many stories without lengthy discussion (book 8.4.3), which fits sizing 120 stories for a first release map.

n.1: Agile estimates should harness the whole team so that everyone contributes; one person's estimates lose the team's knowledge and shared commitment (book 8.4.3).
n.2: Velocity is a team's rate of delivery used for forecasting, not a way to size stories, and forecasts should use the team's own figures (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile uses relative estimates from the whole team, not hour-by-hour estimates from one person, and time is already fixed by Welcome Week (book 8.4.3, Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Daniel Ferreira says his team will not commit to any feature more than one sprint ahead. Jamal Hussain accepts this and decides that the plan for Release 1 will be the web team's current sprint plan, with no release map, until each new sprint begins. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because detailed task-level planning should be done for the next iteration and not further ahead.
Yes, because empiricism means that no forecast for the release can be made until the work itself is finished.
No, because a high-level release map is still needed for the releases, with detailed planning kept to the next sprint.
No, because the web team should commit during initiation to a detailed plan for every Release 1 sprint.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile plans just in time: a high-level release map serves as the project and stage plan, showing how many releases there are, when, and which features they contain, while task-level planning is done for the next iteration (book 8.3.2, Table 8.1). Ferreira's point is valid for team plans, but the board still needs a release map.

n.0: This is true for team plans, but it does not justify having no release map; the higher-level plan is still needed (book 8.3.2).
n.1: Empiricism means starting work, measuring how much gets done and forecasting from that rate; it supports forecasts during the work (book 8.3).
n.3: Detailed plans for every sprint in advance go against planning just in time; task-level planning belongs to the next iteration (book 8.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: The university's quality team wants evidence that each release has been tested with real students. For Release 1, Maya Kowalczyk's student design panel takes part in three planned test sessions on phones and with screen readers, and the result of each session is recorded. Where should the planned sessions and their results be recorded?
o: In the product register, with the current status of each product.
In the quality register, with planned and actual dates and results.
On the web team's team dashboard, beside the sprint burn-down.
In the lessons log, with what the team learned from each session.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The quality register holds all planned and completed quality activities, with their method, planned and actual dates, responsibilities, results and records (book 9.3.2, Table 9.1). The student test sessions are quality activities, so they and their results go there.

n.0: The product register lists the products required by a plan and their status; it is not the record of quality activities and results (book 9.3.2).
n.2: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and shows the team's progress; it is not the record of planned and completed quality activities (book Table 12.1).
n.3: The lessons log captures lessons; the planned test sessions and their pass or fail results belong in the quality register (book 9.3.2, Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Members of the student design panel disagree about two designs for the first screen of self-referral: one asks students to choose a category of need, the other asks them to describe their concern in their own words. Rebecca Lyle wants evidence of which design more students complete. Which quality technique BEST fits this situation?
o: Refactoring, changing the internal structure of the screen while keeping its behaviour the same for students.
Test-driven development, writing unit tests for each design before the code for that design is written.
A cumulative flow diagram, showing how many stories for each design are in progress and how many are done.
A/B testing, releasing both versions to groups of students and comparing how many complete each one.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A/B testing compares two versions of a product with users to see which performs better (book 9.4.3). It gives Rebecca evidence from students instead of opinions from the panel.

n.0: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing external behaviour; it cannot show which design students prefer (book 9.4.1).
n.1: Test-driven development checks that code works at unit level; it does not compare how real users respond to two designs (book 9.4.3, Glossary).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram is a progress technique that shows work in each workflow state; it says nothing about which design students complete (book 12.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: The web team's definition of done does not include testing with assistive technology, which an external auditor has carried out once a year. Rebecca Lyle proposes keeping the definition of done as it is for Release 1 and booking the auditor's annual check for August, a few weeks before Welcome Week. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because an external auditor gives more independent evidence of accessibility than the team's own checks.
Yes, because the definition of done belongs to the team, so the project should leave it unchanged.
No, because accessibility should be checked by project assurance at each stage boundary instead.
No, because assistive-technology testing should be part of done for each story, so faults are found as work is built.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The definition of done is the shared agreement of what makes an item complete; work that has defects is not done (book 9.3.2.2). PRINCE2 Agile advises deciding early how much can be tested first or tested as the work goes (book 9.4.3). For a hub used by many disabled students, accessibility is part of done, not a late check.

n.0: An external audit may still be useful, but a single check weeks before go-live finds faults too late to fix, and stories would count as done while untested (book 9.3.2.2, 9.4.3).
n.1: The definition of done is a shared agreement that the team and product owner should keep fit for the product's quality needs, which here include accessibility (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Project assurance monitors adherence to practices and governance; it does not test products, and a check at stage boundaries is still late (book Table 7.2, 9.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In the project initiation workshop, the participants assess the Agilometer for the hub. Peter Langley insists that the early-warning feature must be in Release 1, and several senior staff describe every requested feature as essential for Welcome Week. The group rates the related slider low. Which action is MOST LIKELY to improve that slider?
o: Hold more frequent stand-ups with the wellbeing staff on both campuses, to raise the level of collaboration.
Move the Northmere agreement to one fixed price for the whole project, to protect the scope already agreed.
Challenge with the board and stakeholders whether so many features really are Must haves, using Greer's stated minimum.
Ask the council for extra budget for more web developers, so that every requested feature can fit into Release 1 before Welcome Week.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Stakeholders treating every feature as essential lowers the 'flexibility on what is delivered' slider. One way to raise it is to challenge whether too many requirements are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them (book 10.3.2.2, 10.3.2.3). Greer's statement that self-referral and booking are the minimum gives a basis for that conversation.

n.0: More stand-ups might help collaboration, but the low reading here comes from stakeholders' unwillingness to flex scope, which is a different slider (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: A fixed-price contract for all the scope would make flexing what is delivered harder, and contracts that inhibit agile lower another slider (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: Cost has zero tolerance and the council has fixed the budget; adding money avoids, rather than improves, flexibility on what is delivered (book Table 3.1, 10.3.2.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Professor Greer, whose council has a very low appetite for risks to student data, asks Jamal Hussain to show whether the total exposure from the data security risks that the web team is tracking is falling from sprint to sprint during stage 2. Which technique BEST meets her request?
o: A cumulative risk burn-down chart, with the team updating the likelihood of each tracked risk at every planning session.
A release burn-up chart, showing the story points completed against the scope of Release 1 over the sprints of the stage.
A cumulative flow diagram, showing how many data security stories sit in each workflow state over the weeks of the stage.
An Agilometer, with its sliders reassessed at each agile enablement workshop held by the board during the stage.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In a cumulative risk burn-down chart the team sets the likelihood of each tracked risk at the first planning meeting and updates it at each planning session; the chart shows total risk exposure across iterations, which should fall over time (book 10.4.2).

n.1: A burn-up chart tracks completed work against scope; it does not show risk exposure (book 12.4.3).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram shows work in each workflow state and reveals bottlenecks; it does not measure risk exposure (book 12.4.2).
n.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working itself, such as flexibility and collaboration, not the exposure from specific data security risks (book 10.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Dr Ruth Sefton requires two responses to the risk of a breach of student health data: encryption of stored case notes, and access to notes limited by staff role. Both need development work. Rebecca Lyle adds them as stories to the web team's product backlog, prioritized alongside the user stories, and the risk stays in the risk register. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because placing risk responses in the product backlog lets them be prioritized and tracked alongside the stories.
Yes, because once the responses are in the product backlog, the risk no longer needs to be held in the risk register.
No, because responses to data risks should be planned by the board in the agile enablement workshop, not by the team.
No, because data protection risks fall outside the team's tolerances and must be reported in an exception report.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds risk responses together with the user stories, so that the work to manage risk is prioritized and delivered like any other work (book 10.4.1). The risk register still records the risk and its status (book 10.3.2).

n.1: The risk register is the record of identified risks with their status and history; adding responses to the backlog does not replace it (book 10.3.2, Table 10.1).
n.2: The agile enablement workshop deals with risks to agile adoption found through the Agilometer, not with planning responses to specific product risks (book Table 13.5).
n.3: An exception report is needed when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; nothing suggests that, and the responses can be planned within the team's work (book Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In stage 2, Peter Langley asks again for the early-warning feature to be moved from Release 3 into Release 1 as a Must have. Professor Greer has said that self-referral and booking are the minimum for Welcome Week, and the ethics committee has asked to review any use of predictive analytics before it is built. How should Langley's request be handled?
o: As a detail change, agreed by Rebecca Lyle with the web team at the next team planning workshop in stage 2.
As a request for change to the baseline, assessed formally and decided by the board or delegated change authority.
As a trade, swapping the early-warning epic for Release 1 stories of similar effort within the web team.
As an off-specification, because Release 1 will not include a feature that a senior stakeholder expects.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline. Making a whole epic a Must have for Release 1 changes the approved scope in the project backlog and the release map, so it is handled formally and decided by the project board or whoever holds delegated change authority (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2). The ethics review would also have to come first.

n.0: A detail change does not affect the project backlog; moving an epic into Release 1 changes the agreed scope, so the product owner cannot decide it at team level (book 11.3.2).
n.2: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort inside a team's work; it is not a way to bring a new epic into a release without a baseline decision (book 11.4.1, 11.3.2).
n.3: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; the early-warning feature was never part of Release 1's scope (book 11.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Late in stage 2, testing with screen readers shows that the appointment booking screens will not meet the university's accessibility standard, which forms part of their quality criteria. The fix will not be ready before Welcome Week. What type of issue is this, and why?
o: A request for change, because the accessibility standard will have to be changed for Release 1.
An off-specification, because a product will not meet its quality specification.
A business opportunity, because the fault shows where the booking screens can be improved.
A problem, because the fault has an immediate effect on the web team's velocity this sprint.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification (book 11.3.1). The booking screens are forecast to miss the accessibility standard set in their quality criteria.

n.0: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline; nobody has proposed changing the standard, and the facts are that the product will fall short of it (book 11.3.1).
n.2: A business opportunity is an unexpected positive consequence; a failure to meet a quality standard is not (book 11.3.1).
n.3: The problem type covers issues with a negative impact that are not a product failing its specification; this issue is specifically about the screens missing their quality criteria (book 11.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In sprint 5, the link between the hub's booking screens and the student records system fails testing, blocking three of the Northmere team's stories. Before the team has looked at it together, its product owner reports it to Jamal Hussain, who writes an issue report and asks the project board how to proceed. Release 1 is still forecast to be on time. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a fault that blocks stories should be recorded in an issue report for the board to decide on.
Yes, because faults in a supplier's work under the per-iteration agreement need a decision from the board.
No, because the blocked stories should be traded for other Northmere stories of similar effort instead.
No, because the team should first swarm on the blocker together and escalate it if it cannot resolve it.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Swarming means the team focuses together on a stuck task or blocker, and it should be tried before an issue is escalated to the project manager (book 11.4.2). The board is involved when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded, and Release 1 is still on time (book Table 12.1).

n.0: Formal issue handling is for matters the team cannot resolve or that affect the baseline; a blocker should be swarmed first (book 11.4.2).
n.1: The per-iteration agreement does not turn every technical fault into a board decision; the team should try to resolve it first (book 11.4.2, Table 12.1).
n.2: Trading absorbs change by swapping requirements of similar effort; it is not a way to remove a blocker (book 11.4.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Midway through stage 2, the web team's cumulative flow diagram shows the 'waiting for data protection sign-off' band growing wider each week, while the 'done' band rises slowly. Chloe Hartley asks the team what the chart is telling them. Which reading is correct?
o: The team is ahead of plan, because more stories are moving through the workflow each week than before.
Work is queuing at data protection sign-off, a bottleneck the team should address before starting more stories.
Total risk exposure is rising, so the data protection risks in the risk register should be reassessed.
The team's velocity is falling because its data stories were underestimated, so the remaining stories should be re-estimated.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A cumulative flow diagram shows how many items are in each workflow state over time and reveals bottlenecks; a band that keeps widening shows work queuing at that state (book 12.4.2).

n.0: A widening waiting band with a slowly rising 'done' band shows work piling up, not faster delivery (book 12.4.2).
n.2: Total risk exposure is shown by a cumulative risk burn-down chart, not by a cumulative flow diagram (book 10.4.2, 12.4.2).
n.3: The chart shows where work is waiting, not that estimates were wrong; velocity and estimates are read from burn charts and story points (book 12.4.2, 12.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Professor Greer asks Jamal Hussain for a detailed weekly written report. To produce it, Jamal asks the web team to stop updating its online team dashboard and instead email him a status note every Friday, which he will rewrite into a report for her. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project executive decides the format and frequency of the reports that she receives.
Yes, because written reports give the board a more reliable record of progress than visual dashboards.
No, because the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report, and Greer should pull from a project dashboard.
No, because the web team should send its weekly status note directly to Greer rather than through Jamal.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and the project manager pulls information from it; the project dashboard replaces the highlight report and the board pulls information from it (book Table 12.1). Replacing the team dashboard with emailed notes removes the team's visual management and pushes reports instead.

n.0: The board's information needs matter, but in PRINCE2 Agile they are met through a project dashboard it can pull from, not by dismantling the team's dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.1: Written reports are not more reliable; people tend to adjust what they report to what seems acceptable, while dashboards keep progress visible (book 4.4, 12.3.1).
