n.3: Sending status notes to the executive bypasses the project manager and still pushes reports; the board should pull from the project dashboard (book Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Four weeks into Stage 4, the store operations team's Kanban board shows that, in addition to the 10 pilot stores, it has taken 24 stores live, a steady rate of about six stores a week. Patrick Dunne must forecast whether the remaining 51 stores will be ready before Easter. Bill Rowntree suggests using the rate of ten stores a week that a contractor achieved in last year's store refit programme. How should Patrick forecast the roll-out?
o: Use the store operations team's own measured rate of about six stores a week to forecast the finish, and update the release map with the result.
Use the contractor's rate of ten stores a week, because it comes from a larger programme and so gives a more reliable basis for the forecast.
Ask each area manager to estimate a go-live date for each remaining store, and combine their estimates into a detailed schedule for the stage.
Work back from the Easter deadline to set the rate needed each week, and plan the remaining stores so that this rate is met.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile planning is empirical: start the work, measure how much gets done and use that to forecast (book 8.3). The rate should be the team's own, not another person's or team's. The store operations team has a steady measured rate, so it is the right basis, and the release map is updated with the forecast.

n.1: Another organization's rate on different work is not evidence of what this team can do; forecasts should use the team's own measured rate (book 8.3).
n.2: Estimates from people outside the team are reasoned predictions rather than measured experience, and they ignore the data the team already has (book 8.3).
n.3: Working back from the deadline sets a target; it does not forecast what the team will actually achieve from its measured rate (book 8.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During initiation, the teams turn their user story map into a release map. Live stock levels on the website depend on Tallis's new interface, and Tallis's quarterly releases fall in months 2, 5 and 8. Elena Marsh has confirmed that Tallis will not change these dates for Pinewick. How should Patrick Dunne and the teams reflect this in the release map?
o: Leave the Tallis dates out of the release map and record them in the risk register, because they are outside the project's control.
Plan every sprint for both teams in detail for the full nine months, so that each task linked to the Tallis interface can be scheduled exactly.
Ask Elena Marsh to bring forward Tallis's month 5 release, so that the interface work for Release 2 arrives earlier in the stage.
Show the dependency on each Tallis release and place the features that need the interface in releases that follow the matching Tallis date.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Turning a story map into a release map also defines the interdependencies, and releases are planned around them (book 8.3.1.1). The release map shows how many releases there are, when they happen and which features they contain (book 8.3.2), so it should show the Tallis dates and sequence the dependent features after them.

n.0: The dependency may also be a risk, but release planning must take known interdependencies into account rather than leave them out (book 8.3.1.1).
n.1: Detailed task-level planning is done just in time for the next iteration in a team plan, not for the whole project in advance (book 8.3.2).
n.2: Tallis has confirmed that its dates will not change, so the plan has to work around them rather than depend on a request already refused.

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In initiation, Patrick Dunne builds a release map with both teams from their story map, showing the three releases with their epics and main user stories. Detailed plans for each sprint and each store are left to the teams' planning workshops. Gwen Tallowby asks for a day-by-day plan of every task for the nine months because the date cannot move, but Patrick keeps his approach. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the release map is owned by the chief product owner, so the project manager is not the right person to produce detailed plans.
Yes, because plans are made just in time: the release map stays high level and the teams make task-level plans for the next iteration.
No, because zero tolerance on time means the board must approve a detailed baseline of every task before the project can start.
No, because a release map covers a single release, so Patrick needs a separate stage plan for each of the three releases as well.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the release map is kept at a high level and updated at stage boundaries, while task-level planning is done by the delivery team in a team plan for the next iteration (book 8.3.2). Planning every task for nine months would rest on guesses; the plan is refined empirically as the teams learn (book 8.3).

n.0: The chief product owner owns the project backlog; the release map is the project plan, which the project manager prepares with the teams (book 8.3.2, Table 7.2).
n.2: With time fixed, PRINCE2 Agile flexes what is delivered; a detailed baseline of every task is not needed and would not stay accurate (book Table 3.1, 8.3).
n.3: The release map serves as both the project plan and the stage plan, with the stage view covering a shorter horizon (book 8.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In Stage 2, the e-commerce team twice pulls stories about showing stock levels into a sprint and then finds that the field names and test data for the Tallis interface are not yet available. Both stories stall and roll over to the next sprint. Anita Shah asks how to stop this happening again. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on quality?
o: Add 'interface tested with Tallis data' to the Definition of Done, so that the stories cannot be counted as complete until the data is available.
Agree a Definition of Ready requiring the interface details and test data to be available before a story that needs them enters a sprint.
Let the team start the stories anyway and swarm on them once the data arrives, so that the sprint can still finish with them complete.
Ask Elena Marsh to set the order of the stories that use the interface, so that Tallis decides when the work is pulled into a sprint.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A Definition of Ready is a shared team agreement on the criteria an item must meet before work begins, such as clear information, resources and dependencies being in place (book 9.3.2.1). The stories stalled because they entered sprints before their dependency was met.

n.0: The Definition of Done sets the criteria for an item to be complete; the problem is that work started before the story was ready (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Swarming helps a team clear a blocker, but starting stories that cannot progress would repeat the stalls; readiness should be checked first (book 11.4.2, 9.3.2.1).
n.3: The product owner owns and orders the team's product backlog; handing that to the supplier would not ensure stories are ready (book Table 7.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In Stage 3, the e-commerce team cannot agree whether customers are more likely to complete a reservation if the 'reserve and collect' button appears above or below the delivery options on the product page. Marcus Lindell prefers it above, while Anita Shah prefers it below. Both layouts are quick to build. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Ask Marcus Lindell to decide, because he represents online customers' needs and owns the roadmap for the website and app.
Refactor the product page so that both layouts are coded cleanly, then choose one of them at the next sprint review.
Run an A/B test, showing each layout to a share of real customers and comparing how many go on to complete a reservation.
Survey the 85 store managers on which layout they think customers would prefer, and build the one the majority favours.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A/B testing compares two versions of a product with real users to see which performs better (book 9.4.3). It replaces opinion with evidence about which layout leads more customers to complete a reservation.

n.0: Marcus's preference is still an opinion; testing with users gives evidence of what customers actually do (book 9.4.3).
n.1: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour; it does not tell the team which layout customers respond to (book 9.4.1).
n.3: Store managers are not the users of the product page, and a survey of opinions is not a test with customers (book 9.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Early in Stage 4, Bill Rowntree proposes that the store operations team marks a store's card as done once staff are trained and the collection point works, and that stock accuracy is checked in the weeks after the store goes live, to save time during the peak. Patrick Dunne agrees and updates the quality management approach accordingly. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the quality management approach can record the organization's own procedures, and Bill is responsible for store standards.
Yes, because stock accuracy is a risk rather than a quality criterion, so it belongs in the risk register instead of the Definition of Done.
No, because the Definition of Done must be set by the project board, so Patrick cannot change it through the quality management approach.
No, because a store is done once every agreed criterion is met, including 97% stock accuracy, and there is no such state as almost done.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The Definition of Done is a shared agreement on the criteria an item must meet to be complete, and an item is either done or not done, with no almost done (book 9.3.2.2). The go-live condition for each store includes stock accuracy of at least 97%, so a store cannot be counted as done before that is met.

n.0: An organization's own procedures can be recorded as a tailoring decision, but this change removes an agreed acceptance criterion from the meaning of done (book 9.3.1, 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Whether accuracy will reach 97% in time is a risk, but the 97% threshold itself is a go-live criterion that each store must meet (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: A Definition of Done is a shared agreement among those doing and accepting the work; it is not reserved to the board, and the reason the change fails is that it drops a criterion (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In the agile enablement workshop at the start of Stage 3, the participants review the Agilometer. Lucy Fenn has insisted that every feature to be advertised in February must be in Release 3, and the board has started to treat almost every item in the project backlog as a Must have. Which slider does this MOST directly affect, and how could it be improved?
o: Level of collaboration; it could be improved by inviting Lucy Fenn to the e-commerce team's sprint reviews so that she sees progress first-hand.
Ease of communication; it could be improved by sending the board a summary of the project backlog at the end of each sprint.
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally; it could be improved by moving the national campaign to after Easter.
Flexibility on what is delivered; it could be improved by challenging whether so many requirements are really Must haves.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The flexibility on what is delivered slider reflects how comfortable stakeholders are with flexing scope and with their role in prioritizing work (book 10.3.2.2). One way to raise it is to challenge whether too many requirements are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them (book 10.3.2.3).

n.0: Collaboration concerns how closely people work together; treating everything as a Must have is about willingness to flex scope (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: Ease of communication is about how easily all parties communicate; more summaries would not change the board's view of what must be delivered (book 10.3.2.2).
n.2: This slider concerns delivering benefit through regular partial deliveries; the issue here is stakeholders' unwillingness to flex scope, and moving the campaign does not change that (book 10.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: George Ahmed asks how the e-commerce team can show whether its overall exposure to the main delivery risks, such as payment security weaknesses and interface delays, is falling from one sprint to the next. Patrick Dunne wants a technique that the team can keep up to date itself as part of its normal planning. Which technique should the team use?
o: A cumulative risk burn-down chart, with the team rating the likelihood of each tracked risk at every sprint planning session.
The Agilometer, reassessed at every sprint planning session, so that the board can see how the team's delivery risks change.
A cumulative flow diagram, showing how many risk responses are in each state of the team's workflow at the end of each day.
A burn-up chart of the risk responses completed in each sprint, plotted against the total number of responses planned.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In a cumulative risk burn-down chart the team rates the likelihood of each tracked risk at the first planning meeting and updates it at each planning session; the chart shows total risk exposure across iterations, which should fall over time (book 10.4.2).

n.1: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, not the project's delivery risks such as payment security (book 10.3.2).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram shows how many items are in each workflow state over time and reveals bottlenecks; it does not show risk exposure (book 12.4.2).
n.3: Counting completed responses shows work done, not whether the likelihood of the risks, and so the exposure, is falling (book 10.4.2, 12.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In the project initiation workshop, all participants assess the Agilometer and the results are combined into a single project view. Patrick Dunne then files it with the PID and tells the board that it will not need to be repeated, because the e-commerce team has used agile for three years. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the Agilometer is a progress tool, and progress against the release map is reported through the project dashboard instead.
Yes, because a team with several years of agile experience already understands the risks that agile working brings to its projects.
No, because the Agilometer should be reassessed regularly in later stages, and this project adds a store team new to agile and a supplier.
No, because the Agilometer should be completed by Nikhil Rao as agile coach rather than by the participants of the workshop.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The Agilometer identifies and monitors the risks of agile working (book 10.3.1, 10.3.2). It is first assessed in the project initiation workshop and then reassessed regularly in later stages, for example in the agile enablement workshop, with trends shown on the project dashboard (book Table 13.5). Pinewick has never run a project combining technology, store operations and an external supplier, and the store team is new to agile.

n.0: The Agilometer belongs to the risk practice; it assesses risks of agile working, not progress (book 10.3.2).
n.1: One team's experience does not cover the store operations team or the supplier, and the book expects regular reassessment (book Table 13.5).
n.3: In the project initiation workshop all participants assess the Agilometer and the results are combined, so the workshop assessment is the intended approach (book Table 13.7).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During a Stage 3 sprint, staff in the pilot stores say the reservation confirmation email confuses customers because the collection point is described at the bottom. They ask for the store's collection point details to appear at the top. The change does not alter any epic or requirement in the project backlog. How should this change be handled?
o: As a request for change, recorded in an issue report and sent to the project board for a decision before the email is altered.
As an off-specification, because the email does not meet its quality specification and must be reported to Patrick Dunne.
As a detail change, agreed informally between the team and Anita Shah and handled within the team's product backlog.
As an exception, because changing a feature already released to the pilot stores means the stage is forecast to exceed tolerance.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change. It is seen as making the final product more accurate and is handled informally at team level (book 11.3.2), here between the team and its product owner, Anita Shah.

n.0: Formal handling by the board or change authority is for changes to the project baseline, which in PRINCE2 Agile means the project backlog; this change does not affect it (book 11.3.2).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; the email works as specified, and staff are suggesting an improvement (book 11.3.1).
n.3: An exception arises when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; nothing suggests a small wording change threatens any tolerance (book Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In Stage 4, the collection point at one large store is stuck in the preparation column because the store's handheld scanners cannot connect to the new stock system. Rather than raising an issue straight away, the store operations team stops starting new stores for a day and works on the problem together with one e-commerce developer. They agree to tell Patrick Dunne if it is still unresolved by the end of the week. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because swarming focuses the team on a blocker together, and it should be tried before an issue is escalated to the project manager.
Yes, because trading lets the team swap the blocked store for another store of similar effort, which keeps the roll-out on schedule.
No, because every problem should be captured in the issue register and reported to the project board before the team acts on it.
No, because pausing new work for a day breaks the team's work-in-progress limits, so the blocked store should go back to the backlog.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Swarming is when the team focuses together on a stuck task or blocker, which can also speed up time-critical work; the book suggests trying it before escalating an issue to the project manager (book 11.4.2). The team escalates if it cannot resolve the problem.

n.1: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort to absorb a change; the team has not swapped anything, and trading is not a way to remove a blocker (book 11.4.1).
n.2: Swarming comes first; a problem is escalated as an issue if the team cannot resolve it, and the board is involved for decisions beyond the project manager's tolerance (book 11.4.2).
n.3: Stopping new work to clear a blocker keeps work in progress down, which is consistent with limiting it; moving the store back would leave the problem unsolved (book 11.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: George Ahmed asks how the board will know, between stage boundaries, whether the project is still on track. Patrick Dunne, used to sending weekly written reports on construction projects, wants to meet this need while following PRINCE2 Agile guidance on the progress practice. What should Patrick propose?
o: A highlight report emailed to each board member every Friday, summarizing both teams' progress in the same format he used for construction projects.
Board members taking turns to attend the e-commerce team's daily stand-ups, so that they hear about progress directly from the developers.
An end stage report at each stage boundary, with a detailed list of the tasks completed and the costs incurred in that stage.
A project dashboard, built from the team dashboards and showing release status, burn charts and current risks, that the board can view at any time.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project dashboard replaces the highlight report and end stage report. The board pulls information from it rather than having reports pushed to it, and it shows items such as release status, burn charts, current risks and issues, and Agilometer trends (book Table 12.1, 12.3.2.1). It is updated from the team dashboards and reviewed in progress review workshops.

n.0: A pushed weekly report is what the project dashboard replaces in PRINCE2 Agile; the board pulls the information it needs (book Table 12.1).
n.1: Stand-ups are the team's own events, which even the project manager attends with the team's agreement, and they do not give the board a project-level view (book Table 12.1).
n.2: George asked about the period between stage boundaries; an end stage report comes at the boundary itself (book Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In Stage 2, Patrick Dunne sets up progress control as he did in construction. Each week he measures the percentage of the budget spent and the percentage of the nine months used, and reports the project as on track while both figures stay below 100%. He does not track which user stories or store tasks have been completed. Which is the MAIN weakness of this approach?
o: Spend should be tracked monthly rather than weekly, because weekly figures on an agile project change too often to show a reliable trend.
With zero tolerance on time and cost, the aspect of interest is how much is being delivered, which burn charts of completed work would show.
The board should receive these figures in an exception report each week, because the stage plan has no tolerance for time or cost.
The time measure should be replaced by velocity, because the date can move if the teams' velocity shows that more time is needed.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Because time and cost have zero tolerance, flexibility in what is delivered is the main aspect of interest, and burn charts suit every level; tracking spend against a budget or time tolerance adds little when both are fixed (book 12.3.1). Patrick's measures cannot show whether the Must haves will be delivered.

n.0: The frequency is not the problem; whatever the interval, budget and time used say nothing about how much has been delivered (book 12.3.1).
n.2: An exception report is raised when a plan is forecast to exceed its tolerances, not as a routine weekly report (book Table 12.1).
n.3: Time has zero tolerance; velocity is used to forecast what can be delivered in the fixed time, not to move the date (book Table 3.1, 12.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: After three sprints in stage 2, the Care Online digital team has completed 21, 25 and 23 story points. Joan Whitaker wants to know which Release 1 stories will be ready by month four. Gita Bhatt mentions that a team at one of her previous councils averaged 35 points a sprint on similar work. How should Simon Archer forecast the Release 1 scope?
o: Use the team's own average of 23 points a sprint to forecast how many remaining stories, in priority order, fit by month four.
Use the 35-point average from Gita's previous council, as it comes from a more experienced team that delivered similar work.
Ask each developer to estimate in hours every task of every remaining Release 1 story, and fix the release scope from the total.
Average the digital team's figures with the 35-point figure, so that the forecast reflects both experience and the team's current rate.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile plans empirically: start work, measure how much gets done and forecast from that rate (calibration, or calculating velocity). The forecast should use the team's own velocity, not another team's (book 8.3). Here that is (21 + 25 + 23) / 3 = 23 points a sprint.

n.1: A team forecasts from its own measured velocity; another council's figure, however experienced that team was, does not show what this team will deliver (book 8.3).
n.2: Detailed task estimates for a whole release are rationalist planning; agile planning is empirical, and task-level plans are made for the next iteration (book 8.3, 8.4.3).
n.3: Mixing in another team's velocity still distorts the forecast; empiricism uses the rate this team has actually achieved (book 8.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Early in initiation, the digital team, Amy Fletcher and two practitioners have written about 140 user stories across the three Care Online releases. Before the project initiation workshop, they need a rough relative size for every story so that a first release map can be drafted, and they have one short session in which to do it. Which estimating technique fits BEST?
o: Planning-poker style estimation, with each person revealing a card for every story at the same time and discussing any differences.
A product flow diagram, which shows the sequence of and dependencies between the stories across the three releases.
Magic estimation, a quick collaborative technique for sizing a large number of stories early in planning without long debate on each.
Task-level estimation in hours for each story, so that the release map is built from actual rather than relative effort.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique for early planning, for example at project product level, that sizes many stories relative to one another without lengthy discussion (book 8.4.3).

n.0: Simultaneous card estimation is a valid relative technique, but revealing and discussing cards for each of 140 stories takes far longer than one short session allows (book 8.4.3).
n.1: A product flow diagram shows sequence and dependencies, not the size of each story (book 8.4.2).
n.3: Agile estimation is relative rather than in actual hours, and task-level estimates belong to planning the next iteration (book 8.4.3, 8.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During initiation, Simon Archer runs a session with the digital team, Amy Fletcher, two practitioners and Bev Lomax. Starting from the personas, they set out in order what carers and people who may need care do, break those activities into user stories, and then group the stories into the three releases. Simon does not draw up a separate product breakdown structure. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because product-based planning is not part of PRINCE2 Agile, so the team is free to plan from what users do instead of from products.
Yes, because PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map that breaks products into stories.
No, because a product breakdown structure is still needed to show the board which products will be delivered in each stage.
No, because the product owner should group the stories into releases on their own before users and practitioners see the story map.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Product-based planning still applies in PRINCE2 Agile, but the product breakdown structure is recommended to be replaced by a user story map: start from personas, set out user activities in order, break them into stories, then turn the story map into the release map (book 8.3.1, 8.3.2.4).

n.0: Product-based planning is still part of PRINCE2 Agile; it is carried out through story mapping rather than dropped (book 8.3.1).
n.2: The story map removes the need for a separate PBS, and the release map shows the board what each release and stage will deliver (book 8.3.1, 8.3.2.5).
n.3: Story mapping is collaborative and starts from users and their activities, so involving users and practitioners is a strength here (book 8.3.2.4).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Carol Mbeki must approve how personal data flows between the online service and the case system. She asks Simon Archer where she can see which information governance reviews of the interface have been planned and held, who carried them out, on what dates and whether each one passed. Which artifact holds this information?
o: The product register, because it records every product the plan requires and the current status of each of those products.
The issue register, because a failed review of personal data flows is an issue that must be captured and assessed.
The team dashboard, because the Abacus team updates it every sprint and the project manager pulls progress from it.
The quality register, because it records planned and completed quality activities with dates, responsibilities and results.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The quality register records all planned and completed quality activities, with identifiers, method, planned and actual dates, responsibilities, pass or fail results and references to quality records (book 9.3.2, Table 9.1).

n.0: The product register tracks products and their status; the reviews, dates, reviewers and results belong in the quality register (Table 9.1).
n.1: A failed review could lead to an issue being raised, but the record of planned and completed reviews and their results is the quality register (Table 9.1, 11.3.1).
n.2: The team dashboard shows a team's progress through the iteration; it is not the formal record of quality activities and results (Table 12.1, Table 9.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During initiation, Simon Archer drafts the Care Online quality management approach. It records the council's document standards and the accessibility checks for the online pages, and names Carol Mbeki as the reviewer for personal data. It does not say how the digital team or Abacus will test their work within sprints, as Simon expects each team to use its usual methods. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because Abacus works on fixed-price change requests, so its testing methods are covered by its contract rather than by the project.
Yes, because the quality management approach describes standards and responsibilities, while testing belongs in each team plan.
No, because the agile ways of working and the agile testing methods to be used, including the supplier's, should be recorded in the approach.
No, because in PRINCE2 Agile the team Definition of Done takes the place of a quality management approach, so none should be drafted.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the quality management approach must incorporate, document and assure agile ways of working and behaviours, and should record the agile testing methods to be used, including those of suppliers (book 9.3.2, Table 9.1).

n.0: A supplier's contract terms do not take its testing outside the project's quality approach; suppliers' agile testing methods should be recorded there (Table 9.1).
n.1: Standards and responsibilities belong in the approach, but so do the agile testing methods; a team plan sets out the work for the next iteration (Table 9.1, Table 8.1).
n.3: The quality management approach is kept and tailored in PRINCE2 Agile; the Definition of Done sits alongside it (Table 9.1, 9.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In the project initiation workshop, the participants assess the Care Online Agilometer. The 'flexibility on what is delivered' slider is rated low: senior managers have marked 92 of the 100 user stories as Must haves, because they expect every feature named in the mandate to be delivered. Which action is MOST LIKELY to improve this slider?
o: Ask the cabinet to add time tolerance to the twelve-month deadline, so that all of the Must haves can still be delivered.
Challenge whether so many stories are really Must haves, and test the assumptions behind each one with the senior managers.
Arrange co-location days for the digital team and practitioners, so that collaboration between them improves before stage 2.
Record the low rating as an issue in the issue register and report it to the board on the next project dashboard.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The Agilometer is a risk tool that assesses the areas where agile working could cause problems. Flexibility on what is delivered can be raised by challenging whether too many requirements are Must haves, or the assumptions behind them (book 10.3.2.2, 10.3.2.3).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance and the cabinet has said the date cannot move; extending time does not make stakeholders more comfortable flexing scope (Table 3.1, 10.3.2).
n.2: Co-location may help the level of collaboration and the ease of communication, but those are different sliders (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: A low Agilometer rating is a risk to agile working to be managed, not an issue that has already happened, and reporting it does not raise the rating (book 10.3.2, 11.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: The council has a very low appetite for any risk to the safeguarding of adults at risk. In stage 3, the digital team adds risk responses to its product backlog as stories, such as 'flag answers that suggest a safeguarding concern to the duty social worker on the same day', and its product owner prioritizes them alongside the features. The risks stay in the risk register. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a risk-adjusted product backlog keeps stories and risk responses together, so responses are prioritized and built in sprints.
Yes, because once the responses are held in the product backlog, the risk register no longer needs to be updated for these safeguarding risks.
No, because responses to safeguarding risks should be held in the risk register and kept apart from the team's user stories and features.
No, because a risk with a very low appetite has to be escalated to the board as an exception rather than handled by the team.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds user stories and risk responses together, so that responses are prioritized and built within the iteration cycle, while the risk register still records the risks and their status (book 10.4.1, Table 10.1). With a very low appetite for safeguarding risk, building responses into the product is sound.

n.1: The risk register remains the record of identified risks with their status and history, so it continues to be updated (Table 10.1).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile recommends combining stories and risk responses in a risk-adjusted product backlog (book 10.4.1).
n.3: An exception arises when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; planning responses in the backlog is normal risk management (Table 12.1, 10.4.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In sprint 4, carers testing the online assessment through the carers' network say that the question 'Do you provide substantial care?' is confusing. Amy Fletcher suggests plainer wording that asks how many hours a week they spend caring. The change fits within the existing user story and does not affect the project backlog. How should this change be handled?
o: As a request for change to the project baseline, raised in an issue report and decided by the project board.
As an off-specification, because the question as written does not meet the quality criteria agreed for the carers' assessment story.
As an exception, because the story will now take longer than planned and the sprint may not deliver its forecast.
As a detail change, handled informally by the team with its product owner, as it makes the final product more accurate.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change. It is seen as making the final product more accurate and is handled informally at team level rather than through formal baseline change control (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Formal handling by the board or change authority is for changes to the project baseline, and this change leaves the project backlog untouched (book 11.3.2).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; this is a refinement found in testing, within the story as agreed (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2).
n.2: An exception means tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; a small wording change within one story does not do that (Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In sprint 9, the story that sends a completed self-assessment into the Abacus test environment has been stuck for three days. One developer has tried several fixes alone while the rest of the digital team carries on with other stories. The sprint ends in four days. What should the team do FIRST?
o: Swarm on the blocked story, with the whole team focusing on it together until the work can move again.
Trade the blocked story for another story of similar effort, so that the sprint's scope stays the same size.
Raise an issue report to Simon Archer, so that he can escalate the blocker to the project board for a decision.
Ask Simon Archer to prepare an exception report, as the sprint goal is now at risk of being missed.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Swarming means the team focusing together on a stuck task or blocker, and it also speeds up time-critical work. The team should try swarming before escalating an issue to the project manager (book 11.4.2).

n.1: Trading or swapping absorbs a change by replacing requirements of similar effort; it is not a tool for removing a blocker (book 11.4.1).
n.2: Escalation comes after the team has tried to resolve the blocker itself by swarming (book 11.4.2).
n.3: An exception report is for a stage or project plan forecast to exceed tolerance, not for a sprint goal at risk (Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In stage 2, Paul Henshaw asks for a staff screen in Release 1 so that the front door team can triage online carers' assessments. Amy Fletcher, acting as the digital team's product owner, adds a new epic for it to the team's backlog. To keep the month four date, she removes the easy-read versions of the carers' assessment, which are Must haves in the project backlog, without referring the change to anyone. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because trading lets the product owner swap requirements of similar effort so that the release date can still be met.
Yes, because the product owner owns the product backlog and can reprioritize it to absorb change requested by users.
No, because removing Must haves from the project backlog changes the baseline, so it needs formal handling by the board or change authority.
No, because requests for change are considered at stage boundaries, so Paul's request should have waited until the end of stage 2.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A change that alters the project backlog, here removing Must haves agreed in it, is a change to the project baseline and must be handled formally by the project board or whoever holds delegated change authority. Detail changes inside the backlog can be handled at team level, but this is not one (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Trading swaps items of similar effort within agreed scope; it cannot be used to drop Must haves from the project backlog without formal approval (book 11.4.1, 11.3.2).
n.1: The product owner owns the team's product backlog, but the project backlog is the baseline, owned by the chief product owner, and changes to it go formal (book 8.3.2.1, 11.3.2).
n.3: Issues and changes are captured and assessed as they arise during a stage, not held back to its end; what makes this inappropriate is that a baseline change was made informally (Table 13.9, book 11.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: On day 7 of a ten-day sprint in stage 2, the digital team's burn-down chart shows 30 story points still outstanding. The ideal line stands at 9 points for day 7, and the actual line has been above the ideal line since day 3. What does the chart show, and what should the team do?
o: The team is behind and will not finish every story at this rate, so it should focus on the highest-priority stories for the rest of the sprint.
The team is ahead, because more points remain in hand than the ideal line shows, so it can pull further stories into the sprint.
The team is behind, so the product owner should extend the sprint by three days to give the team enough time to finish every story it chose.
The chart shows completed work against the release date, so Simon Archer should update the release map before the team changes its plans.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A burn-down shows outstanding work over time. An actual line above the ideal line means not enough work has been done, so the team cannot finish everything at this rate and should concentrate on the highest-priority items (book 12.4.3).

n.1: Points remaining above the ideal line mean less work has been burned than planned, which is behind, not ahead (book 12.4.3).
n.2: A sprint is a timebox and time has zero tolerance; the content flexes rather than the end date (Table 3.1, Glossary).
n.3: That describes a burn-up at project or product level; this team-level chart shows remaining work over the days of one sprint (book 12.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Midway through stage 3, the Release 2 burn-up chart shows that, at the current velocity, about 80% of the Release 2 Must haves will be complete by month eight. Time and cost have zero tolerance, and the forecast is outside the scope tolerance agreed for the stage. What should Simon Archer do NEXT?
o: Move the Release 2 date to month nine, using the time tolerance in the stage plan to protect delivery of all the Release 2 Must haves.
Record the forecast on the next monthly project dashboard and let the board decide what to do about it at the end of stage 3.
Ask the digital team to work longer hours, including weekends, until its velocity rises enough to deliver every Release 2 Must have by month eight.
Hold an immediate meeting with the product owners and teams to explore options, then raise an exception report if tolerance will be breached.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: An exception occurs when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded, and an updated burn chart can trigger it. The book suggests holding an immediate meeting to discuss options before escalating to the board in an exception report with options and a recommendation (Table 12.1).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, and the cabinet has said the end date cannot move (Table 3.1).
n.1: A forecast breach of tolerance should be raised promptly as an exception rather than left to routine reporting at the end of the stage (Table 12.1).
n.2: Pushing the team to work longer hours does not deal with a forecast tolerance breach; the board needs to see the options in an exception report (Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Simon Archer, who is new to agile, asks the digital team whether he may attend its daily stand-ups. The team agrees that he can listen in to two stand-ups a week. On other days he takes progress information from the team dashboard, and he updates the project dashboard for the board after each progress review. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager is responsible for running the stand-ups so that he can assign the day's tasks to developers.
Yes, because the project manager may attend stand-ups with the team's agreement, and he pulls progress from the team dashboard.
No, because the project manager should receive a written checkpoint report from the product owner instead of using the team dashboard.
No, because the delivery team, rather than the project manager, should update the project dashboard for the board to pull from.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups only with the delivery team's agreement. The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report and the project manager pulls information from it; the project dashboard is updated in progress reviews so that the board can pull from it (Table 12.1).

n.0: Stand-ups belong to the delivery team, and the project manager attends with its agreement; assigning daily tasks would undermine self-management (Table 12.1).
n.2: In PRINCE2 Agile the team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report, and the project manager pulls information from it (Table 12.1).
n.3: In reporting highlights, the project manager assembles the team dashboards and updates the project dashboard so that the board can pull information from it (Table 13.9).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Graham Doyle asks when the software team will finish the remaining Release 2 dashboard work, estimated at 105 story points. The team's velocity over its last three two-week sprints was 18, 24 and 21 points. A contractor says a team he worked with elsewhere managed 30 points a sprint on similar work. Using an empirical approach, what forecast should Andrea Lucas give?
o: About three and a half sprints, using the contractor's figure of 30 points a sprint for similar work.
Between four and five sprints, using the team's best recent sprint of 24 points as the rate.
Close to six sprints, using the team's slowest recent sprint of 18 points as a cautious rate.
About five sprints, using the team's own average velocity of 21 points a sprint.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Empirical planning forecasts from what the team has actually done. Velocity is the average rate of story points delivered per timebox: (18 + 24 + 21) / 3 = 21, and 105 / 21 = 5 sprints, about ten weeks. Use the team's own velocity, not another team's (book 8.3, 12.4.3).

n.0: Another team's velocity on another project is not evidence of this team's rate; empiricism uses your own team's history (book 8.3).
n.1: Velocity is an average over recent timeboxes; picking the best sprint overstates the rate and gives an optimistic forecast (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.2: Picking the slowest sprint understates the rate; the empirical forecast uses the average velocity, which is 21 points (book 8.3, 12.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In initiation, the teams have built a user story map for Smart Maintenance, and Andrea Lucas is turning it into the release map. Sensor hardware has a ten-week lead time, and each fitting needs the machine stopped for four hours, which Colin Ashby must schedule. What should Andrea do as she creates the release map?
o: Write task-level plans now for every sprint in all three releases, so that each fitting date is fixed for Colin Ashby.
Identify interdependencies such as the sensor lead time and machine stops, and plan the releases around them.
Draw a product breakdown structure alongside the story map, so that sensors and gateways appear as separate products.
Fix the number of machines in each release, so that Senticore's fitting schedule cannot change later in the project.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Turning a story map into a release map also defines interdependencies and plans the releases accordingly (book 8.3.1.1). The ten-week lead time and the need to schedule machine stops are exactly such dependencies.

n.0: Planning is just in time: the release map stays high level, and task-level planning is done for the next iteration in managing product delivery (book 8.3, Table 13.12).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, so a separate PBS is not needed (book 8.3.1).
n.3: The board has said the number of machines per release can be adjusted; fixing it removes the flexibility in what is delivered (Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: At the end of Stage 2, Andrea Lucas prepares for the board to approve Stage 3. Because the board is used to detailed plans, she writes a task-by-task plan for every sprint in Release 2, assigns tasks to named developers, and gives it to Leanne Park to follow. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the board must approve a plan for the next stage before Stage 3 can be authorized.
Yes, because a detailed plan suits a board that is used to monthly written reports against a detailed plan.
No, because the team plans tasks for the next iteration only, and the stage plan is a high-level release map.
No, because in PRINCE2 Agile the board approves the team plan for each sprint rather than a stage plan.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The release map serves as the stage plan and stays high level; the team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts a work package and covers the next iteration at task level (book 8.3.2, Table 8.1). Planning is just in time.

n.0: The board does approve the next stage plan, but in PRINCE2 Agile that is the updated release map, not a task-level plan written by the PM (book 8.3.2, 13.7.1).
n.1: The board's habits do not change who plans at task level; detailed plans for later sprints would be out of date before the team reached them (book 8.3).
n.3: Team plans belong to the delivery team in managing product delivery; the board approves the stage plan in the form of the release map (Table 8.1, Table 13.4).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: The software team's Definition of Done says a feature that changes how machines are maintained is done when Mei Chen has approved it under the aerospace quality system. At the sprint review, the new alert-driven maintenance checklist has been built and tested, but Mei's approval is still pending. Leanne Park reports it as 'almost done'. How should the team treat the checklist?
o: Count it as done for this sprint's velocity, and ask Mei Chen to approve it during the next sprint.
Show it as 90% complete on the team dashboard, so that the board can see how close it is to being done.
Treat it as not done, keep it out of the release, and return it to the product backlog for reprioritization.
Ask a tester to sign it off against its acceptance criteria, so that Mei Chen's approval is not needed for it.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The Definition of Done is the shared agreement on what makes an item complete; an item is either done or not done, and there is no 'almost done'. Unfinished work goes back to the backlog to be reprioritized (book 9.3.2.2).

n.0: Counting unfinished work as done inflates velocity and breaks the agreed Definition of Done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Percentages hide the fact that the item is not done; PRINCE2 Agile treats work as done or not done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: Testers check work against acceptance criteria and the team DoD, but they cannot remove an approval step that the DoD itself requires (Table 7.2, book 9.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In initiation, Andrea Lucas writes the quality management approach. It records the software team's automated tests run as each dashboard feature is built, and Senticore's checks agreed before each fitting so that a mounting is proven safe before the machine restarts. It also notes A/B testing of two alert screen designs with engineers. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because it decides early what is tested first or as you go, and records agile testing methods, including the supplier's.
Yes, because A/B testing confirms that the system has been built right against its technical specification.
No, because physical products such as sensor fittings should follow the same fast build-and-fix cycle as the software.
No, because a supplier's own testing methods belong in its contract rather than in the quality management approach.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile advises deciding early how much can be tested first and how much as you go, transferring software practices carefully to other products, and recording agile testing methods, including suppliers', in the quality management approach (book 9.3.2, 9.4.3).

n.1: A/B testing compares two versions with users, which supports validation (building the right thing), not verification against a specification (book 9.4.3).
n.2: Software practices do not transfer directly to physical work: a fitting needs a four-hour stop and must not affect safety certification, so it cannot be rebuilt in minutes (book 9.4.3).
n.3: The quality management approach should record agile testing methods, including those used by suppliers (book 9.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: At the project initiation workshop, participants assess the Agilometer. Senticore's contract requires a formal variation, with legal review and a fee, before any change can be made to the agreed fitting schedule. Several participants mark one slider low because of this. Which Agilometer slider are they MOST LIKELY to have marked low?
o: Advantageous environmental conditions
Ability to work iteratively and deliver incrementally
Level of collaboration
Ease of communication
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The 'advantageous environmental conditions' slider covers how far the overall working environment supports agile, including contracts that do not inhibit agile working (book 10.3.2.2). A contract that makes every schedule change a legal variation is such an inhibitor.

n.1: This slider is about how easily benefit can be delivered through regular partial deliveries; the releases are still planned in increments here (book 10.3.2.2).
n.2: Level of collaboration reflects how well people work together; the problem described is a contractual constraint in the environment (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: Ease of communication concerns how easily all parties can talk to each other; the contract terms are an environmental condition (book 10.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Hannah Reece's cleansing of the old maintenance records, and the IT security review that must pass before sensors connect to the network, are both responses to risks in the risk register. Leanne Park wants the software team to plan and prioritize this work alongside its user stories in each sprint. Which technique supports this?
o: A cumulative risk burn-down chart, updated at each sprint planning session to show the total risk exposure for the project.
The Agilometer, reassessed at each agile enablement workshop to show the risks of agile working.
A cumulative flow diagram, showing how many risk responses sit in each workflow state over time.
A risk-adjusted product backlog, holding risk responses and user stories together in one prioritized list.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A risk-adjusted product backlog places risk responses in the product backlog alongside user stories, so they are prioritized and planned together (book 10.4.1).

n.0: A cumulative risk burn-down tracks total risk exposure across iterations; it does not plan the response work alongside stories (book 10.4.2).
n.1: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, such as collaboration or contracts, not project risks like data quality or security (book 10.3.2).
n.2: A cumulative flow diagram shows work in each workflow state to reveal bottlenecks; it does not prioritize risk responses (book 12.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: From Stage 2, Andrea Lucas asks Tomasz Zielinski to make risk identification a fixed agenda item in every team planning workshop and every team retrospective. New risks, such as gateways losing signal near the large presses, are recorded and assessed by the team before Andrea updates the risk register. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the Agilometer should be reassessed by the team at every planning session and retrospective.
Yes, because in agile, identifying risks is a fixed part of every planning session and retrospective.
No, because risks should be identified by the project manager and recorded before they are shared with the teams.
No, because new risks should be gathered at progress reviews, where the project dashboard shows current risks.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile adapts the five-step risk technique so that identification is a fixed part of every planning session and team or project retrospective, where risks are gathered and documented (book 10.3.1).

n.0: The Agilometer is assessed in the project initiation workshop and reassessed in agile enablement workshops; it is not the identification step in team workshops (book 10.3.2, Table 13.5).
n.2: The team often sees risks first; the book builds identification into team planning and retrospectives rather than leaving it to the PM (book 10.3.1).
n.3: Progress reviews look at current risks, but identification is built into every planning session and retrospective, where risks can surface early (book 10.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During a Release 1 sprint, engineers trialling the dashboard ask for the vibration trend to appear above the temperature trend on each machine screen. The change sits within an existing user story, takes the team about an hour, and does not affect the project backlog. How should it be handled?
o: Raise a request for change to the board, because any change to an agreed product alters the project's baseline.
Handle it as a detail change at team level with Leanne Park, without the formal change procedure.
Record it as an off-specification, because the screen no longer matches the layout first agreed.
Ask Ruth Kenyon as chief product owner to approve it as a change to the project backlog before work starts.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change: it makes the final product more accurate and is handled informally at team level. Changes that alter the project backlog are baseline changes and go through the formal route (book 11.3.2).

n.0: Only changes that alter the project backlog are baseline changes needing a formal decision; this one sits inside an existing story (book 11.3.2).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; here the users are improving a layout within the story (book 11.3.1).
n.3: The project backlog is not affected, so there is nothing for the chief product owner to approve formally; the team handles it with its product owner (book 11.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In a Release 2 sprint, one developer has been stuck for three days because data from two gateways drops out at random. The other developers carry on with their own stories. Leanne Park records the blocker as an issue and asks Andrea Lucas to raise it with the board straight away. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a problem with an immediate negative impact is a type of issue that should go to the board.
Yes, because trading lets the blocked story be swapped for another story of similar effort from the backlog.
No, because blockers belong on the team dashboard and are not raised with the project manager as issues.
No, because the team should first swarm on the blocker together, and escalate it if they cannot resolve it.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Swarming means the team focuses together on a stuck task or blocker. PRINCE2 Agile suggests trying swarming before escalating an issue to the project manager, and escalating further only if needed (book 11.4.2).

n.0: A problem is an issue type, but that does not mean it goes straight to the board; the team should first try to resolve it, and the PM handles issues within tolerance (book 11.3.1, 11.4.2).
n.1: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort to absorb change; it is not a way to remove a blocker (book 11.4.1).
n.2: Blockers the team cannot resolve should be escalated to the PM as issues; the point is to swarm first, not to keep them off the PM's desk (book 11.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Graham Doyle tells Andrea Lucas that the board expects a monthly written report against a detailed plan, as on previous Draycott projects. Andrea wants to apply the progress practice in an agile way while keeping the board in control. What should she propose?
o: Send the board each team's dashboard every month, so that it can see the detailed status of every team.
Send the board an exception report each month, setting out options and a recommendation for the next month.
A project dashboard with release status, burn charts and current risks and issues, reviewed at progress reviews.
A monthly chart of spend against budget and days used against the end date, to show how much tolerance remains.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report: it shows release status, burn charts and current risks and issues, is updated and reviewed in progress review workshops, and the board pulls information from it (Table 12.1, book 12.3.2.1).

n.0: Team dashboards replace checkpoint reports and serve the PM; the board's view is the project dashboard (Table 12.1).
n.1: An exception report is produced when a plan is forecast to exceed tolerance, not as a routine monthly report (Table 12.1).
n.3: With zero tolerance on time and cost, tracking them against tolerance adds little; the main aspect to monitor is what is delivered, through burn charts (book 12.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In Stage 4, Dev Patel warns that a component shortage will delay the Factory B sensors by six weeks. The updated burn-up chart now forecasts that the Must have stories for Release 3 cannot all be delivered by month 12, which would exceed the project's scope tolerance. What should Andrea Lucas do NEXT?
o: Move the closure date back by six weeks, as the delay is caused by the supplier rather than by the project.
Record the delay in the daily log and report it on the project dashboard when Stage 4 comes to an end.
Send the board an exception report straight away, recommending that Release 3 be cancelled.
Hold an immediate meeting with the people involved to explore the options, before escalating to the board.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: An updated burn chart can trigger an exception. PRINCE2 Agile advises holding an immediate meeting to discuss options before escalating to the board, which is then done through an exception report with options and a recommendation (Table 12.1).

n.0: Time has zero tolerance and the end date is fixed by the aerospace contract; the PM cannot move it (Table 3.1).
n.1: A forecast breach of tolerance must be acted on now; waiting until the end of the stage removes the board's chance to decide (Table 12.1).
n.2: Escalation comes after options have been explored; jumping straight to a recommendation skips that step (Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During the busy weeks before Release 1, Andrea Lucas asks the software team whether she may attend some of its daily stand-ups to hear about blockers first hand. The team agrees, and Andrea listens without assigning work, then reads the rest of the status from the team dashboard. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager may attend stand-ups with the team's agreement, and pulls status from the team dashboard.
Yes, because the project manager should attend stand-ups to replace the checkpoint reports the team would send her.
No, because the stand-up is a team event, and the project manager should get status from the team coach's weekly report.
No, because status should come from the project dashboard, which the project manager updates after each progress review.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups when the delivery team agrees, and pulls progress information from the team dashboard, which replaces the checkpoint report (Table 12.1).

n.1: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report; stand-ups are the team's own event, which the PM attends by agreement, not as a reporting channel (Table 12.1).
n.2: The PM may attend with the team's agreement, and PRINCE2 Agile uses the team dashboard for team status, not a weekly report from the team coach (Table 12.1).
n.3: The project dashboard serves the board; the PM pulls team-level status from the team dashboards (Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: The service design team completed 14, 18 and 16 story points in its first three iterations of Stage 3, and about 96 points of its Release 2 work remain. Ellen Price suggests using the digital team's velocity of 24 points per iteration, which would show Release 2 finishing sooner. How many more iterations should Sally Greaves forecast for the service design team's remaining work?
o: Four, based on the digital team's velocity of 24 points per iteration.
Six, based on the team's own average of 16 points per iteration.
About five, based on the team's best iteration so far of 18 points.
Seven, based on the team's first iteration of 14 points.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile plans empirically: start work, measure how much gets done and forecast from that rate, using the team's own velocity rather than another team's (book 8.3). The team's average is (14 + 18 + 16) / 3 = 16 points, and 96 / 16 = 6 iterations.

n.0: Velocity should come from the team doing the work; another team's rate says nothing about this team's capacity (book 8.3).
n.2: Velocity is the average rate over timeboxes; using the best iteration gives an optimistic forecast (book 8.3, 12.4.3).
n.3: A single early iteration is not the team's measured average; the forecast should use 16 points per iteration (book 8.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In initiation, the service design and digital teams have built a story map. Starting from their personas, they listed tenant activities from reporting a repair to confirming it is fixed, ordered them in time and broke them into user stories. Sally Greaves now needs a plan for the project. What should she do NEXT?
o: Create a product breakdown structure from the story map, to act as the formal basis for the project plan and for its releases.
Ask each team to write task-level plans for all of its iterations in Stages 2 to 4 before the project is authorized.
Estimate each user story in hours with Coastline, so that a fixed completion date can be set for every story in Release 3.
Cluster the user stories into releases on a release map, showing dependencies such as the diagnosis guide before appointment slots.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: Turning a story map into a release map clusters stories into releases and defines interdependencies, so releases can be planned accordingly; the release map serves as the project plan (book 8.3.1.1, 8.3.2.5, 8.4.4).

n.0: In PRINCE2 Agile the product breakdown structure is recommended to be replaced by the user story map, so a separate PBS is not needed (book 8.3.1).
n.1: Planning is just in time: task-level plans are made for the next iteration in managing product delivery, not for the whole project in initiation (book 8.3.2).
n.2: Agile estimation is relative (for example story points), and plans fix the timebox rather than a date for each story (book 8.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: At the end of Stage 2, Sally Greaves prepares for the board's decision on Stage 3. She spends two weeks producing a detailed plan of every task for every iteration of Releases 2 and 3, with each task assigned to a named team member, so that the board can see exactly who will do what until month 12. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the board must see a detailed plan for the whole of the next stage before it can authorize that stage to begin.
Yes, because detailed plans for Releases 2 and 3 help to keep time and cost within their zero tolerances.
No, because task-level planning is for the next iteration, done by the teams; a stage boundary needs a high-level release map.
No, because the chief product owner plans each team member's tasks when it sets the priorities across all of the teams.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile plans just in time: the stage boundary produces a high-level update of the release map, and task-level planning happens for the next iteration only, by the team in managing product delivery (book 8.3.2, 8.4.4). Planning every task to month 12 wastes effort and removes the teams' self-management.

n.0: The board approves the next stage plan, which in PRINCE2 Agile is the updated release map, not a task-level plan of every iteration (book 8.3.2, 13.7.1).
n.1: Time and cost are protected by flexing what is delivered, not by detailed upfront task plans that will change as the teams learn (book Table 3.1, 8.3).
n.3: The CPO prioritizes the project backlog across teams; the delivery team produces its own team plan when it accepts a work package (book Table 7.2, 8.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: At the end of an iteration in Stage 2, the digital team reviews the story 'As a tenant, I want to upload a photo of my repair so that the engineer brings the right parts'. Photo upload from smartphones meets the team's Definition of Done, but upload from tablets has not yet been tested with tenants. Ellen Price says the story is 'almost done'. How should the team treat the story?
o: Report it as 90% done on the team dashboard and finish testing the tablet upload early in the next iteration.
Count the whole story as done, because the way most tenants upload photos already meets the Definition of Done.
Split it: count the smartphone part as done and return the tablet part to the product backlog to be reprioritized.
Leave the whole story as not done and carry it into the next iteration without changing its priority.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The Definition of Done allows only 'done' or 'not done'; there is no 'almost done'. A partly done story is split, with the done part counted and the rest returned to the backlog for reprioritization (book 9.3.2.2).

n.0: Percentage-complete reporting is the 'almost done' the Definition of Done rules out; the story should be split (book 9.3.2.2).
n.1: Untested work does not meet the Definition of Done, so the whole story cannot count as done (book 9.3.2.2).
n.3: The done part should be recognized and the remainder returned to the backlog for reprioritization, rather than carried over as one block (book 9.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Some appointments are wasted because nobody is at home when the engineer arrives. Ellen Price has two versions of the text message sent the day before an appointment: one gives the engineer's name and arrival window, the other adds a reply option to rearrange. She wants evidence from tenants on the pilot estate about which version reduces missed appointments. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
o: Refactoring, improving the structure of the message while keeping what it does the same.
A/B testing, sending each version to similar groups of tenants and comparing the results.
Technical debt, recording the cost of the weaker version so that it can be removed later.
Test first, writing the message's acceptance criteria before either version is sent.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A/B testing compares two versions with users to see which performs better (book 9.4.3). Sending each message to comparable groups on the pilot estate and comparing missed appointments gives the evidence Ellen needs.

n.0: Refactoring changes internal structure without changing behaviour; it does not compare two versions with users (book 9.4.1).
n.2: Technical debt describes the consequences of poor design owed as future work; it is not a way of comparing versions with users (book 9.4.2).
n.3: Deciding tests first is useful, but it does not give comparative evidence from tenants on which version works better (book 9.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Every new phone script must pass the association's existing compliance review before advisers use it with tenants. In initiation, the service design team decides to keep this review as part of its quality control for scripts instead of designing a new method, and Sally Greaves records the decision in the project initiation documentation. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because an organization's own procedures may be used, and recording this as a tailoring decision in the PID is correct.
Yes, because the compliance review removes the need for a Definition of Done for the service design team's scripts.
No, because the quality management approach must describe agile testing methods rather than existing procedures.
No, because tailoring decisions about quality should be recorded in the quality register rather than in the PID.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In PRINCE2 Agile, an organization's own design, development and testing procedures may be used instead of the standard quality cycle, and this should be recorded as a tailoring decision in the PID (book 9.3.1). Keeping the compliance review is sensible for scripts used with tenants.

n.1: The review is one quality control activity; the team still needs a Definition of Done to agree when a script is complete (book 9.3.2.2).
n.2: The quality management approach records agile ways of working and testing methods, but it may include an organization's own procedures as a tailoring choice (book 9.3.1, 9.3.2).
n.3: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities and their results; tailoring decisions are recorded in the PID (book 9.3.1, 9.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: The risk management approach for Repairs Reimagined is being updated. In Stage 1, risks were identified only at the monthly board meeting, and several risks that advisers raised in team meetings were never recorded. How should risk identification be built into the service design team's iterations?
o: Hold a separate risk workshop at each stage boundary, where the board identifies the risks for the next release.
Ask project support to identify the risks each month from the team dashboards and add them to the risk register.
Reassess the Agilometer with the board at the end of each iteration, so that the risks to the repairs service are identified there.
Make risk identification a fixed part of each team planning session and retrospective, where risks are gathered and recorded.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: PRINCE2 Agile adapts the five-step risk technique to iterations: identification is a fixed part of every planning session and team or project retrospective, where risks are gathered and documented, while implementing and communicating responses run through the iteration cycles (book 10.3.1, Figure 10.1).

n.0: Risks can surface at any time; leaving identification to stage boundaries repeats the Stage 1 problem of missed risks (book 10.3.1).
n.1: Project support can help with risk administration, but identification should happen with the team in its planning sessions and retrospectives (book 10.3.1, Table 7.2).
n.2: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, reviewed in initiation and the agile enablement workshop; it is not the tool for identifying all project risks each iteration (book 10.3.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In the project initiation workshop, participants assess the Agilometer. They note that Coastline is paid per job, that any change to how engineers work must be agreed with Coastline, and that the current contract gives engineers no reason to trial new ways of working. Which Agilometer slider is MOST affected by these points?
o: Level of collaboration, covering how closely the customer and the supplier work together on the project.
Ease of communication, covering how easily information passes between all the parties involved.
Advantageous environmental conditions, covering whether the environment, including contracts, supports agile.
Flexibility on what is delivered, covering how comfortable the stakeholders are with flexing the scope.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The advantageous environmental conditions slider covers whether the overall working environment supports agile, including contracts that do not inhibit agile working (book 10.3.2.2). A pay-per-job contract that discourages trialling new ways of working sits here.

n.0: The points describe how the pay-per-job contract and its terms shape the working environment, not how closely the parties work together; contracts that inhibit agile sit under environmental conditions (book 10.3.2.2).
n.1: Nothing in the points concerns how information flows; they concern contract terms (book 10.3.2.2).
n.3: This slider is about stakeholders' comfort with prioritizing and flexing scope, not about contracts (book 10.3.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In the project initiation workshop, Sally Greaves asks everyone present, including Frank Tolley from Coastline, Winston Clarke from the tenants' panel and members of both teams, to rate the Agilometer sliders anonymously in small groups. She then combines their ratings into one Agilometer for the project. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the Agilometer helps identify agile working risks, and all participants assess it before the views are combined.
Yes, because the Agilometer is a progress tool that shows the board how quickly each of the delivery teams is completing work.
No, because the project manager should rate the Agilometer, as the person who runs the project day to day.
No, because the Agilometer belongs to the agile enablement workshop, so it should not be assessed during the initiation stage.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: The Agilometer identifies and monitors the risks of agile working. In the project initiation workshop all participants assess it, anonymously or in groups, and the results are combined into one project Agilometer (book 10.3.1, 10.3.2, Table 13.7). Including Coastline and tenants gives a fuller view.

n.1: The Agilometer is a risk tool in the risk practice; it does not measure delivery speed (book 10.3.2).
n.2: The book has all participants assess it so that different views are captured; one person's rating would miss them (Table 13.7).
n.3: The Agilometer is first assessed in the project initiation workshop and reassessed in agile enablement workshops in later stages (Table 13.5, Table 13.7).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: During Stage 2, Winston Clarke asks for online reporting in Release 1 to be available in five community languages. The request would add a new Must have epic to the project backlog and would need extra work from the digital team. How should this request be handled?
o: As a request for change: record it in the issue register, assess it and refer it to the board or the delegated change authority.
As a detail change: ask the digital team's product owner to add it to the product backlog and trade out a story of similar effort.
As a problem: ask the digital team to swarm on the translation work until it is finished within the current iteration.
As an exception: prepare an exception report at once, because a new requirement takes the project beyond its scope tolerance.
