Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A new requirement that changes the project backlog is a change to the project baseline, handled formally and decided by the project board or the person(s) with delegated change authority; it is captured as an issue (request for change) and assessed before the decision (book 11.3.1, 11.3.2, Table 11.1).

n.1: Detail changes do not affect the project backlog; a new Must have epic does, so it needs formal handling (book 11.3.2).
n.2: Swarming helps with a stuck task or blocker; a new requirement is a request for change, not a problem (book 11.3.1, 11.4.2).
n.3: An exception arises when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; the request has not yet been assessed or approved (book Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: In Stage 3, tenants testing the diagnosis guide ask for a short question about boiler error codes to be added to the heating section. The request fits within an existing epic and does not change the project backlog. Raj Malhotra, the team's product owner, agrees with the team to swap out a lower-priority story of similar effort so that the iteration's scope does not grow. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because swarming lets the whole team focus together on the new question so that it is finished quickly.
Yes, because trading swaps in work of similar effort, absorbing a detail change at team level with the product owner.
No, because a request from tenant testers is a request for change that the project board has to decide.
No, because trading is a technique for removing blockers, so it is not the way to absorb a new request.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change, handled informally at team level (book 11.3.2). Trading or swapping replaces requirements with others of similar effort so that change is absorbed without growing scope, with priorities agreed with the product owner (book 11.4.1).

n.0: Swarming is the team focusing together on a stuck task or blocker; what Raj and the team did is trading (book 11.4.2, 11.4.1).
n.2: Who raises a request does not make it a baseline change; this one does not change the project backlog, so it is a detail change for the team (book 11.3.2).
n.3: Trading absorbs change by swapping work of similar effort; removing blockers is swarming (book 11.4.1, 11.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: The board, which includes tenant members, is used to receiving quarterly written reports. For Repairs Reimagined, Sally Greaves wants the board to be able to see release status, burn charts and current risks and issues between its meetings, without waiting for a written report. What should she set up?
o: Team dashboards for each team, sent to the board after each iteration so that members can see the detailed tasks.
A project dashboard, updated and reviewed in progress review workshops, from which the board pulls the information it needs.
Fortnightly checkpoint reports from each product owner, combined by project support into a written report sent to the board between meetings.
An end stage report at the end of each iteration, so that the board can decide whether each iteration should continue.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: In PRINCE2 Agile the project dashboard replaces the highlight report: it shows release status, burn charts, current risks and issues and other trends, is updated and reviewed in progress review workshops, and the board pulls information from it (book 12.3.2.1, Table 12.1).

n.0: Team dashboards replace checkpoint reports; the project manager pulls from them, and they are too detailed for board-level control (book Table 12.1).
n.2: Checkpoint reports are team-to-PM reports, replaced in PRINCE2 Agile by team dashboards; the board needs the project dashboard (book Table 12.1).
n.3: End stage reports belong to stage ends, not iterations, and the board does not authorize individual iterations (book Table 12.1, 13.7.1).

Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.q: Because the £1.3 million budget and the twelve-month timescale are both fixed, Sally Greaves proposes that the main progress measure reported to the board each fortnight should be spend against budget and days used against the timescale. She does not plan to report which features or user stories have been delivered until the end of each stage. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because time and cost are the aspects the board has said will not change, so they need the closest fortnightly tracking.
Yes, because reporting delivered features each fortnight would add detail that belongs on the team dashboards.
No, because the reports should be written in the quarterly format that the tenant board members are used to.
No, because with zero tolerance on time and cost, what is delivered is the key aspect, and burn charts suit every level.
Agile Practitioner: Plans to Progress.w: With zero tolerance on time and cost, flexibility in what is delivered is the primary performance aspect of interest, so burn charts suit every level; tracking spend and time against tolerances that are zero adds little (book 12.3.1). The board should see progress in delivered features each period.

n.0: Fixing time and cost is exactly why they are not the useful measure: the aspect that moves is what is delivered (book 12.3.1, Table 3.1).
n.1: Team dashboards hold team detail, but the board still needs to see what is being delivered at project level, for example burn-up charts on the project dashboard (book 12.3.1, 12.4.3).
n.2: PRINCE2 Agile favours informal, visual reporting such as dashboards and burn charts; the problem is what is measured, not the board's preferred format (book 12.2, 12.3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In starting up a project, Bronwen Hale runs the project canvas workshop for Fair Fares. The participants agree that daily commuters, passengers with a disability or long-term condition, and occasional leisure travellers are the key groups the app must serve, and they rank the three groups in order of importance. Under which topic of the project canvas workshop is this discussed?
o: Persona definition.
User group definition.
Benefits analysis.
Business value definition.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In the project canvas workshop, the user group definition topic identifies one to three key user groups and prioritizes them (book 13.2.4.1, Table 13.2). Persona definition comes later, in the project initiation workshop.

n.0: Personas are defined in the project initiation workshop during initiation; the canvas workshop identifies and ranks the key user groups (Table 13.7, Table 13.2).
n.2: Benefits analysis identifies benefits and dis-benefits and their tolerances, not which user groups matter most (Table 13.2).
n.3: Business value definition concerns the value the project brings to the organization, not the identification and ranking of user groups (Table 13.2).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: After the mandate is issued, Rhys Pengelly works with Matteo Ricci, Gemma Lowther and Bronwen Hale to agree what Fair Fares will deliver, and creates the project backlog with epics for delay detection, payment and alerts. At the same time, Bronwen leads work on the project canvas. Which activity of the 'starting up a project' process is this, and why?
o: Select the project approach, as the team is deciding how the epics will be delivered by the three teams.
Assemble the project brief, as the scope and exclusions of the project are being confirmed for the board.
Plan the initiation stage, as the epics will be refined further while the project is being initiated.
Prepare the outline business case, as the project canvas and the project backlog are drafted in it.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In PRINCE2 Agile's version of 'prepare the outline business case', the project executive leads the project canvas from the mandate, and the project manager, with the CPO, senior supplier and executive, defines what is to be delivered and creates the project backlog (book Table 13.1).

n.0: Selecting the project approach evaluates delivery solutions and tailoring needs; drafting the canvas and creating the project backlog belong to preparing the outline business case (Table 13.1).
n.1: Assembling the brief confirms objectives, scope, tolerances, constraints and dependencies once the outline business case exists; it is not where the canvas and backlog are first drafted (Table 13.1).
n.2: Planning the initiation stage sets the constraints, release map and controls for initiation; it does not cover defining the deliverables or the canvas (Table 13.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In stage 2, the project board, Priyanka Desai and two business representatives hold an agile enablement workshop. They have already agreed that resistance in customer relations is the most serious threat to agile adoption, and they now agree practical actions, such as inviting Yusuf Bello's supervisors to each product demo. Under which topic of the workshop is this done?
o: Risk planning.
Agilometer assessment review.
Risk identification.
Risk assessment.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The agile enablement workshop moves through Agilometer assessment review, risk identification, risk assessment and risk planning, where practical mitigation steps are agreed (book Table 13.5). The risk has already been prioritized, so agreeing actions is risk planning.

n.1: This topic links the Agilometer's risk areas to agile values and transformation objectives to build a shared view of key risks; it precedes the planning of actions (Table 13.5).
n.2: Risk identification looks for further agile-adoption threats and opportunities; this risk has already been identified (Table 13.5).
n.3: Risk assessment estimates probability and impact and prioritizes; the group has already ranked this risk and is now deciding responses (Table 13.5).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Midway through stage 3, Rhys Pengelly asks Bronwen Hale whether passengers with paper season tickets should be included in Release 2. The question is outside his authority but does not threaten any tolerance. Bronwen discusses it with the other board members by phone and gives him an answer the next day. Which activity of the 'directing a project' process is this?
o: Authorize a stage or exception plan.
Authorize the project.
Give ongoing direction.
Authorize initiation.

Dr Kwame Mensah, Daniel Ferreira and Jamal agree who will support the hub after the project, what the wellbeing service needs to run it day to day, and the actions for measuring waiting times after the project ends. In which workshop, and under which topic, is this agreed?
o: The project closure workshop, under final product demo
The project closure workshop, under final handover planning
The project closure workshop, under progress review
The release planning workshop, under release planning
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The project closure workshop formally concludes the project; its final handover planning topic agrees support responsibilities, operational requirements and the actions for benefits after the project (book 13.8.4, Table 13.19).

n.0: The final product demo shows the product for user acceptance and readiness for handover; it does not agree support responsibilities and benefits actions (book Table 13.19).
n.2: The progress review topic of the closure workshop updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer, not the support and benefits arrangements (book Table 13.19).
n.3: The release planning workshop is held at stage boundaries to plan the next stage; at the end of the project the handover is planned in the closure workshop (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.19).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Most of the university's leaders are used to annual plans and committee approvals. The project board decides to hold an agile enablement workshop in each stage with an agile coach from the IT department and two business representatives, to reassess the Agilometer and agree practical steps to reduce risks to agile adoption. Is this an appropriate application of the directing a project process, and why?
o: Yes, because the agile enablement workshop is where the agile transformation plan for the whole university is produced.
Yes, because regular Agilometer reassessment with the board, coaches and business representatives keeps agile risks under review.
No, because the Agilometer is assessed once in the project initiation workshop and is not revisited in later stages.
No, because risks to agile adoption are a progress matter and belong in the progress review workshop instead.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The agile enablement workshop in directing a project provides regular Agilometer assessments in initiation and later stages, so that agile maturity and agile risks are reviewed; it is for the project board, agile coaches and business representatives (book Table 13.5). That suits a university with leaders new to agile.

n.0: The agile transformation plan, where needed, is produced in initiation through the project initiation workshop, not in the agile enablement workshop (book Table 13.7).
n.2: The Agilometer is first assessed in the project initiation workshop, but it is reassessed regularly in later stages through agile enablement workshops (book 10.3.2, Table 13.5).
n.3: The Agilometer is a risk tool, and reviewing risks to agile adoption with the board is the purpose of the agile enablement workshop (book 10.3.2, Table 13.5).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the release planning workshop at the end of stage 2, Jamal Hussain asks the web team and the Northmere team to plan every task for all the sprints of Release 2 in detail, with named developers and hours, so that the board can approve the stage 3 plan at task level. Is this an appropriate application of the managing a stage boundary process, and why?
o: Yes, because the board approves the next stage plan, so it needs the full detail of each task to authorize the stage.
Yes, because time is fixed for Release 2, so every task has to be planned before the stage begins to protect the date.
No, because the stage boundary updates the release map at a high level, and task planning is done before each sprint.
No, because the release planning workshop is for the project board, and the delivery teams should not take part in it.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: At a stage boundary the release map is updated at a high level for the next stage; detailed task planning is done for the next iteration in managing product delivery, through the team planning workshop (book 13.7.4.1, 8.3.2).

n.0: The board approves the next stage plan as an updated release map; it does not need task-level detail, which the teams plan each sprint (book Table 13.4, 8.3.2).
n.1: Time is fixed, but it is protected by flexing what is delivered, not by planning every task in advance (book Table 3.1, 8.3.2).
n.3: The release planning workshop aligns the teams with the vision and plans the next stage, so the teams take part (book 13.7.4.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In starting up a project, Jamal Hussain learns that the university council usually expects a long written business case before it backs a project. He must produce the business justification for the hub in a way that fits PRINCE2 Agile while keeping the council's confidence. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
o: Professor Greer leads a project canvas workshop with key stakeholders, adding supporting detail where the council needs it.
Jamal writes a 40-page business case on his own, because the council's committees expect a full written document before approval.
The business justification is postponed until Release 1 has shown value, because agile projects learn as they go along.
The web team defines the hub's business value in its first sprint review, using the feedback it gathers from students.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In starting up, the executive leads development of the project canvas from the mandate, and the project canvas workshop builds a shared understanding of the project's core elements (book Table 13.1, 13.2.4.1). Tailoring to suit the project allows extra detail where the organization's governance needs it (book 5.2.1.7).

n.1: The executive should lead the canvas with stakeholders; a long document written by one person loses the shared understanding the canvas workshop builds (book Table 13.1, 13.2.4.1).
n.2: Every project needs business justification from the start; agile tailors the business case into a canvas rather than postponing it (book 5.2.1.1, 6.3.1).
n.3: Business value is defined in the project canvas workshop in starting up, before delivery begins, not by a delivery team in its first sprint (book Table 13.2).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: To save time before Welcome Week, Daniel Ferreira suggests that the web team hold its team planning workshop and team retrospective once per release rather than every sprint. Jamal Hussain wants to tailor managing product delivery without losing the purpose of these workshops. Which tailoring is MOST appropriate?
o: Hold both workshops once per release as suggested, since a release of two to four sprints is a natural point to plan and reflect.
Replace the team retrospective with a written review by Jamal at the end of each stage, and keep team planning once per release.
Plan all the Release 1 sprints in one team planning workshop in initiation, and hold one retrospective after Welcome Week.
Keep a short team planning workshop before each sprint and a team retrospective at the end of each sprint, sized to two weeks.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The team planning workshop prepares for the next iteration and the team retrospective reflects on the last one (book 13.6.4.1, 13.6.4.2). Both are tied to the iteration, and risks are also identified in every planning session and retrospective (book 10.3.1); they can be kept short to suit two-week sprints.

n.0: Planning and reflecting once per release loses the iteration-by-iteration planning, feedback and risk identification these workshops exist for (book 13.6.4.1, 13.6.4.2, 10.3.1).
n.1: A retrospective is the team's own reflection on its last iteration; a project manager's written stage review cannot replace it (book 13.6.4.2).
n.2: Task-level planning is done for the next iteration only, and retrospectives happen at the end of each iteration (book 8.3.2, 5.6.3.3).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Release 2 hands the staff case view over to the wellbeing service, whose 45 staff work across two campuses and often part-time. Dr Kwame Mensah asks Jamal Hussain what the transition to operations should include so that the service can run and keep improving the hub. Which approach BEST follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Send the full technical documentation to every member of staff, and close the teams' dashboards and backlogs at handover.
Keep the web team handling triage until staff feel confident, and begin training the staff once the project has closed.
Hand over the backlog, dashboards and tools, give tailored training with quick guides, and set up regular feedback loops.
Leave feedback from staff until the post-project benefits review, so that they have time to get used to the hub first.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Transition to operations hands over agile artifacts and tools so agile practices continue, provides tailored end-user training with guides and videos, sets out operational procedures and escalation paths, and creates regular feedback loops such as surveys and check-ins (book 14.2.1).

n.0: Closing the artifacts and tools stops agile practices continuing after handover, and technical documentation is no substitute for tailored training (book 14.2.1).
n.1: Training should help staff adopt the product at handover; delaying it leaves the service unable to run the hub (book 14.2.1).
n.3: Regular feedback loops should start at transition so that actionable insights are collected early (book 14.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: The project will close in the spring term. Dr Kwame Mensah already has more ideas, such as text reminders before appointments and a live chat with advisers, and the web team will keep working on the hub as part of normal business. How should these further enhancements BEST be handled after the project closes?
o: Manage the hub as a product, with a vision and a flexible roadmap adjusted from feedback, prioritizing work in short cycles.
Start a new PRINCE2 Agile project for each enhancement, so that each has its own business justification and board.
Freeze the hub for a year after closure so that it stays stable, then gather all the ideas into one large upgrade.
Fix a detailed three-year roadmap of enhancements now, so that the web team knows what it will build each term.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Agile product management keeps a high-level product vision with a flexible roadmap that is adjusted from stakeholder and customer feedback, and works in short cycles prioritized by value (book 14.2.2.1). Enhancements after a project are handled through product management iterations.

n.1: Enhancements after the project are handled through agile product management iterations, not by starting a new project for each one (book 14.2.2.1).
n.2: Agile product management delivers value in short cycles from feedback; holding ideas back for one large upgrade loses that (book 14.2.2.1).
n.3: A detailed fixed roadmap cannot be continually adjusted from feedback, which agile product management relies on (book 14.2.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Jamal Hussain can use an AI assistant approved by the university. Staff keep asking him the same questions about how the hub will work, and he wants more time for conversations with doubtful staff such as Tom Brierley. Separately, Peter Langley suggests that AI could pick out students who need support. Which statement BEST describes how AI can support the project?
o: AI could decide which students are at risk for Release 3, removing the need for the ethics committee's review of the early-warning feature.
A project chatbot could answer staff's common questions, freeing Jamal for key conversations, while decisions stay with people.
AI could replace the communication management approach by writing and sending every project update to staff each week.
AI could approve the release map at each stage boundary, because it forecasts time and cost more accurately than the board.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: AI can support people by automating the collection and sharing of information and by running a project chatbot for common questions, freeing leaders for strategic communication. It supports, but does not remove, human decision-making or the need to communicate with stakeholders (book 15.4.2).

n.0: AI does not remove human decision-making; the ethics committee's review and the decision on the feature stay with people (book 15.4.2).
n.2: AI can help spread information, but it does not remove the need to communicate with stakeholders, which the communication management approach plans (book 15.4.2, 4.4).
n.3: AI can refine forecasts for time, cost and benefits, but approving the next stage plan stays with the project board (book 15.4.1, Table 13.4).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In starting up a project, Gwen Tallowby runs the project canvas workshop. The group compares doing nothing, building click and collect in-house with Tallis exposing stock levels, buying a ready-made module from a retail platform, and selling through a third-party marketplace that offers collection. They agree which of these to take forward. Under which topic of the project canvas workshop is this discussed?
o: Business option selection.
Business value definition.
Scope definition.
Benefits analysis.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Business option selection is the project canvas workshop topic in which the group weighs the alternative ways of meeting the need, including doing nothing, and chooses the one to pursue (book Table 13.2).

n.1: Business value definition sets out the value the project should bring to the organization; it does not compare alternative solutions (book Table 13.2).
n.2: Scope definition covers the timeline and tolerance, the scope as epics prioritized with MoSCoW, and dependencies, once an option has been chosen (book Table 13.2).
n.3: Benefits analysis identifies benefits and dis-benefits, usually in small groups, and their tolerances; it does not choose between options (book Table 13.2).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Near the end of starting up a project, Patrick Dunne confirms the project's objectives, scope, tolerances and constraints. He also records that Release 1 depends on Tallis's quarterly release in month 2, and that Lucy Fenn's February campaign depends on the service being ready in the stores it will advertise. Which activity of the 'starting up a project' process is Patrick carrying out?
o: Select the project approach.
Assemble the project brief.
Plan the initiation stage.
Prepare the outline business case.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In assembling the project brief, the project manager confirms the objectives, outcomes, scope, exclusions, tolerances, constraints, assumptions and dependencies, including dependencies on other initiatives (book Table 13.1).

n.0: Selecting the project approach evaluates delivery solutions, decides the approach and defines any known tailoring requirements (book Table 13.1).
n.2: Planning the initiation stage sets the time and cost constraints for initiation and produces a high-level release map for it (book Table 13.1).
n.3: Preparing the outline business case is where the executive leads the project canvas and the project backlog is created (book Table 13.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the start of Stage 3, the board, Nikhil Rao and several area managers hold an agile enablement workshop. After reviewing the latest Agilometer results, they list further threats to agile working that the Agilometer does not cover, such as area managers asking stores for weekly written reports instead of using the team dashboard. Under which topic of the workshop does this listing take place?
o: Agilometer assessment review.
Risk identification.
Risk assessment.
Risk planning.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In the agile enablement workshop, the risk identification topic looks for additional threats and opportunities to agile adoption that the Agilometer does not capture (book Table 13.5).

n.0: The Agilometer assessment review links the Agilometer's risk areas to agile values and transformation objectives and builds a shared view of them; the threats here lie outside the Agilometer (book Table 13.5).
n.2: Risk assessment estimates the probability and impact of risks already identified and prioritizes them (book Table 13.5).
n.3: Risk planning agrees practical steps to mitigate the risks; the group is still listing them (book Table 13.5).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the end of starting up a project, the board reviews the project brief and the high-level release map for the one-month initiation stage. Gwen Tallowby confirms that the board is content, lets the store managers and Tallis know that initiation is beginning, and asks Patrick Dunne to start work. Which activity of the 'directing a project' process is the board carrying out?
o: Authorize the project.
Give ongoing direction.
Authorize a stage or exception plan.
Authorize initiation.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In authorizing initiation, the board approves the project brief and the release map for initiation, informs stakeholders and authorizes the project manager to initiate the project (book Table 13.4).

n.0: Authorizing the project comes after initiation, when the board approves the PID and commits resources for delivery (book Table 13.4).
n.1: Ongoing direction is informal guidance given at any time in response to requests, issues or reports, not the formal start of initiation (book Table 13.4).
n.2: Authorizing a stage or exception plan approves an updated release map at a stage boundary or after an exception (book Table 13.4).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In the project initiation workshop, the teams, Elena Marsh and Bill Rowntree agree criteria that any epic must meet before a team starts work on it, such as the interface details being confirmed with Tallis and the store's current stock accuracy figure being available. Under which topic of the project initiation workshop should this be agreed?
o: Management approaches.
Project Definition of Done.
Project Definition of Ready.
High-level release planning.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The project Definition of Ready topic of the project initiation workshop agrees the product-wide criteria that work must meet before it starts (book Table 13.7).

n.0: The management approaches topic co-creates approaches such as risk and quality; criteria for starting work belong to the project Definition of Ready (book Table 13.7).
n.1: The project Definition of Done sets the criteria for work to be acceptable to users, not the conditions for starting it (book Table 13.7).
n.3: High-level release planning develops or updates the release map; it does not set entry criteria for epics (book Table 13.7).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the project kickoff workshop, the store operations team lists who can train staff on the handheld scanners, who has designed store signage before and who knows the stock system. They find that one trainer is the sole person able to teach the scanner process, and plan for a second member to learn it. Under which topic of the project kickoff workshop does this take place?
o: Team delegation matrix.
Team values and norms.
Psychological safety.
Team skill matrix.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The team skill matrix topic of the project kickoff workshop maps the team's skills, gaps and overlaps (book Table 13.8), giving an overview of capabilities and training needs (book 7.4.1).

n.0: The team delegation matrix clarifies who decides what, to simplify decisions and support self-management; it does not map skills (book Table 13.8).
n.1: Team values and norms build an agile culture and shared expectations of behaviour (book Table 13.8).
n.2: The psychological safety topic assesses whether people feel safe to speak up and take risks (book Table 13.8).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Midway through Stage 3, Patrick Dunne holds a progress review workshop with the board, Marcus Lindell and Sophie Draper. After the welcome, they look at the project dashboard metrics, including the burn-up chart for Release 2 and the number of pilot stores live, and celebrate the first four stores taking collection orders. Under which topic of the workshop does this take place?
o: Product demo.
Current risks and issues.
Project highlights.
Welcome.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In the progress review workshop, the project highlights topic reviews the project dashboard metrics and achievements, which supports the workshop's aim of assessing status and celebrating success (book Table 13.10).

n.0: The product demo shows completed features to gather user acceptance and feedback; the group is reviewing dashboard metrics, not using the product (book Table 13.10).
n.1: Current risks and issues looks at open risks and issues and how to address them (book Table 13.10).
n.3: The welcome opens the session; the stem says the review of metrics comes after it (book Table 13.10).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the e-commerce team's team planning workshop for sprint 9, the stories at the top of the product backlog have already been refined and estimated. The team now selects stories in priority order until the total matches its recent velocity of about 30 points, and agrees a team plan for the sprint. Under which topic of the team planning workshop does this take place?
o: Iteration planning.
Product backlog refinement.
Effort estimation.
User story refinement.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Iteration planning is the team planning workshop topic in which the team selects stories by priority and estimate and agrees a realistic team plan for the next iteration (book Table 13.13).

n.1: Product backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes backlog items, for example with MoSCoW; the stem says this is already done (book Table 13.13).
n.2: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's effort; the stories are already estimated (book Table 13.13).
n.3: User story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable; that has already happened (book Table 13.13).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the store operations team's retrospective after the first pilot stores go live, the team notes that two stores missed their go-live date because stock counts started late. The team then proposes running a stock count a week before staff training at every remaining pilot store, and agrees to try this in the next cycle. Under which topic of the team retrospective workshop is the proposal captured?
o: The good.
The bad.
The learning.
Team building.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The learning topic of the team retrospective workshop captures lessons, improvement suggestions and actionable insights (book Table 13.14). The proposal to start stock counts earlier is an improvement the team will act on.

n.0: The good covers positives and celebrating success, not improvement proposals (book Table 13.14).
n.1: The bad captures issues, risks and challenges and their causes, such as the late stock counts; the proposal that follows belongs under the learning (book Table 13.14).
n.3: Team building uses a game or food to strengthen bonds within the team (book Table 13.14).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the end of Stage 3, Patrick Dunne holds a release planning workshop for Stage 4. After the introduction, the teams agree an objective of making click and collect part of everyday store life, with key results such as all 85 stores live with stock accuracy of at least 97% and 90% of orders ready within two hours. Under which topic of the workshop is this agreed?
o: Release planning.
OKR definition.
Introduction.
Wrap-up.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The OKR definition topic of the release planning workshop defines or updates the teams' objectives and key results (book Table 13.16). OKRs pair a clear, aspirational objective with specific, measurable key results (book 12.3.2.3).

n.0: The release planning topic breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map (book Table 13.16).
n.2: The introduction opens the workshop and sets the context; the stem says the OKRs were agreed after it (book Table 13.16).
n.3: The wrap-up closes the workshop; objectives and key results are agreed under their own topic, OKR definition (book Table 13.16).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In closing the project, Patrick Dunne holds the project closure workshop. Store staff and a group of regular customers use the locker collection process at one of the largest stores, and the users' representatives confirm that it meets the agreed requirements and is ready to be handed over. Under which topic of the project closure workshop does this take place?
o: Final product demo.
Final handover planning.
Project lessons.
Progress review.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The final product demo topic of the project closure workshop shows the final product so that users can confirm acceptance and that it is ready for handover (book Table 13.19).

n.1: Final handover planning agrees support responsibilities, operational requirements and benefits actions after the product is accepted (book Table 13.19).
n.2: Project lessons is where participants share insights from the project (book Table 13.19).
n.3: The progress review topic updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer (book Table 13.19).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Before the project kickoff workshop, Patrick Dunne designs a team dashboard for each team himself, using the same layout and measures for both, so that he can combine them easily into the project dashboard. At the workshop he presents the finished dashboards and asks the teams to start updating them. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager pulls information from the team dashboards, so the project manager should decide what they contain.
Yes, because both teams must report in the same format so that the board can compare them in the progress review workshops.
No, because team dashboards are created in the team planning workshop for each iteration, not in the project kickoff workshop.
No, because the kickoff aims to build self-management, and each team should co-create its own dashboard rather than have one dictated.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The project kickoff workshop aims to create an agile culture of openness and self-management, and its team dashboards topic has each team co-create its own dashboard rather than have one imposed (book Table 13.8). Designing them for the teams undermines that purpose.

n.0: The project manager does pull information from team dashboards, but that does not make the project manager their designer; teams co-create them (book Table 13.8, Table 12.1).
n.1: The board pulls information from the project dashboard, which the project manager assembles; the teams' dashboards do not need an identical format (book Table 12.1, Table 13.8).
n.2: Team dashboards are created in the project kickoff workshop and later updated in team planning and retrospective workshops (book Table 13.8, Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In starting up a project, Gwen Tallowby is busy with the spring peak, so she asks Patrick Dunne to write the project canvas on his own from the mandate and send it to her for approval. Patrick does so without holding a project canvas workshop or involving the user, supplier or finance representatives. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'starting up a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the fixed budget and date in the mandate mean that the content of the canvas has in effect already been decided.
Yes, because a project canvas is a one-page summary, so there is little to gain from involving other people in writing it.
No, because the executive should lead the canvas from the mandate, working with others so that they share an understanding of the project.
No, because the project canvas is prepared in initiating a project, so it should not be written while the project is still starting up.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In starting up a project the executive leads the development of the project canvas from the mandate (book Table 13.1), and the project canvas workshop exists to build a shared understanding of the project's core elements in line with organizational goals (book 13.2.4.1). A canvas written alone by the project manager loses both.

n.0: Budget and date are only part of the canvas, which also covers vision, users, business options, scope, benefits and major risks (book 6.3.2).
n.1: The canvas is short, but its value comes from the shared understanding built by defining it together (book 13.2.4.1).
n.3: The canvas is first developed in starting up a project and then refined in initiation; writing it in starting up is correct (book Table 13.1, Table 13.6).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: As Stage 2 nears its end, Patrick Dunne holds a release planning workshop with both teams, Marcus Lindell and Elena Marsh. They review the project canvas and project backlog, break the Release 2 features into user stories and update the release map for Stage 3. Sprint-level and store-level task planning is left to the teams. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'managing a stage boundary' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the stage boundary updates the release map for the next stage, while detailed task plans are made in managing product delivery.
Yes, because the release map produced at the stage boundary removes the need for team plans in the managing product delivery process.
No, because the release map should be updated in the team planning workshop, where each team plans the work for its next sprint.
No, because the board approves the next stage plan, so the board rather than the teams should plan Release 2 in this workshop.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: At a stage boundary the release planning workshop reviews the project canvas, project backlog and release map, breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map for the next stage (book Table 13.16). Detailed task-level plans are made by the teams in managing product delivery (book Table 13.12, 8.3.2).

n.1: Team plans are still needed; the delivery team produces one when it accepts a work package, at task level for the next iteration (book Table 13.12).
n.2: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration; the stage-level release map update belongs to the release planning workshop (book Table 13.13, Table 13.16).
n.3: The board approves the updated release map in directing a project, but the project manager prepares it with the teams at the stage boundary (book 13.7.1, Table 13.4).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In Stage 4, Patrick Dunne begins attending the store operations team's daily stand-up every morning without asking the team, and uses it to tell members which stores to prepare next. He says this saves time compared with agreeing work packages with Sophie Draper, the team's product owner. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the 'managing product delivery' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager runs the project day to day for the board and can therefore direct the delivery team members.
Yes, because attending stand-ups lets the project manager pull progress information without asking the team for a report.
No, because stand-ups belong to the Scrum framework, and a Kanban team such as the store operations team should not hold them.
No, because the project manager attends stand-ups with the team's agreement and agrees work with the product owner as work packages.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups only with the delivery team's agreement (book Table 12.1). Work reaches the team through work packages, sets of user stories agreed between the project manager and the product owner, who is the role with direct authority over delivery team members (book 7.3.1, Table 13.9).

n.0: The project manager runs the project day to day, but the product owner is the role with direct authority over delivery team members (book 7.3.1).
n.1: Pulling information from the team dashboard is encouraged, but joining stand-ups without agreement and directing the team is not (book Table 12.1, Table 13.9).
n.2: Kanban teams can hold short daily stand-ups; the problem is the project manager attending uninvited and bypassing the product owner (book Table 12.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: As Release 3 nears completion, Bill Rowntree's area managers will take over the daily running of click and collect in all 85 stores, and the store operations team will disband at closure. Bill asks what the handover should include so that the stores keep running the service well. Which approach follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance on transition to operations?
o: Give each store a printed manual of the collection process and close the project, so that store managers can adapt the process locally as they see fit.
Hand over the team's Kanban board and dashboards, tailored training and quick guides, clear procedures, escalation routes and regular feedback loops.
Keep the store operations team in place for a year after closure, so that it can run the service in each store until staff feel confident.
Transfer responsibility for the stores' collection process to Kieran Walsh's IT operations team, as it already supports the website.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: For transition to operations the book recommends handing over agile artifacts and tools, tailored end-user training with guides and other aids, explicit operational procedures, escalation pathways, and regular feedback loops such as surveys and retrospectives (book 14.2.1).

n.0: A manual alone gives no training, escalation routes or feedback loops, which the book recommends to support adoption after handover (book 14.2.1).
n.2: The project is temporary; keeping the project team running the service delays handover to the business rather than preparing operations to take it on (book 1.3.1, 14.2.1).
n.3: IT operations supports the website, but the daily collection process is run by the stores, which need the training, procedures and feedback loops themselves (book 14.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: The e-commerce team deploys small website changes several times a week. Kieran Walsh, who is responsible for keeping the website running, wants every change to go through his weekly change board, especially during the spring peak. After the project, the team will keep improving the service. Which approach is MOST LIKELY to keep the website stable while keeping the benefits of frequent releases?
o: Bring Kieran's team into the e-commerce team's work, with automated testing and deployment, and live monitoring that feeds back into development.
Group all changes into a single weekly release approved by the change board, so that IT operations reviews each change before it goes live.
Let the e-commerce team deploy without involving IT operations, because frequent small changes carry little risk to the website.
Freeze changes to the website from February until after Easter, and release the remaining features in one deployment after the peak.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Continuous agile development and operations aims for rapid, automated delivery so the product is always deployable. In DevOps, development, testing and operations work closely together without silos, small releases go to production often, and monitoring of the live service feeds back into development (book 14.2.2.2).

n.1: Batching changes into a weekly release slows feedback and keeps development and operations apart, which is what DevOps seeks to avoid (book 14.2.2.2).
n.2: Leaving operations out creates the silo that DevOps removes and ignores the person responsible for website stability (book 14.2.2.2).
n.3: A freeze stops feedback from live use, and holding features until after Easter would break the fixed date for the service (book 14.2.2.2, Table 3.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Patrick Dunne wants to use an AI assistant to reduce the load on the store operations team during the Stage 4 roll-out, when store managers are sending many questions about the new collection process. Which use of AI is consistent with PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Set up a project chatbot that answers common store questions, so that Sophie Draper's team has more time to talk to store managers about concerns.
Let the assistant decide whether each store meets the go-live conditions and send its manager the go-live date, to save the store operations team's time.
Upload customer orders, including payment details, to a public AI tool so that it can predict which stores will be busiest at Easter.
Use the assistant to write and send all messages to store managers, so that the team no longer needs to hold meetings with them.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: AI can support people by automating the collection and sharing of information, for example a project chatbot answering frequent questions, which frees leaders for more important communication. It supports human judgement and does not remove the need to make decisions or to communicate with stakeholders (book 15.4.2).

n.1: Go-live decisions remain human decisions; AI supports decision-making but does not replace it (book 15.4.2).
n.2: Sharing customer payment data with a public tool ignores data care set out in the digital and data management approach, and the board has a very low appetite for payment security risks (book 15.4, Table 12.1).
n.3: AI does not remove the need to communicate with stakeholders; store managers' concerns need direct conversation (book 15.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In starting up a project, Sarah Pennington runs the project canvas workshop for Care Online. Benefits analysis
Scope definition

n.2: Benefits analysis identifies benefits and dis-benefits and their tolerances, not who the users are (Table 13.2).
n.3: Scope definition sets the timeline, tolerance and the epics prioritized with MoSCoW, not the user groups (Table 13.2).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Once Sarah Pennington has led the development of the project canvas from the mandate, Simon Archer meets her, the chief product owner and Martin Sallis to define what Care Online will deliver. Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In the project initiation workshop, Dr Rajesh Iyer, Carol Mbeki and the chief product owner agree the criteria that any part of Care Online must meet before it is acceptable to users, including an easy-read version, approval of the personal data flows and a route to a practitioner assessment where eligibility is likely. n.3: The workshop is designed for the project board together with agile coaches and business representatives (Table 13.5).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The project Definition of Done topic sets the criteria that work must meet to be acceptable to the users and the chief product owner (book 13.4.4.1, Table 13.7).
