n.1: The management approaches topic co-creates the approaches themselves; completion criteria have their own topic, the project Definition of Done (Table 13.7).
n.3: Project canvas refinement updates the business justification, not the criteria for accepting work (Table 13.7).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the project kickoff workshop, the software team and the engineers' trial team meet together for the first time. They want to avoid waiting for answers during sprints, so they agree which decisions they can take themselves, such as the alert threshold for a single machine, and which must go to Ruth Kenyon or Mei Chen. Under which topic of the project kickoff workshop does this agreement belong?
o: Team delegation matrix
Team values and norms
Team skill matrix
Psychological safety
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The team delegation matrix topic of the project kickoff workshop clarifies who decides what, simplifying decisions and empowering self-management (book 13.4.4.2, Table 13.8, 7.4.3).

n.1: Team values and norms build an agile culture and shared expectations of behaviour, not decision rights (Table 13.8).
n.2: The team skill matrix maps skills, gaps and overlaps, not who may take which decisions (Table 13.8, 7.4.1).
n.3: The psychological safety topic assesses whether people feel safe to speak up, not the split of decision authority (Table 13.8).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At a progress review workshop in Stage 3, the board and several engineers from both factories attend. Stuart Bell shows them how the new alert on machine 14 warned of a spindle bearing failure two days before it happened, walks through the screens he used, and gathers their feedback on whether the alert is ready for wider use. Under which topic of the progress review workshop does this take place?
o: Project highlights
Product demo
Current risks and issues
Welcome
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The product demo topic of the progress review workshop shows completed features and gathers user acceptance and feedback (book 13.5.4.1, Table 13.10).

n.0: Project highlights reviews the metrics on the project dashboard rather than demonstrating a working feature (Table 13.10).
n.2: Current risks and issues reviews open risks and issues; Stuart is showing a working feature and seeking acceptance (Table 13.10).
n.3: The welcome opens the workshop and sets its purpose; demonstrations come under the product demo (Table 13.10).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Release 2 is behind its forecast and the board has asked for a closer watch on the software team. In the middle of a sprint, Andrea Lucas checks the team's updated team dashboard, has an informal conversation with Leanne Park about a new gateway risk, and then updates the release map with actuals and forecasts for the work package. Which activity of the 'controlling a stage' process is she carrying out?
o: Report highlights
Receive completed work package
Authorize a work package
Evaluate work package status
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In evaluate work package status, the PM talks informally with the product owner about issues and risks, pulls progress from the updated team dashboard and updates the release map with actuals, forecasts and adjustments (Table 13.9).

n.0: Report highlights assembles team dashboards and release map changes to update the project dashboard for the board (Table 13.9).
n.1: Receiving a completed work package confirms that the set of user stories was delivered; this work package is still in progress (Table 13.9).
n.2: Authorizing a work package is when the PM co-creates the work package description with the PO and team and authorizes the work (Table 13.9).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At a team planning workshop, the software team and two engineers look at the story 'As an engineer, I want an alert when bearing vibration rises, so that I can plan a repair'. The story is already near the top of the backlog. They agree testable acceptance criteria, such as the alert threshold and how quickly the alert must appear, and what will count as done. Under which topic of the team planning workshop does this happen?
o: User story refinement
Product backlog refinement
Effort estimation
Iteration planning
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: User story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable and agrees what counts as done for each story (book 13.6.4.1, Table 13.13).

n.1: Product backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes the backlog as a whole, for example with MoSCoW (Table 13.13).
n.2: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's complexity and effort, not its acceptance criteria (Table 13.13).
n.3: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate into a realistic team plan (Table 13.13).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At a team retrospective after a Release 2 sprint, Tomasz Zielinski asks the software team to look back honestly. The team lists what went wrong: two stories were missed because gateways dropped data, and the security review of a new data connection took longer than planned. The team then discusses what caused each problem, before moving on. Under which topic of the team retrospective does this discussion belong?
o: The learning
The good
The bad
Team building
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The bad covers the issues, risks and challenges of the last iteration and their causes (book 13.6.4.2, Table 13.14).

n.0: The learning turns experience into lessons, improvement suggestions and actions; listing problems and their causes comes under the bad (Table 13.14).
n.1: The good looks at what went well and celebrates it (Table 13.14).
n.3: Team building uses a game or food to strengthen bonds within the team (Table 13.14).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Release 2 has been accepted and the board has asked for Factory B to be brought up to the same standard. At the release planning workshop before Stage 4, the team leads set an objective to make Factory B as reliable as Factory A, with measurable key results such as every Factory B machine sending data by month 10 and every alert acknowledged within one shift. Under which topic of the release planning workshop does this belong?
o: Release planning
OKR definition
Introduction
Wrap-up
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The OKR definition topic of the release planning workshop defines or updates team objectives and key results; objectives are clear, aspirational goals and key results are specific, measurable outcomes (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16, 12.3.2.3).

n.0: Release planning breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map, rather than setting objectives and key results (Table 13.16).
n.2: The introduction sets out the workshop's purpose and context before the planning work starts (Table 13.16).
n.3: The wrap-up closes the workshop by confirming outcomes and next steps (Table 13.16).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: The final release has been demonstrated and accepted by the engineers. At the project closure workshop, Ruth Kenyon, Leanne Park and Andrea Lucas agree who will support the dashboard after closure, what the maintenance team needs in order to run it day to day, and which actions will track the fall in breakdown costs over the coming year. Under which topic of the project closure workshop does this belong?
o: Final product demo
Project canvas refinement
Progress review
Final handover planning
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Final handover planning in the project closure workshop agrees support responsibilities, operational requirements and the actions for benefits realization (book 13.8.4, Table 13.19).

n.0: The final product demo confirms user acceptance and readiness for handover; it does not assign support or benefits actions (Table 13.19).
n.1: Project canvas refinement is a topic of the project initiation workshop, where the business justification is refined; support and benefits actions at closure come under final handover planning (Table 13.7, Table 13.19).
n.2: The progress review topic updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer (Table 13.19).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Release 1 is due at month 4 and Senticore's sensors have a ten-week lead time. To keep to the date on this large, complex project, Andrea Lucas uses the 'controlling a stage' process during initiation to authorize a work package for ordering and preparing sensors for the ten Release 1 machines, as the board-approved initiation plan allows. Is this an appropriate way to tailor the processes, and why?
o: Yes, because once the project brief is approved the project manager may commit the project's resources.
Yes, because controlling a stage can be used during initiation for large or complex projects like this one.
No, because no work package can be authorized until the board has approved the PID and the project.
No, because initiation must be complete before any spending, so that no expenditure is committed early.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Controlling a stage is normally first used after the project is authorized, but it can be used during initiation for large or complex projects (book 13.5.1). Here it lets long-lead sensors be ordered in time for Release 1 within the approved initiation plan.

n.0: Committing the project's resources is a board decision in 'authorize the project', not something the PM does after the brief is approved (Table 13.4).
n.2: The book allows controlling a stage, and so work packages, during initiation for large or complex projects (book 13.5.1).
n.3: Initiating avoids committing significant expenditure before the work is understood; it does not forbid a planned, board-approved early order on a complex project (book 13.4.1, 13.5.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In starting up, Graham Doyle passes the mandate to Andrea Lucas and asks her to write the project canvas on her own, saying he will review it once it is finished. Andrea has not yet met Ruth Kenyon or Dev Patel. Is this an appropriate application of the 'starting up a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager prepares the outline business case and the executive approves it later.
Yes, because the project canvas is a one-page artifact that one person can draft quickly from the mandate.
No, because the executive should lead the development of the project canvas from the mandate.
No, because the project canvas is created in initiation, after the board has approved the project brief.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In 'prepare the outline business case', the executive leads the development of the project canvas from the mandate, while the PM works with the CPO, senior supplier and executive on the project backlog (Table 13.1).

n.0: In PRINCE2 Agile the executive leads the development of the project canvas in starting up; it is not handed to the PM to write alone (Table 13.1).
n.1: Being one page does not change who leads it; the canvas is developed under the executive's lead, normally in a collaborative project canvas workshop (Table 13.1, Table 13.2).
n.3: The project canvas is first developed in starting up and refined into a more detailed canvas in initiation (Table 13.1, Table 13.6).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the end of Stage 2, Andrea Lucas holds a release planning workshop with Leanne Park, Ruth Kenyon, Dev Patel and the trial team lead. They review the project canvas, project backlog and release map, break the Release 2 work into user stories and update the release map. Senticore's fitters do not work in sprints but are represented. Which statement BEST assesses Andrea's use of this workshop?
o: It is well tailored: it plans the next stage and aligns all teams, including the supplier, on the release map.
It is well tailored: holding the workshop means the board no longer needs to approve the next stage plan.
It is poorly tailored: release map updates belong in the team planning workshop at the start of each sprint.
It is poorly tailored: Senticore should be left out because its fitters do not plan their work in sprints.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The release planning workshop at a stage boundary builds shared understanding, aligns the teams with the vision and plans the next stage by reviewing the project canvas, project backlog and release map (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16). Including the supplier helps align the fitting schedule with the release map.

n.1: The workshop prepares the plan, but the board still reviews the stage and approves the next stage plan in directing a project (book 13.7.1, Table 13.4).
n.2: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration in managing product delivery; release map updates for the next stage belong at the stage boundary (Table 13.13, Table 13.16).
n.3: Aligning all teams with the vision is the workshop's purpose; Senticore's fittings drive the release dates even though the fitters do not work in sprints (Table 13.16).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: For Stage 3, Andrea Lucas plans that the agile enablement workshops will be attended by the software team and Tomasz Zielinski, as they have the most agile experience; the board will read the results on the project dashboard. Apart from the software team, nobody at Draycott, including the board, has used agile before. Is this an appropriate application of the 'directing a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the people with the most agile experience give the most accurate Agilometer assessment.
Yes, because the board pulls information from the project dashboard rather than attending workshops.
No, because the Agilometer is assessed once, in the project initiation workshop, and not in later stages.
No, because the workshop is for the board, agile coaches and business representatives to assess agile risks.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The agile enablement workshop in directing a project is for the project board, agile coaches and organizational or business representatives, who regularly reassess the Agilometer and the risks to agile adoption (Table 13.5). With a board new to agile, its own involvement matters most.

n.0: Experience does not make the software team the right audience; the workshop exists so the board and business representatives understand the risks of agile adoption (Table 13.5).
n.1: The board does pull dashboard information, but the agile enablement workshop is a directing workshop that the board itself attends (Table 13.5).
n.2: The Agilometer is first assessed in the project initiation workshop and then reassessed regularly in agile enablement workshops in later stages (Table 13.5, Table 13.7).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Near the end of Stage 4, Ruth Kenyon's maintenance team is preparing to take over the dashboard as part of normal work, with the software team continuing to improve it. Andrea Lucas is planning the transition to operations. Which plan BEST follows PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
o: Hand over a full user manual at closure, and ask the engineers to email the software team if they need help.
Keep the project board in place for six months after closure, so that it can approve every change the engineers and the software team ask for.
Hand over the backlog, dashboards and tools, give tailored training and clear procedures, and set up regular feedback loops.
Ask the software team to stop changing the dashboard for a year, so that the engineers can settle into using it.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Transition to operations should hand over agile artifacts and tools so agile practices continue, provide tailored training and materials, set out explicit operational procedures and escalation paths, and create regular feedback loops such as surveys, retrospectives and check-ins (book 14.2.1).

n.0: A manual alone, with ad hoc email support, lacks tailored training, clear procedures, escalation paths and structured feedback loops (book 14.2.1).
n.1: The project board ends at closure; after the project the dashboard moves into normal business with its own feedback and improvement loops (book 14.2.1, 14.2.2.1).
n.3: Regular feedback loops after transition are meant to drive continued improvement; freezing the product ignores them (book 14.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: After Release 1, the software team plans to release small dashboard improvements every week and, after closure, to keep improving it as part of normal business. At present each release needs two days of manual testing and a manual installation by IT on the factory servers. Which approach BEST supports continuous agile development and operations?
o: Group the weekly improvements into one large release each quarter, so that manual testing and installation happen less often.
Bring development, testing and IT operations together to automate testing and deployment, so the dashboard is always deployable.
Ask the engineers to test each weekly release on the shop floor during their shifts, so that the two days of manual testing can be dropped.
Hand the dashboard over to IT operations after closure, so that the software team can move on to other work.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Continuous agile development and operations aims for rapid, automated delivery with minimal manual effort so the product is always deployable. In DevOps, development, testing and operations work closely together, and continuous delivery releases small increments to production with fast feedback (book 14.2.2.2).

n.0: Batching changes into large, infrequent releases is the opposite of continuous delivery's small, frequent increments (book 14.2.2.2).
n.2: User feedback is valuable, but replacing tests with shop-floor trials does not automate delivery or keep the product always deployable (book 14.2.2.2).
n.3: Handing over to a separate operations silo works against DevOps, where development and operations collaborate closely (book 14.2.2.2).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Draycott has approved an AI assistant for project use. As Senticore's fitters and the engineers' trial team join the project, Andrea Lucas wants to use the assistant to support the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle. Which use of the assistant would do this?
o: Analyse skills and workload data to suggest who could take which role, and flag gaps or overlaps for Andrea to review.
Forecast from velocity and spend data whether the project canvas still shows a viable investment for the board.
Search the lessons logs and retrospective notes of earlier Draycott projects and give each role a prioritized list of relevant lessons.
Decide on Andrea's behalf who should fill each role, so that appointments can be made without any delay.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: AI can support defined roles by analysing data, skills and workload to suggest role assignments and flag gaps or overlaps. It supports, but does not remove, human decision-making (book 15.4.1, 15.4.2).

n.1: Forecasting viability supports the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, not defined roles (book 15.4.1).
n.2: Turning lessons into prioritized, role-specific insights supports 'learn from experience', not defined roles (book 15.4.1).
n.3: AI supports human decision-making but does not replace it; appointing people stays with the project's managers (book 15.4.2).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In starting up a project, Margaret Oyelaran runs the project canvas workshop. The group agrees that the key users are tenants who report repairs by phone, tenants who will report online and the contact centre advisers who take the reports, and it ranks these three groups in order of priority. Under which topic of the project canvas workshop is this being discussed?
o: User group definition
Persona definition
Benefits analysis
Business value definition
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The user group definition topic of the project canvas workshop identifies one to three key user groups and prioritizes them (book 13.2.4.1, Table 13.2).

n.1: Personas are written in the project initiation workshop and describe fictional users' needs; this group is naming and ranking the key user groups (Table 13.7, 6.4.1).
n.2: Benefits analysis identifies benefits and dis-benefits with tolerances; it does not define who the users are (Table 13.2).
n.3: Business value definition sets out the value the project brings to the organization; identifying and ranking user groups is user group definition (Table 13.2).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Still in starting up a project, Sally Greaves confirms the project's objectives, scope and exclusions, the fixed budget and end date, the requirement that phone reporting must remain, and the fact that the project depends on the renewal of the Coastline contract at month 12. Which starting up activity is she carrying out?
o: Prepare the outline business case
Select the project approach
Assemble the project brief
Plan the initiation stage
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Assembling the project brief confirms the objectives, outcomes, scope, exclusions, tolerances, constraints, assumptions and dependencies, such as dependencies on other initiatives (book Table 13.1).

n.0: This activity develops the project canvas from the mandate, led by the executive, and creates the project backlog; Sally is confirming objectives, constraints and dependencies (Table 13.1).
n.1: Selecting the project approach evaluates delivery solutions and determines how the work will be done; it does not confirm scope, constraints and dependencies (Table 13.1).
n.3: Planning the initiation stage sets out the time, cost, release map and controls for initiation itself (Table 13.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: During Stage 2, the board, an external agile coach and business representatives meet for the agile enablement workshop. After reviewing the latest Agilometer, Joy Ansah raises a threat that it does not cover: high turnover in the contact centre means advisers trained in the new ways of working may leave before Release 3. Under which topic of the workshop should this threat FIRST be discussed?
o: Agilometer assessment review
Risk assessment
Risk planning
Risk identification
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: In the agile enablement workshop, the risk identification topic captures additional threats and opportunities to agile adoption that the Agilometer does not cover; assessment and planning of responses follow (book Table 13.5).

n.0: That topic reviews the Agilometer itself and links its risk areas to agile values; Joy's threat is outside the Agilometer (Table 13.5).
n.1: Risk assessment estimates the probability and impact of risks that have already been identified; the threat must first be identified (Table 13.5).
n.2: Risk planning agrees practical mitigation steps after risks are identified and assessed (Table 13.5).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Midway through Stage 3, Frank Tolley says Coastline will not trial the new parts list on more estates unless trial jobs are paid at a higher rate. The stage is still forecast to finish within tolerance, but Sally Greaves escalates the issue to the board for advice. Margaret Oyelaran replies the same day with guidance. Which directing a project activity is this?
o: Authorize a stage or exception plan
Give ongoing direction
Authorize the project
Authorize initiation
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Give ongoing direction covers the board's informal guidance at any time, in response to business advice, informal requests and escalated issues (book Table 13.4). No exception has arisen and no stage decision is being made.

n.0: That activity reviews the project dashboard and approves an updated release map at a stage end or after an exception; neither applies here (Table 13.4).
n.2: Authorizing the project approves the PID and commits resources at the end of initiation, not mid-stage advice (Table 13.4).
n.3: Authorizing initiation approves the project brief and the release map for initiation before the project starts (Table 13.4).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In the project initiation workshop, both teams and Deborah Kiely agree criteria that any piece of work must meet before either team starts it: the tenant need is clear, any effect on Coastline's engineers has been checked, and the acceptance criteria can be tested. Under which topic of the workshop does this belong?
o: Project Definition of Ready
Project Definition of Done
Management approaches
High-level release planning
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The project Definition of Ready topic of the project initiation workshop sets product-overarching criteria that work must meet before it starts (book Table 13.7, 9.3.2.1).

n.1: The project Definition of Done sets criteria for work to be acceptable to users and the CPO when complete, not before it starts (Table 13.7, 9.3.2.2).
n.2: Management approaches are co-created there too, but criteria for starting work belong under the project Definition of Ready topic (Table 13.7).
n.3: Release planning develops or updates the release map; it does not set entry criteria for work (Table 13.7).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the project kickoff workshop, several advisers on the service design team seem uneasy, and one says privately that she is afraid to admit mistakes in case her job is cut. Before the team agrees its values, Raj Malhotra runs a short anonymous check of how safe people feel to speak up and take risks. Which topic of the kickoff workshop is Raj covering?
o: Team values and norms
Icebreaker, project intro and team intro
Team delegation matrix
Psychological safety
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The project kickoff workshop includes a psychological safety topic, assessing whether people feel safe to speak up, take risks and challenge ideas (book Table 13.8, 2.7.4).

n.0: Values and norms come next in Raj's plan; the anonymous check of how safe people feel is the psychological safety topic (Table 13.8).
n.1: These build familiarity and connections; they do not assess whether people feel safe to speak up (Table 13.8).
n.2: The delegation matrix clarifies who decides what to support self-management; it does not measure how safe people feel (Table 13.8, 7.4.3).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In Stage 2, Sally Greaves has an informal conversation with the digital team's product owner about risks to the photo upload feature, pulls the team's latest progress from its team dashboard and updates the release map with actuals and a revised forecast. Which controlling a stage activity is she carrying out?
o: Evaluate stage status
Report highlights
Evaluate work package status
Receive completed work package
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Evaluating work package status involves informal conversations with the product owner on issues and risks, pulling progress from the updated team dashboard and updating the release map with actuals and forecasts (book Table 13.9).

n.0: Evaluating stage status reviews the progress of the whole stage in a progress review and decides on actions; Sally is checking one team's work package (Table 13.9).
n.1: Reporting highlights assembles team dashboards and log and release map changes to update the project dashboard for the board (Table 13.9).
n.3: This confirms that the set of user stories has been delivered; the photo upload work is still in progress (Table 13.9).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the progress review workshop near the end of Stage 2, tenants from the pilot estate try the new online reporting form and the text updates, say what works for them and what does not, and confirm which features they accept. Under which topic of the progress review workshop does this take place?
o: Project highlights
Product demo
Current risks and issues
Final product demo
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The product demo topic of the progress review workshop shows completed features and gathers user acceptance and feedback (book 13.5.4.1, Table 13.10).

n.0: Project highlights reviews the project dashboard metrics; tenants trying the features and giving feedback is the product demo (Table 13.10).
n.2: This topic covers open risks and issues, not users trying and accepting completed features (Table 13.10).
n.3: The final product demo is a topic of the project closure workshop at the end of the project, not of a progress review (Table 13.19).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the team planning workshop, the service design team works through the stories it may take on next. For the story about a new damp and mould question in the diagnosis guide, members agree that its acceptance criteria are vague and rewrite them so that tenant testing can show clearly whether it is done. Under which topic is the team working?
o: User story refinement
Product backlog refinement
Effort estimation
Iteration planning
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: User story refinement in the team planning workshop makes acceptance criteria clear and testable and agrees what counts as done (book 13.6.4.1, Table 13.13).

n.1: Backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes the backlog, for example with MoSCoW; sharpening one story's acceptance criteria is user story refinement (Table 13.13).
n.2: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's size; the team is rewriting acceptance criteria, not estimating (Table 13.13).
n.3: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate into a realistic team plan; it comes after stories are refined (Table 13.13).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In managing a stage boundary, the teams meet for the release planning workshop before Stage 3. They agree an objective of getting repairs right first time, with key results such as cutting second visits on the pilot estate from 30% to 20% by month 8. Under which topic of the workshop is this agreed?
o: Release planning
Introduction
Project canvas refinement
OKR definition
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The release planning workshop includes an OKR definition topic, where team objectives and key results are defined or updated; objectives are aspirational goals and key results are measurable outcomes (book 13.7.4.1, Table 13.16, 12.3.2.3).

n.0: Release planning breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map; setting objectives and key results is OKR definition (Table 13.16).
n.1: The introduction sets the scene for the workshop; it does not define objectives and key results (Table 13.16).
n.2: Project canvas refinement is a topic of the project initiation workshop, not the release planning workshop (Table 13.7).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: In the project closure workshop at month 12, Sally Greaves, Joy Ansah, Ian Thursby and Ellen Price agree who will support the new repairs service after the project, what the contact centre and repairs team need in order to run it as normal business, and which actions will track the benefits. Under which topic of the workshop is this being agreed?
o: Final product demo
Current risks and issues
Final handover planning
Progress review
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Final handover planning in the project closure workshop agrees support responsibilities, operational requirements and benefits actions for handover (book 13.8.4, Table 13.19).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Before the project kickoff workshop, Sally Greaves designs a team dashboard template with fixed charts and columns. At the workshop she tells the service design and digital teams to use it unchanged, so that all reporting looks the same, and moves on to the next topic. Is this an appropriate application of the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because one template makes it easier for the project manager to pull progress from the teams' dashboards.
Yes, because the project dashboard is created in the kickoff workshop, so the team dashboards should match it.
No, because team dashboards are created at a stage boundary, in the release planning workshop for Stage 2.

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The project kickoff workshop aims to build an agile culture of openness and self-management; team dashboards are co-created by each team there, not dictated (book Table 13.8). Imposing a fixed template works against that purpose.

n.0: The project manager does pull from team dashboards, but convenience for the PM does not outweigh the teams co-creating them (Table 13.8, Table 12.1).
n.1: The project dashboard is created in the kickoff workshop, but that does not mean team dashboards should be dictated to match it (Table 13.8).
n.2: Team dashboards are a topic of the project kickoff workshop in initiation, not of the release planning workshop (Table 13.8, Table 13.16).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: At the end of Stage 2, Sally Greaves updates the release map for Stage 3 using what was learned in the pilot, updates the project canvas with early results on repair satisfaction, and presents both with the project dashboard. The board reviews them and approves Stage 3. Is this an appropriate application of the 'managing a stage boundary' process, and why?
o: Yes, because a stage boundary is where the teams write task-level plans for every iteration of the next stage.
Yes, because the board needs the updated release map and canvas to review the stage and confirm continued justification.
No, because the release map is updated in the team planning workshop, rather than at the end of a stage.
No, because the project canvas is fixed once the project is authorized and should not change at a stage boundary.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Managing a stage boundary gives the board enough information to review the current stage, approve the next stage plan (the updated release map) and confirm continued business justification, which in PRINCE2 Agile means the updated project canvas (book 13.7.1).

n.0: Task-level plans are made by teams for the next iteration in managing product delivery; the stage boundary updates the high-level release map (book 8.3.2).
n.2: Team planning workshops produce team plans for the next iteration; the release map for the next stage is updated at the stage boundary (book 13.7.1, Table 13.16).
n.3: The project canvas is kept up to date so that continued business justification can be confirmed at each stage boundary (book 13.7.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Sally Greaves runs the agile enablement workshop for Stage 3 with members of the service design and digital teams. The board members do not attend, as they prefer to read a summary later. The teams review the Agilometer and agree actions on the agile risks they identify. What is the MOST significant weakness in how this workshop is being run?
o: The board is absent, yet the workshop is for the board, agile coaches and business representatives to assess agile risks and maturity.
The Agilometer should not be reviewed after initiation, as the risks of agile working are set at the start of the project.
The workshop should produce the agile transformation plan, which the teams have not been asked to write.
The teams should estimate the effort of their Stage 3 stories in the workshop, so that the board's summary includes a forecast for Release 2.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The agile enablement workshop sits in directing a project. It brings together the project board, agile coaches and organizational or business representatives so that agile maturity and agile risks are assessed regularly through the Agilometer (book Table 13.5). Running it without the board defeats its purpose.

n.1: The agile enablement workshop exists to reassess the Agilometer regularly in initiation and later stages (Table 13.5).
n.2: The agile transformation plan is considered in the project initiation workshop, not the agile enablement workshop (Table 13.7, 2.7.1).
n.3: Effort estimation is a team planning workshop topic in managing product delivery, not part of agile enablement (Table 13.13).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: Near month 12, Sally Greaves proposes to save time by leaving the final product demo out of the project closure workshop. Instead she plans to send the end project report to the repairs team and the contact centre, noting that they have seen the project dashboard throughout. What is the MOST significant weakness in this tailoring?
o: The project dashboard would be out of date, because it is updated when a product demo takes place.
The lessons report could not be written, because lessons are gathered during the final product demo.
Users would lose the chance to confirm that the final service meets their requirements and is ready for handover.
Benefits could not be measured, because the final product demo is where the benefits review of the fall in second visits takes place.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: The final product demo in the project closure workshop lets users accept the final product and confirms it meets requirements and is ready for handover, which is central to the workshop's purpose of formally concluding the project (book 13.8.4, Table 13.19). A report and dashboards do not replace users confirming acceptance.

n.0: The project dashboard is updated in progress reviews, including the closure workshop's progress review topic; that is not the main loss here (Table 13.19).
n.1: Lessons are gathered under the project lessons and lessons report topics, not the product demo (Table 13.19).
n.3: Benefits reviews are planned in the benefits management approach and largely happen after closure; the demo is about user acceptance (book 6.3.1, Table 13.19).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: As Repairs Reimagined nears closure, the repairs team and the contact centre prepare to run the new repairs service as normal business. Ian Thursby suggests handing over the final scripts and portal settings and switching off the project's boards and dashboards. Which approach BEST supports the transition to operations?
o: Hand over the final scripts and portal settings as Ian suggests, as operational teams set their own ways of working.
Hand over the agile artifacts and tools, with tailored training, clear procedures and escalation routes, and regular feedback loops.
Keep the project open until advisers and engineers have used the new service for a year, so the project team can support them.
Ask the digital team to run the whole repairs service, as it will continue to improve the portal after the project ends.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Transition to operations should hand over agile artifacts and tools so agile practices continue, provide tailored training and guides, set out explicit operational procedures and escalation pathways, and keep regular feedback loops such as surveys and retrospectives (book 14.2.1).

n.0: Handing over products without the artifacts, training, procedures and feedback loops risks the new ways of working being lost (book 14.2.1).
n.2: The project is temporary and has a fixed end at month 12; support continues through operational arrangements agreed at handover (book 14.2.1, 1.3.1).
n.3: The scenario says the repairs team and contact centre will run the service; the digital team's continuing role is improving the portal (book 14.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: After the project closes, Ellen Price's digital team will keep improving the tenant portal. Tenants are already asking for new features, such as tracking the engineer's arrival on a map. Ian Thursby suggests starting a new PRINCE2 Agile project for each enhancement. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
o: Start a separate project for each enhancement, so that each one has its own business case, project board, release map and closure.
Freeze the portal after closure and collect the requests for a single large upgrade project in two years' time.
Pass the requests to Coastline, as its engineers will be the main users of any arrival-tracking feature.
Manage the portal as a product, with a flexible roadmap and short cycles prioritized by value and tenant feedback.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: Agile product management uses a high-level product vision with a flexible roadmap continually adjusted from feedback, and short cycles prioritized by business value and feedback; enhancements after a project are handled through product management iterations rather than a new project each time (book 14.2.2.1).

n.0: A project for every small enhancement adds needless overhead; ongoing improvements fit agile product management (book 14.2.2.1).
n.1: Agile product management keeps adjusting the product in short cycles from feedback rather than batching changes for years (book 14.2.2.1).
n.2: The feature serves tenants, and the scenario gives the digital team the role of improving the portal after the project (book 14.2.2.1).

Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.q: The digital team wants to pilot an AI assistant on the tenant portal that suggests the likely repair type from a tenant's description and photo. The tenants' panel asks for it to be tested with older tenants and with tenants whose first language is not English. Which statement BEST describes how AI should support PRINCE2 Agile on this project?
o: AI can draft suggestions and speed diagnosis, but people keep the decisions and still need to engage tenants and stakeholders.
AI can take over the contact centre's diagnosis once its suggestions are accurate, so phone reporting can be withdrawn.
AI can set the project's priorities from tenant data, so the chief product owner no longer needs to consult tenants.
AI tools sit outside PRINCE2 Agile, so the portal pilot should be managed apart from the project's practices, controls and reporting.
Agile Practitioner: Processes & Wider Co.w: AI can support principles, people and practices, for example by automating information collection or helping define products, but it does not remove human decision-making or the need to communicate with stakeholders (book 15.4.1, 15.4.2).

n.1: AI supports rather than replaces human judgement, and phone reporting must remain for tenants who do not use the internet (book 15.4.2).
n.2: AI can help prioritize backlogs, but people decide and the CPO still engages users; AI does not remove the need to communicate (book 15.4.1, 15.4.2).
n.3: PRINCE2 Agile describes how AI can support its principles, people and practices, so the pilot is managed within the project (book 15.4).
